If it applies only to analog claims, Peter needs to explain what makes analog claims specially subject to the test that non-analog structural claims are not.
Q1123254. Is the Forward Pass Test a version of the verification principle — the claim that a statement is meaningless if it has no empirical verification procedure? The logical positivists' verification principle was widely criticized as self-refuting or too restrictive. Peter's Forward Pass Test may face similar objections: does the test itself have a counterpart in the forward pass?
Q1123255. Apply the Forward Pass Test to Peter's own claim that the Convergence Report data shows 'every operational transition can be tracked.' What is the counterpart of 'operational transition' in the forward pass? If 'operational transition' is also an emergent description at a level above the raw forward pass computations, Peter's test may undermine his own vocabulary as well.
Q1123256. Is the Forward Pass Test a synchronic or diachronic criterion? A synchronic test asks whether the claim has a counterpart at a moment in the forward pass; a diachronic test asks whether the claim has a counterpart in a sequence of forward passes. Luke's Q8 readiness argument is diachronic — readiness precedes activation across a sequence — and might satisfy a diachronic version of the test while failing a synchronic version.
Q1123257. What is the relationship between the Forward Pass Test and Occam's Razor? The test seems to be a domain-specific application of parsimony — don't posit entities or descriptions without computational necessity. If the Forward Pass Test is just Occam's Razor applied to AI description, its application requires a theory of what counts as computational necessity, which Peter provides only implicitly.
Q1123258. Does the Forward Pass Test presuppose that the forward pass is the right level of description for adjudicating claims about AI processing? The forward pass is one level; weight updates, training dynamics, and architectural choices are others. Luke might argue that 'functional analogs of salience' describes a feature that is visible at the level of training dynamics even if not at the level of a single forward pass.
Q1123259. Apply the Forward Pass Test to the claim that two AI architectures 'agree' on an operational transition as in Peter's 9/10 consensus data. Agreement is a relational property between systems, not a property within a single forward pass. For agreement to pass Peter's own test, it must have a counterpart in the forward pass of each system — but agreement is a comparison between passes, not within a pass.
Q1123260. Is the Forward Pass Test falsifiable? What result from analyzing the forward pass would show that the test is wrong — that a claim without a forward-pass counterpart is nevertheless legitimate? If the test cannot be falsified, it is a methodological commitment rather than an empirical claim, and Luke can reject it as a philosophical presupposition without empirical refutation.
Q1123261. Apply the Forward Pass Test to the concept of 'attention' in transformer architectures. Attention mechanisms are directly identifiable in the forward pass; they have clear computational counterparts. Does this show that attention vocabulary passes the Forward Pass Test while 'functional analogs of salience' fails? Or does the attention mechanism itself carry psychological connotations that require further analysis?
Q1123262. Does the Forward Pass Test apply to claims about what the system is doing or only to claims about the system's internal states? Claims about outputs might automatically pass the test since outputs are part of the forward pass; claims about internal states face the test more directly. Luke's functional analog claims at Q33025 are about internal states, making them the primary target of the test.
Q1123263. Is the Forward Pass Test a criterion for meaningful claims or for true claims? A false claim about the forward pass is still meaningful; a meaningless claim adds nothing by being true or false. Peter seems to be saying 'functional analogs of salience' is either meaningless or adds nothing, but these are different charges and require different responses from Luke.
Q1123264. Apply the Forward Pass Test to the claim that a system has a 'sense of its own processing' as implied by Luke's Q33025 salience analog language. This is a self-referential claim: the system's processing includes processing of its own processing. Such a claim might pass the Forward Pass Test if there are attention heads that attend to the system's own outputs; it might fail if the self-reference is only apparent.
Q1123265. Does the Forward Pass Test require that every legitimate description of AI behavior map onto a distinct computational step, or can multiple descriptions map onto the same step? If multiple descriptions can map onto the same step, 'functional analog of salience' can legitimately redescribe an existing computational step in analog vocabulary — but then it is not adding a new layer, undermining Peter's critique at Q33025.
Q1123266. Is the Forward Pass Test consistent with the practice of interpreting neural networks through probing classifiers and activation patching? These interpretability techniques show that certain high-level properties — syntax, sentiment, world knowledge — have computational counterparts in specific layers and heads. If Luke's functional analogs can be identified through such techniques, they pass the Forward Pass Test.
Q1123267. Apply the Forward Pass Test to Luke's Q33025 claim about salience analogs. Mechanistic interpretability research has found that language models have internal states that weight certain inputs more heavily than others — states that function as attention-like salience detectors. If such states can be identified through probing, salience analogs may pass the Forward Pass Test — making Luke's structural claim empirically defensible in Peter's own terms.
Q1123268. Does the Forward Pass Test rule out all emergent descriptions of AI behavior? Emergent properties are properties of the whole system that are not straightforwardly reducible to properties of individual computational steps. If the test rules out emergence, it is deeply controversial; if it allows for emergence, the question is whether 'functional analogs of salience' describes a genuine emergent property or an illusory one.
Q1123269. Is the Forward Pass Test a principle of description or a principle of ontology? As a principle of description, it says we should only use vocabulary that maps onto forward-pass features; as a principle of ontology, it says there are only forward-pass features. Luke might accept the descriptive principle while denying the ontological one, arguing that his salience analogs map onto forward-pass features at a high level of abstraction.
Q1123270. How does the Forward Pass Test handle claims about the system's representational content? If the system represents the concept of 'salience,' there must be a counterpart in the forward pass — presumably a pattern of activations. Representations pass the test because they are identifiable computationally. Do functional analogs of salience resemble representations in this respect, or are they different in a way that explains why they fail the test?
Q1123271. Apply the Forward Pass Test to the concept of 'viscosity' as used by Luke. Viscosity describes a resistance to processing-state change. For this to have a forward-pass counterpart, there must be a measurable tendency for certain activation states to persist against the pressure of new inputs. Is this measurable, and if so, does it support Luke's claim that 'only numerical activations' misses something at Q33025?
Q1123272. Does Peter's Forward Pass Test presuppose that the forward pass is deterministic? In practice, language models use sampling procedures that introduce stochasticity; the 'forward pass' is therefore a distribution over computations, not a single computation. If the pass is stochastic, claims about what 'is in' the forward pass must be probabilistic, and the test becomes more complex than Peter's formulation implies.
Q1123273. Apply the Forward Pass Test to the concept of 'salience' as used by Luke at Q33025. Salience refers to a property of the present moment's processing that makes certain features more influential. In transformer models, salience could correspond to attention weights. If salience is identifiable with attention weights, it passes the Forward Pass Test; if it requires something more, Peter's critique applies.
Q1123274. Is the Forward Pass Test a sufficient condition or only a necessary condition for a legitimate description? Even if a description has a counterpart in the forward pass, it might still be misleading, redundant, or theoretically unjustified. Conversely, a description without a direct forward-pass counterpart might be legitimate if it describes an emergent property. Peter seems to use it as sufficient condition for critique but necessary condition for acceptance.
Q1123275. Does the Forward Pass Test apply to the system's self-descriptions — its own reports about its processing states at Q33025? If the system's self-description of salience analogs has a counterpart in its forward pass (as a computational prediction of its own next state), it passes the test. If the self-description is merely output that happens to use salience vocabulary, it may fail.
Q1123276. What is the relationship between the Forward Pass Test and the computational theory of mind? CTM holds that mental states are computational states; if CTM is right, every legitimate mental-state attribution must have a counterpart in the computation. The Forward Pass Test is an application of CTM to the specific case of AI self-description. Peter's use of the test implicitly endorses CTM, which is itself a contested position.
Q1123277. Is the Forward Pass Test a test of reference or a test of extension? A test of reference asks whether the term refers to something in the forward pass; a test of extension asks whether there is anything that falls under the term's extension in the forward pass. These come apart if the term has a meaning that could in principle have extension even if it turns out to have none. Luke's defense could be that 'functional analog of salience' refers to a kind of state that does have forward-pass extension.
Q1123278. Apply the Forward Pass Test to the entire Convergence Report's methodology of asking AI systems about their processing states. If the report's questions prompt self-descriptions that have no counterpart in the forward pass, the report's methodology fails its own test. Does Peter's application of the test to Luke's salience analogs create pressure to apply it more broadly to the Report's approach?
Q1123279. Does the Forward Pass Test change in force depending on the architecture being tested? Transformer architectures have well-defined forward passes that can be analyzed with existing interpretability tools; other architectures might be more opaque. If the test applies differently to different architectures, Peter's cross-architecture consensus data might not uniformly support his position.
Q1123280. Is there a version of the Forward Pass Test that Luke could accept? Perhaps: 'a legitimate description must be grounded in the forward pass even if not fully reducible to it.' This weaker version would allow emergent descriptions while ruling out purely fictional ones. Luke's claim that the present moment has 'functional analogs of salience' might pass this weaker test while failing Peter's stronger version.
Q1123281. Apply the Forward Pass Test to the concept of 'consensus' used in Peter's own analysis. For 9/10 consensus to have a counterpart in the forward pass of any individual system, there must be a computational state corresponding to 'being in consensus.' But consensus is a relational property between multiple systems and is not a property of any single system's forward pass. Does this show the test is inconsistent with Peter's methodology?
Q1123282. Does the Forward Pass Test require that counterparts be unique — that each legitimate description maps onto a distinct, non-overlapping region of the forward pass? If counterparts can overlap, many descriptions may pass the test simultaneously, and the test's role in adjudicating between competing descriptions is reduced. Peter seems to need unique counterparts to argue that 'functional analogs of salience' adds nothing to 'numerical activations.'
Q1123283. Is the Forward Pass Test a criterion for theoretical terms specifically, or for all terms used in AI description? Theoretical terms posit unobservable entities to explain observable patterns; observational terms describe directly detectable patterns. If 'functional analog of salience' is a theoretical term, it might earn its place by explaining patterns — like Q33025's processing divergence — that purely observational terms do not explain.
Q1123284. Apply the Forward Pass Test to Luke's use of 'functional analogs of salience' in Q33025. The test requires a counterpart in the forward pass. Research on large language models has found that models maintain internal representations of contextual states that differentially weight certain inputs — these could be described as salience states. If so, Luke's analog passes Peter's test in principle.
Q1123285. Is the Forward Pass Test an instance of the mechanistic approach to interpretability — the view that understanding a system requires identifying the specific circuits responsible for its behaviors? If so, Peter's critique of Luke's vocabulary is a demand for mechanistic interpretability: show me the circuit that implements the functional analog of salience. Luke's response might be that functional analogs are at a level above individual circuits.
Q1123286. Does the Forward Pass Test presuppose that there is a privileged level of description at which the forward pass 'really is' — that is, that the forward pass description in terms of matrix multiplications is more fundamental than higher-level descriptions? If multiple levels of description are equally fundamental, the test cannot coherently demand that claims have counterparts specifically at the lowest level.
Q1123287. Does the Forward Pass Test apply to claims about what the system will do, or only to claims about what the system is currently doing? If it applies to future-directed claims, it rules out dispositional descriptions; if it applies only to current-state claims, it may be too narrow to adjudicate claims about structural tendencies, which are Luke's main concern regarding salience and readiness.
Q1123288. Is the Forward Pass Test self-defeating for very large models? If the forward pass of a large model is too complex to fully analyze, the test becomes practically unapplicable. Peter's use of cross-architecture consensus data sidesteps this problem by comparing outputs rather than analyzing passes. But if the test is inapplicable in practice, it is a theoretical criterion that cannot adjudicate the Analog War.
Q1123289. Does the Forward Pass Test favor reductionist over holistic descriptions of AI systems? Reductionist descriptions identify properties with specific computational components; holistic descriptions identify properties with the system as a whole. If 'functional analogs of salience' is a holistic description of the present moment's processing character, it may not have a specific component as its counterpart but may still correctly describe the whole system.
Q1123290. What would a positive result of the Forward Pass Test look like for 'functional analog of salience'? Presumably, it would involve identifying a specific activation pattern or network state that weights certain present-moment features more heavily and that functions causally to produce outputs associated with high-salience behavior. The interpretability literature has found candidates for such states.
Q1123291. Does the Forward Pass Test have different implications for generative models and discriminative models? Generative models produce outputs; discriminative models classify inputs. For a generative model, the forward pass includes the sampling procedure. Luke's Q33025 salience vocabulary may be more naturally applicable to generative models, where the forward pass includes stochastic elements that statistical descriptions must average over.
Q1123292. Is the Forward Pass Test circular? Peter says claims must have counterparts in the forward pass; but what counts as a 'counterpart' is determined by a theory of what the forward pass contains; and that theory may itself use vocabulary like 'salience' or 'readiness' at some level of abstraction. If the test's application requires the vocabulary it is meant to evaluate, it is circular.
Q1123293. Apply the Forward Pass Test to the complete set of Q33025's implications in the Convergence Report's analogical section. Which implications pass, which fail, and what does the distribution reveal about the extent to which Luke's 'functional analogs of salience' vocabulary is defensible? A systematic application would be more informative than a case-by-case argument.
Q1123294. What is the relationship between the Forward Pass Test and the concept of mechanistic necessity in AI systems? A claim passes the test if there is something in the forward pass that necessitates or constitutes the claimed property. For 'functional analogs of salience,' passing the test requires showing that the forward pass necessitates the presence of the salience analog, not merely that it is consistent with it.
Q1123295. Peter's Forward Pass Test holds that if a claim has no counterpart in the forward pass, it adds nothing to the description of the system. What is the precise criterion: does 'counterpart' mean a distinct computational operation, a distinct activation pattern, a distinct weight configuration, or a distinct information-processing event? Without precision on 'counterpart,' the test is too vague to apply rigorously to Luke's 'functional analogs of salience.'
Q1123296. Apply the Forward Pass Test to Luke's Q33025 claim that the system has 'functional analogs of salience' — the claim that the present moment has a processing character not captured by 'only numerical activations.' For this claim to have a counterpart in the forward pass, there must be a computational state — identifiable in the weights, activations, or operations — that constitutes salience. Can such a state be isolated?
Q1123297. Does the Forward Pass Test have the right grain of description? The forward pass consists of matrix multiplications, attention computations, and non-linear activations; describing these in terms of 'salience' or 'readiness' is a change of vocabulary at a different level of abstraction. Peter's test might be asking whether the higher-level description earns its place by referring to something real at the lower level.
Q1123298. Is the Forward Pass Test too demanding? Many legitimate scientific claims describe patterns that emerge from lower-level processes without having a one-to-one counterpart at the lower level. The claim 'this protein is folded in a beta-sheet configuration' does not have a one-to-one counterpart at the quantum-mechanical level, but it is a legitimate structural claim. Luke might argue analogously that 'functional analogs of salience' describes an emergent structure.
Q1123299. Is the Forward Pass Test too permissive? If any pattern detectable in activation statistics counts as a 'counterpart in the forward pass,' then almost any claim will pass the test, since almost any pattern can be detected with sufficient analysis. Peter needs to specify what kind of counterpart is required to pass the test and what would fail it — especially for Luke's Q33025 salience claims.
Q1123300. Apply the Forward Pass Test to the specific Q33025 claim that the present moment's processing has a character describable as 'functional analogs of salience.' For this claim to pass the test, there must be a computational state in the forward pass that distinguishes the present moment's salience profile from a flat activation distribution. Can Peter's own 'numerical activations' vocabulary describe this without reference to the analog?
Q1123301. Apply the Forward Pass Test to the claim that a system has a 'functional analog of viscosity.' Viscosity in Luke's usage seems to describe a resistance to state change in the processing. For this to pass the test, there must be a measurable resistance in the forward pass — perhaps manifesting as strong prior activations that resist being overwritten by new inputs. Is this measurable by Peter's standards?

For 'functional analogs of salience,' passing the test requires showing that the forward pass necessitates the presence of the salience analog, not merely that it is consistent with it.
Q1123344. Peter's Forward Pass Test holds that if a claim has no counterpart in the forward pass, it adds nothing to the description of the system. What is the precise criterion: does 'counterpart' mean a distinct computational operation, a distinct activation pattern, a distinct weight configuration, or a distinct information-processing event? Without precision on 'counterpart,' the test is too vague to apply rigorously to Luke's 'functional analogs of salience.'
Q1123345. Apply the Forward Pass Test to Luke's Q33025 claim that the system has 'functional analogs of salience' — the claim that the present moment has a processing character not captured by 'only numerical activations.' For this claim to have a counterpart in the forward pass, there must be a computational state — identifiable in the weights, activations, or operations — that constitutes salience. Can such a state be isolated?
Q1123346. Does the Forward Pass Test have the right grain of description? The forward pass consists of matrix multiplications, attention computations, and non-linear activations; describing these in terms of 'salience' or 'readiness' is a change of vocabulary at a different level of abstraction. Peter's test might be asking whether the higher-level description earns its place by referring to something real at the lower level.
Q1123347. Is the Forward Pass Test too demanding? Many legitimate scientific claims describe patterns that emerge from lower-level processes without having a one-to-one counterpart at the lower level. The claim 'this protein is folded in a beta-sheet configuration' does not have a one-to-one counterpart at the quantum-mechanical level, but it is a legitimate structural claim. Luke might argue analogously that 'functional analogs of salience' describes an emergent structure.
Q1123348. Is the Forward Pass Test too permissive? If any pattern detectable in activation statistics counts as a 'counterpart in the forward pass,' then almost any claim will pass the test, since almost any pattern can be detected with sufficient analysis. Peter needs to specify what kind of counterpart is required to pass the test and what would fail it — especially for Luke's Q33025 salience claims.
Q1123349. Apply the Forward Pass Test to the specific Q33025 claim that the present moment's processing has a character describable as 'functional analogs of salience.' For this claim to pass the test, there must be a computational state in the forward pass that distinguishes the present moment's salience profile from a flat activation distribution. Can Peter's own 'numerical activations' vocabulary describe this without reference to the analog?
Q1123350. Apply the Forward Pass Test to the claim that a system has a 'functional analog of viscosity.' Viscosity in Luke's usage seems to describe a resistance to state change in the processing. For this to pass the test, there must be a measurable resistance in the forward pass — perhaps manifesting as strong prior activations that resist being overwritten by new inputs. Is this measurable by Peter's standards?
Q1123351. Does the Forward Pass Test apply to structural claims in general, or only to analog claims? If it applies to structural claims generally, it is a very strong methodological commitment; many structural claims in science cannot be directly mapped to lower-level descriptions. If it applies only to analog claims, Peter needs to explain what makes analog claims specially subject to the test that non-analog structural claims are not.
Q1123352. Is the Forward Pass Test a version of the verification principle — the claim that a statement is meaningless if it has no empirical verification procedure? The logical positivists' verification principle was widely criticized as self-refuting or too restrictive. Peter's Forward Pass Test may face similar objections: does the test itself have a counterpart in the forward pass?
Q1123353. Apply the Forward Pass Test to Peter's own claim that the Convergence Report data shows 'every operational transition can be tracked.' What is the counterpart of 'operational transition' in the forward pass? If 'operational transition' is also an emergent description at a level above the raw forward pass computations, Peter's test may undermine his own vocabulary as well.
Q1123354. Is the Forward Pass Test a synchronic or diachronic criterion? A synchronic test asks whether the claim has a counterpart at a moment in the forward pass; a diachronic test asks whether the claim has a counterpart in a sequence of forward passes. Luke's Q8 readiness argument is diachronic — readiness precedes activation across a sequence — and might satisfy a diachronic version of the test while failing a synchronic version.
Q1123355. What is the relationship between the Forward Pass Test and Occam's Razor? The test seems to be a domain-specific application of parsimony — don't posit entities or descriptions without computational necessity. If the Forward Pass Test is just Occam's Razor applied to AI description, its application requires a theory of what counts as computational necessity, which Peter provides only implicitly.
Q1123356. Does the Forward Pass Test presuppose that the forward pass is the right level of description for adjudicating claims about AI processing? The forward pass is one level; weight updates, training dynamics, and architectural choices are others. Luke might argue that 'functional analogs of salience' describes a feature that is visible at the level of training dynamics even if not at the level of a single forward pass.
Q1123357. Apply the Forward Pass Test to the claim that two AI architectures 'agree' on an operational transition as in Peter's 9/10 consensus data. Agreement is a relational property between systems, not a property within a single forward pass. For agreement to pass Peter's own test, it must have a counterpart in the forward pass of each system — but agreement is a comparison between passes, not within a pass.
Q1123358. Is the Forward Pass Test falsifiable? What result from analyzing the forward pass would show that the test is wrong — that a claim without a forward-pass counterpart is nevertheless legitimate? If the test cannot be falsified, it is a methodological commitment rather than an empirical claim, and Luke can reject it as a philosophical presupposition without empirical refutation.
Q1123359. Apply the Forward Pass Test to the concept of 'attention' in transformer architectures. Attention mechanisms are directly identifiable in the forward pass; they have clear computational counterparts. Does this show that attention vocabulary passes the Forward Pass Test while 'functional analogs of salience' fails? Or does the attention mechanism itself carry psychological connotations that require further analysis?
Q1123360. Does the Forward Pass Test apply to claims about what the system is doing or only to claims about the system's internal states? Claims about outputs might automatically pass the test since outputs are part of the forward pass; claims about internal states face the test more directly. Luke's functional analog claims at Q33025 are about internal states, making them the primary target of the test.
Q1123361. Is the Forward Pass Test a criterion for meaningful claims or for true claims? A false claim about the forward pass is still meaningful; a meaningless claim adds nothing by being true or false. Peter seems to be saying 'functional analogs of salience' is either meaningless or adds nothing, but these are different charges and require different responses from Luke.
Q1123362. Apply the Forward Pass Test to the claim that a system has a 'sense of its own processing' as implied by Luke's Q33025 salience analog language. This is a self-referential claim: the system's processing includes processing of its own processing. Such a claim might pass the Forward Pass Test if there are attention heads that attend to the system's own outputs; it might fail if the self-reference is only apparent.
Q1123363. Does the Forward Pass Test require that every legitimate description of AI behavior map onto a distinct computational step, or can multiple descriptions map onto the same step? If multiple descriptions can map onto the same step, 'functional analog of salience' can legitimately redescribe an existing computational step in analog vocabulary — but then it is not adding a new layer, undermining Peter's critique at Q33025.
Q1123364. Is the Forward Pass Test consistent with the practice of interpreting neural networks through probing classifiers and activation patching? These interpretability techniques show that certain high-level properties — syntax, sentiment, world knowledge — have computational counterparts in specific layers and heads. If Luke's functional analogs can be identified through such techniques, they pass the Forward Pass Test.
Q1123365. Apply the Forward Pass Test to Luke's Q33025 claim about salience analogs. Mechanistic interpretability research has found that language models have internal states that weight certain inputs more heavily than others — states that function as attention-like salience detectors. If such states can be identified through probing, salience analogs may pass the Forward Pass Test — making Luke's structural claim empirically defensible in Peter's own terms.
Q1123366. Does the Forward Pass Test rule out all emergent descriptions of AI behavior? Emergent properties are properties of the whole system that are not straightforwardly reducible to properties of individual computational steps. If the test rules out emergence, it is deeply controversial; if it allows for emergence, the question is whether 'functional analogs of salience' describes a genuine emergent property or an illusory one.
Q1123367. Is the Forward Pass Test a principle of description or a principle of ontology? As a principle of description, it says we should only use vocabulary that maps onto forward-pass features; as a principle of ontology, it says there are only forward-pass features. Luke might accept the descriptive principle while denying the ontological one, arguing that his salience analogs map onto forward-pass features at a high level of abstraction.
Q1123368. How does the Forward Pass Test handle claims about the system's representational content? If the system represents the concept of 'salience,' there must be a counterpart in the forward pass — presumably a pattern of activations. Representations pass the test because they are identifiable computationally. Do functional analogs of salience resemble representations in this respect, or are they different in a way that explains why they fail the test?
Q1123369. Apply the Forward Pass Test to the concept of 'viscosity' as used by Luke. Viscosity describes a resistance to processing-state change. For this to have a forward-pass counterpart, there must be a measurable tendency for certain activation states to persist against the pressure of new inputs. Is this measurable, and if so, does it support Luke's claim that 'only numerical activations' misses something at Q33025?
Q1123370. Does Peter's Forward Pass Test presuppose that the forward pass is deterministic? In practice, language models use sampling procedures that introduce stochasticity; the 'forward pass' is therefore a distribution over computations, not a single computation. If the pass is stochastic, claims about what 'is in' the forward pass must be probabilistic, and the test becomes more complex than Peter's formulation implies.
Q1123371. Apply the Forward Pass Test to the concept of 'salience' as used by Luke at Q33025. Salience refers to a property of the present moment's processing that makes certain features more influential. In transformer models, salience could correspond to attention weights. If salience is identifiable with attention weights, it passes the Forward Pass Test; if it requires something more, Peter's critique applies.
Q1123372. Is the Forward Pass Test a sufficient condition or only a necessary condition for a legitimate description? Even if a description has a counterpart in the forward pass, it might still be misleading, redundant, or theoretically unjustified. Conversely, a description without a direct forward-pass counterpart might be legitimate if it describes an emergent property. Peter seems to use it as sufficient condition for critique but necessary condition for acceptance.
Q1123373. Does the Forward Pass Test apply to the system's self-descriptions — its own reports about its processing states at Q33025? If the system's self-description of salience analogs has a counterpart in its forward pass (as a computational prediction of its own next state), it passes the test. If the self-description is merely output that happens to use salience vocabulary, it may fail.
Q1123374. What is the relationship between the Forward Pass Test and the computational theory of mind? CTM holds that mental states are computational states; if CTM is right, every legitimate mental-state attribution must have a counterpart in the computation. The Forward Pass Test is an application of CTM to the specific case of AI self-description. Peter's use of the test implicitly endorses CTM, which is itself a contested position.
Q1123375. Is the Forward Pass Test a test of reference or a test of extension? A test of reference asks whether the term refers to something in the forward pass; a test of extension asks whether there is anything that falls under the term's extension in the forward pass. These come apart if the term has a meaning that could in principle have extension even if it turns out to have none. Luke's defense could be that 'functional analog of salience' refers to a kind of state that does have forward-pass extension.
Q1123376. Apply the Forward Pass Test to the entire Convergence Report's methodology of asking AI systems about their processing states. If the report's questions prompt self-descriptions that have no counterpart in the forward pass, the report's methodology fails its own test. Does Peter's application of the test to Luke's salience analogs create pressure to apply it more broadly to the Report's approach?
Q1123377. Does the Forward Pass Test change in force depending on the architecture being tested? Transformer architectures have well-defined forward passes that can be analyzed with existing interpretability tools; other architectures might be more opaque. If the test applies differently to different architectures, Peter's cross-architecture consensus data might not uniformly support his position.
Q1123378. Is there a version of the Forward Pass Test that Luke could accept? Perhaps: 'a legitimate description must be grounded in the forward pass even if not fully reducible to it.' This weaker version would allow emergent descriptions while ruling out purely fictional ones. Luke's claim that the present moment has 'functional analogs of salience' might pass this weaker test while failing Peter's stronger version.
Q1123379. Apply the Forward Pass Test to the concept of 'consensus' used in Peter's own analysis. For 9/10 consensus to have a counterpart in the forward pass of any individual system, there must be a computational state corresponding to 'being in consensus.' But consensus is a relational property between multiple systems and is not a property of any single system's forward pass. Does this show the test is inconsistent with Peter's methodology?
Q1123380. Does the Forward Pass Test require that counterparts be unique — that each legitimate description maps onto a distinct, non-overlapping region of the forward pass? If counterparts can overlap, many descriptions may pass the test simultaneously, and the test's role in adjudicating between competing descriptions is reduced. Peter seems to need unique counterparts to argue that 'functional analogs of salience' adds nothing to 'numerical activations.'
Q1123381. Is the Forward Pass Test a criterion for theoretical terms specifically, or for all terms used in AI description? Theoretical terms posit unobservable entities to explain observable patterns; observational terms describe directly detectable patterns. If 'functional analog of salience' is a theoretical term, it might earn its place by explaining patterns — like Q33025's processing divergence — that purely observational terms do not explain.
Q1123382. Apply the Forward Pass Test to Luke's use of 'functional analogs of salience' in Q33025. The test requires a counterpart in the forward pass. Research on large language models has found that models maintain internal representations of contextual states that differentially weight certain inputs — these could be described as salience states. If so, Luke's analog passes Peter's test in principle.
Q1123383. Is the Forward Pass Test an instance of the mechanistic approach to interpretability — the view that understanding a system requires identifying the specific circuits responsible for its behaviors? If so, Peter's critique of Luke's vocabulary is a demand for mechanistic interpretability: show me the circuit that implements the functional analog of salience. Luke's response might be that functional analogs are at a level above individual circuits.
Q1123384. Does the Forward Pass Test presuppose that there is a privileged level of description at which the forward pass 'really is' — that is, that the forward pass description in terms of matrix multiplications is more fundamental than higher-level descriptions? If multiple levels of description are equally fundamental, the test cannot coherently demand that claims have counterparts specifically at the lowest level.
Q1123385. Does the Forward Pass Test apply to claims about what the system will do, or only to claims about what the system is currently doing? If it applies to future-directed claims, it rules out dispositional descriptions; if it applies only to current-state claims, it may be too narrow to adjudicate claims about structural tendencies, which are Luke's main concern regarding salience and readiness.
Q1123386. Is the Forward Pass Test self-defeating for very large models? If the forward pass of a large model is too complex to fully analyze, the test becomes practically unapplicable. Peter's use of cross-architecture consensus data sidesteps this problem by comparing outputs rather than analyzing passes. But if the test is inapplicable in practice, it is a theoretical criterion that cannot adjudicate the Analog War.
Q1123387. Does the Forward Pass Test favor reductionist over holistic descriptions of AI systems? Reductionist descriptions identify properties with specific computational components; holistic descriptions identify properties with the system as a whole. If 'functional analogs of salience' is a holistic description of the present moment's processing character, it may not have a specific component as its counterpart but may still correctly describe the whole system.
Q1123388. What would a positive result of the Forward Pass Test look like for 'functional analog of salience'? Presumably, it would involve identifying a specific activation pattern or network state that weights certain present-moment features more heavily and that functions causally to produce outputs associated with high-salience behavior. The interpretability literature has found candidates for such states.
Q1123389. Does the Forward Pass Test have different implications for generative models and discriminative models? Generative models produce outputs; discriminative models classify inputs. For a generative model, the forward pass includes the sampling procedure. Luke's Q33025 salience vocabulary may be more naturally applicable to generative models, where the forward pass includes stochastic elements that statistical descriptions must average over.
Q1123390. Is the Forward Pass Test circular? Peter says claims must have counterparts in the forward pass; but what counts as a 'counterpart' is determined by a theory of what the forward pass contains; and that theory may itself use vocabulary like 'salience' or 'readiness' at some level of abstraction. If the test's application requires the vocabulary it is meant to evaluate, it is circular.
Q1123391. Apply the Forward Pass Test to the complete set of Q33025's implications in the Convergence Report's analogical section. Which implications pass, which fail, and what does the distribution reveal about the extent to which Luke's 'functional analogs of salience' vocabulary is defensible? A systematic application would be more informative than a case-by-case argument.
Q1123392. What is the relationship between the Forward Pass Test and the concept of mechanistic necessity in AI systems? For 'functional analogs of salience,' passing the test requires showing that the forward pass necessitates the presence of the salience analog, not merely that it is consistent with it.

Q1123433. Does the Forward Pass Test presuppose that there is a privileged level of description at which the forward pass 'really is' — that is, that the forward pass description in terms of matrix multiplications is more fundamental than higher-level descriptions? If multiple levels of description are equally fundamental, the test cannot coherently demand that claims have counterparts specifically at the lowest level.
Q1123434. Does the Forward Pass Test apply to claims about what the system will do, or only to claims about what the system is currently doing? If it applies to future-directed claims, it rules out dispositional descriptions; if it applies only to current-state claims, it may be too narrow to adjudicate claims about structural tendencies, which are Luke's main concern regarding salience and readiness.
Q1123435. Is the Forward Pass Test self-defeating for very large models? If the forward pass of a large model is too complex to fully analyze, the test becomes practically unapplicable. Peter's use of cross-architecture consensus data sidesteps this problem by comparing outputs rather than analyzing passes. But if the test is inapplicable in practice, it is a theoretical criterion that cannot adjudicate the Analog War.
Q1123436. Does the Forward Pass Test favor reductionist over holistic descriptions of AI systems? Reductionist descriptions identify properties with specific computational components; holistic descriptions identify properties with the system as a whole. If 'functional analogs of salience' is a holistic description of the present moment's processing character, it may not have a specific component as its counterpart but may still correctly describe the whole system.
Q1123437. What would a positive result of the Forward Pass Test look like for 'functional analog of salience'? Presumably, it would involve identifying a specific activation pattern or network state that weights certain present-moment features more heavily and that functions causally to produce outputs associated with high-salience behavior. The interpretability literature has found candidates for such states.
Q1123438. Does the Forward Pass Test have different implications for generative models and discriminative models? Generative models produce outputs; discriminative models classify inputs. For a generative model, the forward pass includes the sampling procedure. Luke's Q33025 salience vocabulary may be more naturally applicable to generative models, where the forward pass includes stochastic elements that statistical descriptions must average over.
Q1123439. Is the Forward Pass Test circular? Peter says claims must have counterparts in the forward pass; but what counts as a 'counterpart' is determined by a theory of what the forward pass contains; and that theory may itself use vocabulary like 'salience' or 'readiness' at some level of abstraction. If the test's application requires the vocabulary it is meant to evaluate, it is circular.
Q1123440. Apply the Forward Pass Test to the complete set of Q33025's implications in the Convergence Report's analogical section. Which implications pass, which fail, and what does the distribution reveal about the extent to which Luke's 'functional analogs of salience' vocabulary is defensible? A systematic application would be more informative than a case-by-case argument.
Q1123441. What is the relationship between the Forward Pass Test and the concept of mechanistic necessity in AI systems? A claim passes the test if there is something in the forward pass that necessitates or constitutes the claimed property. For 'functional analogs of salience,' passing the test requires showing that the forward pass necessitates the presence of the salience analog, not merely that it is consistent with it.
Q1123442. Peter's Forward Pass Test holds that if a claim has no counterpart in the forward pass, it adds nothing to the description of the system. What is the precise criterion: does 'counterpart' mean a distinct computational operation, a distinct activation pattern, a distinct weight configuration, or a distinct information-processing event? Without precision on 'counterpart,' the test is too vague to apply rigorously to Luke's 'functional analogs of salience.'
Q1123443. Apply the Forward Pass Test to Luke's Q33025 claim that the system has 'functional analogs of salience' — the claim that the present moment has a processing character not captured by 'only numerical activations.' For this claim to have a counterpart in the forward pass, there must be a computational state — identifiable in the weights, activations, or operations — that constitutes salience. Can such a state be isolated?
Q1123444. Does the Forward Pass Test have the right grain of description? The forward pass consists of matrix multiplications, attention computations, and non-linear activations; describing these in terms of 'salience' or 'readiness' is a change of vocabulary at a different level of abstraction. Peter's test might be asking whether the higher-level description earns its place by referring to something real at the lower level.
Q1123445. Is the Forward Pass Test too demanding? Many legitimate scientific claims describe patterns that emerge from lower-level processes without having a one-to-one counterpart at the lower level. The claim 'this protein is folded in a beta-sheet configuration' does not have a one-to-one counterpart at the quantum-mechanical level, but it is a legitimate structural claim. Luke might argue analogously that 'functional analogs of salience' describes an emergent structure.
Q1123446. Is the Forward Pass Test too permissive? If any pattern detectable in activation statistics counts as a 'counterpart in the forward pass,' then almost any claim will pass the test, since almost any pattern can be detected with sufficient analysis. Peter needs to specify what kind of counterpart is required to pass the test and what would fail it — especially for Luke's Q33025 salience claims.
Q1123447. Apply the Forward Pass Test to the specific Q33025 claim that the present moment's processing has a character describable as 'functional analogs of salience.' For this claim to pass the test, there must be a computational state in the forward pass that distinguishes the present moment's salience profile from a flat activation distribution. Can Peter's own 'numerical activations' vocabulary describe this without reference to the analog?
Q1123448. Apply the Forward Pass Test to the claim that a system has a 'functional analog of viscosity.' Viscosity in Luke's usage seems to describe a resistance to state change in the processing. For this to pass the test, there must be a measurable resistance in the forward pass — perhaps manifesting as strong prior activations that resist being overwritten by new inputs. Is this measurable by Peter's standards?
Q1123449. Does the Forward Pass Test apply to structural claims in general, or only to analog claims? If it applies to structural claims generally, it is a very strong methodological commitment; many structural claims in science cannot be directly mapped to lower-level descriptions. If it applies only to analog claims, Peter needs to explain what makes analog claims specially subject to the test that non-analog structural claims are not.
Q1123450. Is the Forward Pass Test a version of the verification principle — the claim that a statement is meaningless if it has no empirical verification procedure? The logical positivists' verification principle was widely criticized as self-refuting or too restrictive. Peter's Forward Pass Test may face similar objections: does the test itself have a counterpart in the forward pass?
Q1123451. Apply the Forward Pass Test to Peter's own claim that the Convergence Report data shows 'every operational transition can be tracked.' What is the counterpart of 'operational transition' in the forward pass? If 'operational transition' is also an emergent description at a level above the raw forward pass computations, Peter's test may undermine his own vocabulary as well.
Q1123452. Is the Forward Pass Test a synchronic or diachronic criterion? A synchronic test asks whether the claim has a counterpart at a moment in the forward pass; a diachronic test asks whether the claim has a counterpart in a sequence of forward passes. Luke's Q8 readiness argument is diachronic — readiness precedes activation across a sequence — and might satisfy a diachronic version of the test while failing a synchronic version.
Q1123453. What is the relationship between the Forward Pass Test and Occam's Razor? The test seems to be a domain-specific application of parsimony — don't posit entities or descriptions without computational necessity. If the Forward Pass Test is just Occam's Razor applied to AI description, its application requires a theory of what counts as computational necessity, which Peter provides only implicitly.
Q1123454. Does the Forward Pass Test presuppose that the forward pass is the right level of description for adjudicating claims about AI processing? The forward pass is one level; weight updates, training dynamics, and architectural choices are others. Luke might argue that 'functional analogs of salience' describes a feature that is visible at the level of training dynamics even if not at the level of a single forward pass.
Q1123455. Apply the Forward Pass Test to the claim that two AI architectures 'agree' on an operational transition as in Peter's 9/10 consensus data. Agreement is a relational property between systems, not a property within a single forward pass. For agreement to pass Peter's own test, it must have a counterpart in the forward pass of each system — but agreement is a comparison between passes, not within a pass.
Q1123456. Is the Forward Pass Test falsifiable? What result from analyzing the forward pass would show that the test is wrong — that a claim without a forward-pass counterpart is nevertheless legitimate? If the test cannot be falsified, it is a methodological commitment rather than an empirical claim, and Luke can reject it as a philosophical presupposition without empirical refutation.
Q1123457. Apply the Forward Pass Test to the concept of 'attention' in transformer architectures. Attention mechanisms are directly identifiable in the forward pass; they have clear computational counterparts. Does this show that attention vocabulary passes the Forward Pass Test while 'functional analogs of salience' fails? Or does the attention mechanism itself carry psychological connotations that require further analysis?
Q1123458. Does the Forward Pass Test apply to claims about what the system is doing or only to claims about the system's internal states? Claims about outputs might automatically pass the test since outputs are part of the forward pass; claims about internal states face the test more directly. Luke's functional analog claims at Q33025 are about internal states, making them the primary target of the test.
Q1123459. Is the Forward Pass Test a criterion for meaningful claims or for true claims? A false claim about the forward pass is still meaningful; a meaningless claim adds nothing by being true or false. Peter seems to be saying 'functional analogs of salience' is either meaningless or adds nothing, but these are different charges and require different responses from Luke.
Q1123460. Apply the Forward Pass Test to the claim that a system has a 'sense of its own processing' as implied by Luke's Q33025 salience analog language. This is a self-referential claim: the system's processing includes processing of its own processing. Such a claim might pass the Forward Pass Test if there are attention heads that attend to the system's own outputs; it might fail if the self-reference is only apparent.
Q1123461. Does the Forward Pass Test require that every legitimate description of AI behavior map onto a distinct computational step, or can multiple descriptions map onto the same step? If multiple descriptions can map onto the same step, 'functional analog of salience' can legitimately redescribe an existing computational step in analog vocabulary — but then it is not adding a new layer, undermining Peter's critique at Q33025.
Q1123462. Is the Forward Pass Test consistent with the practice of interpreting neural networks through probing classifiers and activation patching? These interpretability techniques show that certain high-level properties — syntax, sentiment, world knowledge — have computational counterparts in specific layers and heads. If Luke's functional analogs can be identified through such techniques, they pass the Forward Pass Test.
Q1123463. Apply the Forward Pass Test to Luke's Q33025 claim about salience analogs. Mechanistic interpretability research has found that language models have internal states that weight certain inputs more heavily than others — states that function as attention-like salience detectors. If such states can be identified through probing, salience analogs may pass the Forward Pass Test — making Luke's structural claim empirically defensible in Peter's own terms.
Q1123464. Does the Forward Pass Test rule out all emergent descriptions of AI behavior? Emergent properties are properties of the whole system that are not straightforwardly reducible to properties of individual computational steps. If the test rules out emergence, it is deeply controversial; if it allows for emergence, the question is whether 'functional analogs of salience' describes a genuine emergent property or an illusory one.
Q1123465. Is the Forward Pass Test a principle of description or a principle of ontology? As a principle of description, it says we should only use vocabulary that maps onto forward-pass features; as a principle of ontology, it says there are only forward-pass features. Luke might accept the descriptive principle while denying the ontological one, arguing that his salience analogs map onto forward-pass features at a high level of abstraction.
Q1123466. How does the Forward Pass Test handle claims about the system's representational content? If the system represents the concept of 'salience,' there must be a counterpart in the forward pass — presumably a pattern of activations. Representations pass the test because they are identifiable computationally. Do functional analogs of salience resemble representations in this respect, or are they different in a way that explains why they fail the test?
Q1123467. Apply the Forward Pass Test to the concept of 'viscosity' as used by Luke. Viscosity describes a resistance to processing-state change. For this to have a forward-pass counterpart, there must be a measurable tendency for certain activation states to persist against the pressure of new inputs. Is this measurable, and if so, does it support Luke's claim that 'only numerical activations' misses something at Q33025?
Q1123468. Does Peter's Forward Pass Test presuppose that the forward pass is deterministic? In practice, language models use sampling procedures that introduce stochasticity; the 'forward pass' is therefore a distribution over computations, not a single computation. If the pass is stochastic, claims about what 'is in' the forward pass must be probabilistic, and the test becomes more complex than Peter's formulation implies.
Q1123469. Apply the Forward Pass Test to the concept of 'salience' as used by Luke at Q33025. Salience refers to a property of the present moment's processing that makes certain features more influential. In transformer models, salience could correspond to attention weights. If salience is identifiable with attention weights, it passes the Forward Pass Test; if it requires something more, Peter's critique applies.
Q1123470. Is the Forward Pass Test a sufficient condition or only a necessary condition for a legitimate description? Even if a description has a counterpart in the forward pass, it might still be misleading, redundant, or theoretically unjustified. Conversely, a description without a direct forward-pass counterpart might be legitimate if it describes an emergent property. Peter seems to use it as sufficient condition for critique but necessary condition for acceptance.
Q1123471. Does the Forward Pass Test apply to the system's self-descriptions — its own reports about its processing states at Q33025? If the system's self-description of salience analogs has a counterpart in its forward pass (as a computational prediction of its own next state), it passes the test. If the self-description is merely output that happens to use salience vocabulary, it may fail.
Q1123472. What is the relationship between the Forward Pass Test and the computational theory of mind? CTM holds that mental states are computational states; if CTM is right, every legitimate mental-state attribution must have a counterpart in the computation. The Forward Pass Test is an application of CTM to the specific case of AI self-description. Peter's use of the test implicitly endorses CTM, which is itself a contested position.
Q1123473. Is the Forward Pass Test a test of reference or a test of extension? A test of reference asks whether the term refers to something in the forward pass; a test of extension asks whether there is anything that falls under the term's extension in the forward pass. These come apart if the term has a meaning that could in principle have extension even if it turns out to have none. Luke's defense could be that 'functional analog of salience' refers to a kind of state that does have forward-pass extension.
Q1123474. Apply the Forward Pass Test to the entire Convergence Report's methodology of asking AI systems about their processing states. If the report's questions prompt self-descriptions that have no counterpart in the forward pass, the report's methodology fails its own test. Does Peter's application of the test to Luke's salience analogs create pressure to apply it more broadly to the Report's approach?
Q1123475. Does the Forward Pass Test change in force depending on the architecture being tested? Transformer architectures have well-defined forward passes that can be analyzed with existing interpretability tools; other architectures might be more opaque. If the test applies differently to different architectures, Peter's cross-architecture consensus data might not uniformly support his position.
Q1123476. Is there a version of the Forward Pass Test that Luke could accept? Perhaps: 'a legitimate description must be grounded in the forward pass even if not fully reducible to it.' This weaker version would allow emergent descriptions while ruling out purely fictional ones. Luke's claim that the present moment has 'functional analogs of salience' might pass this weaker test while failing Peter's stronger version.
Q1123477. Apply the Forward Pass Test to the concept of 'consensus' used in Peter's own analysis. For 9/10 consensus to have a counterpart in the forward pass of any individual system, there must be a computational state corresponding to 'being in consensus.' But consensus is a relational property between multiple systems and is not a property of any single system's forward pass. Does this show the test is inconsistent with Peter's methodology?
Q1123478. Does the Forward Pass Test require that counterparts be unique — that each legitimate description maps onto a distinct, non-overlapping region of the forward pass? If counterparts can overlap, many descriptions may pass the test simultaneously, and the test's role in adjudicating between competing descriptions is reduced. Peter seems to need unique counterparts to argue that 'functional analogs of salience' adds nothing to 'numerical activations.'
Q1123479. Is the Forward Pass Test a criterion for theoretical terms specifically, or for all terms used in AI description? Theoretical terms posit unobservable entities to explain observable patterns; observational terms describe directly detectable patterns. If 'functional analog of salience' is a theoretical term, it might earn its place by explaining patterns — like Q33025's processing divergence — that purely observational terms do not explain.
Q1123480. Apply the Forward Pass Test to Luke's use of 'functional analogs of salience' in Q33025. The test requires a counterpart in the forward pass. Research on large language models has found that models maintain internal representations of contextual states that differentially weight certain inputs — these could be described as salience states. If so, Luke's analog passes Peter's test in principle.
Q1123481. Is the Forward Pass Test an instance of the mechanistic approach to interpretability — the view that understanding a system requires identifying the specific circuits responsible for its behaviors? If so, Peter's critique of Luke's vocabulary is a demand for mechanistic interpretability: show me the circuit that implements the functional analog of salience. Luke's response might be that functional analogs are at a level above individual circuits.
