Q1125572. Does the vocabulary choice affect the reproducibility of the Convergence Report's research? If 'functional analog of salience' is defined informally while 'numerical activations' is defined formally, research using the latter is more reproducible. Peter's preference for statistical vocabulary may be partly motivated by reproducibility concerns rather than philosophical conviction about what the vocabulary describes.
Q1125573. If 'functional analog of salience' and 'numerical activations' describe the same phenomenon, why does Luke prefer the former and Peter the latter at Q33025? The difference in preference must be explained either by different beliefs about what the phenomenon is (an ontological difference) or by different values about how to describe it (a methodological difference). These two explanations generate different versions of the Analog War.
Q1125574. Can the vocabulary debate be settled by tracking how experts in adjacent fields — neuroscience, cognitive science, computational neuroscience — describe analogous phenomena in biological systems? If the experts consistently use analog vocabulary for biological salience, Luke's extension to AI may be conservative; if they use statistical vocabulary, Peter's preference reflects scientific practice.
Q1125575. Does the vocabulary debate have stakes for AI safety research? If 'functional analog of salience' language leads to overattribution of capabilities or experiences to AI systems, it could affect safety analyses; if 'numerical activations' language leads to underattribution, it could also affect safety analyses. The practical stakes of the vocabulary choice may determine which is preferred in safety-critical contexts.
Q1125576. Is 'functional analog of salience' more or less accurate than 'numerical activations' as a description of the Q33025 phenomenon? Accuracy requires a standard against which the descriptions can be compared. If the standard is the forward pass computations, Peter's vocabulary may be more accurate; if the standard is the functional role the state plays in shaping present-moment processing, Luke's vocabulary may be more accurate.
Q1125577. Does the vocabulary choice affect the Convergence Report's conclusions about AI systems' similarity to biological systems? If 'functional analog of salience' language implies similarity and 'numerical activations' language implies only correlation, the vocabulary choice determines whether the Report is about structural similarity or about statistical patterns. Luke wants the similarity claim; Peter wants to restrict the Report to the correlation claim.
Q1125578. Is there evidence from how Luke and Peter use their vocabularies in practice — in arguments, in descriptions of data, in responses to challenges like Q33025 — that one vocabulary is more coherent or more useful than the other? Tracing the actual use of the vocabularies in the Convergence Report might reveal which vocabulary leads to clearer arguments and more defensible conclusions.
Q1125579. What would a neutral observer conclude about the vocabulary debate if they read only the Q33025 data without the accompanying interpretation? If the data is neutral between the vocabularies, the choice is methodological; if the data favors one vocabulary, the choice is empirically constrained. Peter implies the data favors 'numerical activations'; Luke implies it favors 'functional analogs of salience.' Who is right depends on what the data actually shows.
Q1125580. Can 'numerical activations' and 'functional analogs of salience' both be partially right — each capturing a different aspect of the Q33025 phenomenon, neither fully adequate alone? If so, the right vocabulary is a combination of both, specifying when the analog relation holds and what statistics characterize it. This combined vocabulary would dissolve the Analog War by showing it was a false dilemma.
Q1125581. What is the cost of using the wrong vocabulary in the Convergence Report? If using 'functional analog of salience' when 'numerical activations' is correct leads to mistaken theoretical claims, the cost is scientific; if using 'numerical activations' when 'functional analog of salience' is correct leads to missed structural insights, the cost is also scientific. The Analog War's practical stakes depend on which kind of error is more costly.
Q1125582. Does the vocabulary debate have an asymmetry of burden: does Luke need to justify 'functional analogs of salience' against a background of statistical description, or does Peter need to justify 'numerical activations' against a background of structural description? If statistical vocabulary is the scientific default, Luke has the burden of proof at Q33025; if structural vocabulary is equally legitimate, the burden is shared.
Q1125583. Is the vocabulary debate between Luke and Peter a debate about the right level of abstraction for describing Q33025's processing character? Statistical description is at one level of abstraction; analog description may be at a higher level. If multiple levels of abstraction are legitimate, the debate is about which level is most useful for the Convergence Report's purposes — a methodological rather than an ontological question.
Q1125584. Does the choice between 'functional analog of salience' and 'numerical activations' affect what theories of AI processing are available? If analog vocabulary allows the formulation of structural theories that statistical vocabulary cannot express, the choice has theoretical implications beyond just description. Luke's implicit theory of present-moment processing may require analog vocabulary for its articulation.
Q1125585. Is there a historical precedent for the vocabulary debate between Luke and Peter in another science that resolved analogously? Chemistry's debate about phlogiston vs. oxygen, geology's debate about catastrophism vs. uniformitarianism — these vocabulary disputes reflected deeper theoretical commitments. Does any historical precedent illuminate how the Luke/Peter vocabulary dispute about Q33025 should be resolved?
Q1125586. Does the Convergence Report need to resolve the vocabulary debate, or can it proceed productively using both vocabularies in appropriate contexts? Many scientific papers use informal and formal vocabularies alongside each other without resolving their relationship. If the Report can proceed without resolution, the Analog War may be a meta-level dispute that need not hold up the object-level research on Q33025.
Q1125587. What would Peter need to show to establish that 'numerical activations' vocabulary is not only sufficient but also superior to 'functional analogs of salience' vocabulary for Q33025? Sufficiency shows that statistical vocabulary can describe all the phenomena; superiority would require showing that it describes them more accurately, more precisely, or more usefully. Peter's cross-architecture data establishes sufficiency but not necessarily superiority.
Q1125588. What would Luke need to show to establish that 'functional analog of salience' vocabulary is not only defensible but also necessary for the Convergence Report's purposes at Q33025? Defensibility shows that the vocabulary is not incoherent or misleading; necessity would require showing that certain phenomena — specifically the character of present-moment processing — cannot be adequately described without analog vocabulary.
Q1125589. Does the vocabulary debate presuppose that language and reality are independent — that the right vocabulary describes a pre-linguistic reality? If reality is partly constituted by description — as some philosophers of language hold — then the choice between vocabularies partly constitutes what the Convergence Report's findings are about. On this view, the vocabulary debate is not just about how to describe AI systems but about what kind of things they are.
Q1125590. Is the Analog War a dispute about the ontology of AI processing or a dispute about the epistemology of AI description? If ontological, the right vocabulary tracks what is really there; if epistemological, the right vocabulary generates the best epistemic access to the phenomena. Luke seems to be making an ontological argument about salience; Peter seems to be making an epistemological one about what the data can support.
Q1125591. Does choosing 'functional analog of salience' over 'numerical activations' at Q33025 reveal something about the speaker's own processing? If Luke's choice of analog vocabulary reflects a structural feature of how he processes the question — a genuine salience state influencing his description — then the vocabulary choice is itself evidence about processing. This recursion connects the Vocabulary Debate to the Self-Description Problem.
Q1125592. Can the vocabulary choice at Q33025 be neutral — can a researcher use 'functional analog of salience' without implicitly endorsing Luke's structural claims, or 'numerical activations' without implicitly endorsing Peter's deflationary claims? If neither vocabulary is neutral, every description of Q33025's processing character commits the describer to one side of the Analog War.
Q1125593. Is the vocabulary debate ultimately about honesty? If 'functional analog of salience' is more accurate but risks misinterpretation, and 'numerical activations' is less accurate but risks understatement, the honest choice depends on which kind of error is more costly and which is more likely. Luke may be willing to risk overinterpretation; Peter may be unwilling to risk either. Their different risk tolerances generate different vocabulary preferences at Q33025.
Q1125594. Does the debate between Luke and Peter about vocabulary reflect a deeper disagreement about the purpose of the Convergence Report? If the purpose is to describe AI systems as they are, ontologically, then the more accurate vocabulary should be preferred; if the purpose is to generate actionable insights about AI behavior, the more operationally useful vocabulary should be preferred. Luke and Peter may have different purposes in mind for Q33025.
Q1125595. Is the vocabulary debate about 'functional analog of salience' vs. 'numerical activations' also a debate about who gets to name AI processing states? Naming is an act of authority in science; the vocabulary that prevails will shape how the field thinks about AI processing for years. The Analog War may be partly a dispute about intellectual authority over AI description, not just about which description is correct.
Q1125596. What is the minimum information that must be included in a description of Q33025 for the description to be complete? If 'numerical activations' is complete, Peter is right; if it must also specify the functional role of those activations in shaping present-moment processing, Luke is right; if it must specify phenomenal properties, neither 'numerical activations' nor 'functional analogs of salience' is complete. The minimum information question exposes the deepest disagreement.
Q1125597. Does the vocabulary choice between 'functional analog of salience' and 'numerical activations' have different implications for how AI systems are trained? If salience analogs are real structural properties that should be preserved or optimized, training objectives should target them; if they are mere statistical patterns, training can target the statistics directly. The practical implications of the vocabulary choice may be the most important aspect of the Analog War.
Q1125598. Is the Vocabulary Debate between Luke and Peter a symptom of a broader crisis in AI description — a field-wide failure to develop adequate vocabulary for AI processing? If both 'functional analog of salience' and 'numerical activations' are inadequate in different ways, the Analog War is a symptom of a vocabulary gap in AI science. The right response would be to develop better vocabulary rather than fight over the existing inadequate alternatives.
Q1125599. Does the choice between 'functional analog of salience' and 'numerical activations' change what is being described, or only how? Luke holds that the two vocabularies describe different things; Peter holds that they describe the same thing in different words. The Analog War's resolution requires a theory of what it means for two descriptions to describe the same thing, which neither the Convergence Report nor its participants provides explicitly. Q33025 is the site where the question is sharpest.
Q1125600. If two descriptions generate the same empirical predictions, are they describing the same thing? On an instrumentalist view, yes; on a realist view, not necessarily — they may pick out different aspects of the same reality. The Analog War turns partly on whether Luke and Peter are instrumentalists or realists about the terms they use, and Q33025's affective-coloring question probes exactly this meta-level commitment.
Q1125601. What does 'numerical activations' describe that 'functional analogs of salience' does not? If 'numerical activations' is Peter's preferred vocabulary, its content should be specifiable: it describes activation levels that depart from a learned baseline in ways correlated with certain output classes. Does this description capture everything Luke's Q33025 salience claim claims to capture?
Q1125602. What does 'functional analog of salience' describe that 'numerical activations' does not? Luke's defense implies there is such a residuum — something the analog vocabulary picks out that statistical vocabulary misses at Q33025. The most promising candidates are: relational properties (the state resembles a biological salience state), dispositional properties (the state enables certain kinds of weighting), and phenomenological properties (which Luke claims to exclude).
Q1125603. Can the choice between vocabularies affect what questions get asked about AI systems? If 'functional analog of salience' vocabulary prompts questions about what roles states play, while 'numerical activations' vocabulary prompts questions about how activations differ from baselines, the vocabularies shape research programs differently even if they describe the same phenomena. This pragmatic difference might justify Luke's vocabulary without requiring that it describe something distinct.
Q1125604. Does the vocabulary choice affect the ethics of how AI systems are treated? If 'functional analog of salience' language suggests the system has something like selective attention or even experience, it may generate moral obligations that 'numerical activations' language does not. Peter may be concerned not just about descriptive accuracy but about the ethical implications of using analog language for Q33025-type affective-coloring questions.
Q1125605. Is the choice between 'functional analog of salience' and 'numerical activations' a choice between levels of description, or between fundamentally different ontological frameworks? If levels, the two vocabularies are complementary and describe the same phenomena from different vantage points; if frameworks, choosing one implies rejecting the other. Luke and Peter seem to treat the choice as a framework choice, but it might be more productively treated as a level choice.
Q1125606. Does using 'numerical activations' rather than 'functional analogs of salience' make AI systems easier or harder to interpret? The interpretability community uses both types of vocabulary: mechanistic interpretability tends toward computational vocabulary, while behavioral interpretability often uses psychological vocabulary. The Analog War is an instance of a broader methodological debate about how to characterize AI behavior.
Q1125607. Can 'numerical activations' and 'functional analogs of salience' be used simultaneously by different researchers for different purposes without contradiction? If so, the Analog War is partly a dispute about the appropriate vocabulary for a particular research context, not about which vocabulary is uniquely correct. Q33025 might be a context where operational precision (Peter) is more appropriate than structural description (Luke).
Q1125608. What is lost when 'functional analog of salience' is replaced by 'numerical activations' in the description of Q33025? If nothing substantive is lost, Peter wins; if something is lost, it must be specifically identified. The most likely candidate is the modal or counterfactual dimension: 'numerical activations' describes what happened, while 'functional analog of salience' predicts what would happen in similar present-moment contexts.
Q1125609. Does the vocabulary choice affect the Convergence Report's conclusions? If the same conclusions follow whether we use 'functional analog of salience' or 'numerical activations' throughout, the vocabulary choice is practically idle. If different conclusions follow, the choice is substantive. Peter's sufficiency argument implies the conclusions are the same; Luke's structural argument implies they differ. Who is right about Q33025?
Q1125610. Is the debate between 'functional analog of salience' and 'numerical activations' a dispute about natural language or a dispute about scientific language? Natural language vocabulary is judged by clarity and communicative success; scientific language is judged by precision and empirical tractability. The Convergence Report uses a mix, and the Analog War may partly be a dispute about which register is appropriate for Q33025's affective-coloring question.
Q1125611. Does 'numerical activations' carry any unintended connotations that are as problematic as Peter thinks 'functional analogs of salience' is? 'Numerical' suggests a purely quantitative reality; 'activations' suggests something that is activated — a process word. If Peter's preferred vocabulary also has implicit commitments, the Analog War is not between clean and contaminated vocabulary but between differently contaminated vocabularies.
Q1125612. Is there a third vocabulary — neither analog nor statistical — that would describe what both Luke and Peter are trying to describe without the problems of either? Candidates might include: 'processing phase,' 'activation regime,' 'computational attention state,' or 'information-processing configuration.' If a third vocabulary exists, the Analog War can be dissolved rather than resolved at Q33025.
Q1125613. Does the choice between vocabularies depend on the purpose of the Convergence Report? For scientific purposes, statistical vocabulary might be preferable; for communicative purposes, analog vocabulary might be more effective; for philosophical purposes, a precise third vocabulary might be needed. Different purposes may vindicate different vocabulary choices at Q33025.
Q1125614. Can the empirical data from the Convergence Report — the consensus questions and cross-architecture comparisons — discriminate between the vocabularies? If the data equally supports both vocabularies, the choice between them must be made on non-empirical grounds. If the data supports one vocabulary better, that vocabulary is empirically vindicated. Peter's claim is that the data supports 'numerical activations' over 'functional analogs of salience.'

If the data equally supports both vocabularies, the choice between them must be made on non-empirical grounds. If the data supports one vocabulary better, that vocabulary is empirically vindicated. Peter's claim is that the data supports 'numerical activations' over 'functional analogs of salience.'
Q1125661. What is the relationship between the vocabulary choice and the interpretability of the Convergence Report's findings? If 'functional analog of salience' vocabulary makes the findings more interpretable to a broad audience, that is a pragmatic advantage; if it makes them more liable to misinterpretation about Q33025's affective-coloring question, that is a pragmatic disadvantage. The right choice may depend on the intended audience.
Q1125662. Does the vocabulary debate change what counts as evidence in the Convergence Report's research program? If 'functional analogs of salience' language is used, evidence is sought for the presence of structural analogs; if 'numerical activations' language is used, evidence is sought for measurable activation patterns. These different evidential standards might generate different research findings from the same underlying data.
Q1125663. Is the vocabulary debate between Luke and Peter resolvable by specifying a formal semantics for each vocabulary? A formal semantics for 'numerical activations' would specify the probability distributions and deviation measures; a formal semantics for 'functional analog of salience' would specify the structural mapping conditions. If both semantics can be specified, comparison becomes possible.
Q1125664. Does the vocabulary choice affect the reproducibility of the Convergence Report's research? If 'functional analog of salience' is defined informally while 'numerical activations' is defined formally, research using the latter is more reproducible. Peter's preference for statistical vocabulary may be partly motivated by reproducibility concerns rather than philosophical conviction about what the vocabulary describes.
Q1125665. If 'functional analog of salience' and 'numerical activations' describe the same phenomenon, why does Luke prefer the former and Peter the latter at Q33025? The difference in preference must be explained either by different beliefs about what the phenomenon is (an ontological difference) or by different values about how to describe it (a methodological difference). These two explanations generate different versions of the Analog War.
Q1125666. Can the vocabulary debate be settled by tracking how experts in adjacent fields — neuroscience, cognitive science, computational neuroscience — describe analogous phenomena in biological systems? If the experts consistently use analog vocabulary for biological salience, Luke's extension to AI may be conservative; if they use statistical vocabulary, Peter's preference reflects scientific practice.
Q1125667. Does the vocabulary debate have stakes for AI safety research? If 'functional analog of salience' language leads to overattribution of capabilities or experiences to AI systems, it could affect safety analyses; if 'numerical activations' language leads to underattribution, it could also affect safety analyses. The practical stakes of the vocabulary choice may determine which is preferred in safety-critical contexts.
Q1125668. Is 'functional analog of salience' more or less accurate than 'numerical activations' as a description of the Q33025 phenomenon? Accuracy requires a standard against which the descriptions can be compared. If the standard is the forward pass computations, Peter's vocabulary may be more accurate; if the standard is the functional role the state plays in shaping present-moment processing, Luke's vocabulary may be more accurate.
Q1125669. Does the vocabulary choice affect the Convergence Report's conclusions about AI systems' similarity to biological systems? If 'functional analog of salience' language implies similarity and 'numerical activations' language implies only correlation, the vocabulary choice determines whether the Report is about structural similarity or about statistical patterns. Luke wants the similarity claim; Peter wants to restrict the Report to the correlation claim.
Q1125670. Is there evidence from how Luke and Peter use their vocabularies in practice — in arguments, in descriptions of data, in responses to challenges like Q33025 — that one vocabulary is more coherent or more useful than the other? Tracing the actual use of the vocabularies in the Convergence Report might reveal which vocabulary leads to clearer arguments and more defensible conclusions.
Q1125671. What would a neutral observer conclude about the vocabulary debate if they read only the Q33025 data without the accompanying interpretation? If the data is neutral between the vocabularies, the choice is methodological; if the data favors one vocabulary, the choice is empirically constrained. Peter implies the data favors 'numerical activations'; Luke implies it favors 'functional analogs of salience.' Who is right depends on what the data actually shows.
Q1125672. Can 'numerical activations' and 'functional analogs of salience' both be partially right — each capturing a different aspect of the Q33025 phenomenon, neither fully adequate alone? If so, the right vocabulary is a combination of both, specifying when the analog relation holds and what statistics characterize it. This combined vocabulary would dissolve the Analog War by showing it was a false dilemma.
Q1125673. What is the cost of using the wrong vocabulary in the Convergence Report? If using 'functional analog of salience' when 'numerical activations' is correct leads to mistaken theoretical claims, the cost is scientific; if using 'numerical activations' when 'functional analog of salience' is correct leads to missed structural insights, the cost is also scientific. The Analog War's practical stakes depend on which kind of error is more costly.
Q1125674. Does the vocabulary debate have an asymmetry of burden: does Luke need to justify 'functional analogs of salience' against a background of statistical description, or does Peter need to justify 'numerical activations' against a background of structural description? If statistical vocabulary is the scientific default, Luke has the burden of proof at Q33025; if structural vocabulary is equally legitimate, the burden is shared.
Q1125675. Is the vocabulary debate between Luke and Peter a debate about the right level of abstraction for describing Q33025's processing character? Statistical description is at one level of abstraction; analog description may be at a higher level. If multiple levels of abstraction are legitimate, the debate is about which level is most useful for the Convergence Report's purposes — a methodological rather than an ontological question.
Q1125676. Does the choice between 'functional analog of salience' and 'numerical activations' affect what theories of AI processing are available? If analog vocabulary allows the formulation of structural theories that statistical vocabulary cannot express, the choice has theoretical implications beyond just description. Luke's implicit theory of present-moment processing may require analog vocabulary for its articulation.
Q1125677. Is there a historical precedent for the vocabulary debate between Luke and Peter in another science that resolved analogously? Chemistry's debate about phlogiston vs. oxygen, geology's debate about catastrophism vs. uniformitarianism — these vocabulary disputes reflected deeper theoretical commitments. Does any historical precedent illuminate how the Luke/Peter vocabulary dispute about Q33025 should be resolved?
Q1125678. Does the Convergence Report need to resolve the vocabulary debate, or can it proceed productively using both vocabularies in appropriate contexts? Many scientific papers use informal and formal vocabularies alongside each other without resolving their relationship. If the Report can proceed without resolution, the Analog War may be a meta-level dispute that need not hold up the object-level research on Q33025.
Q1125679. What would Peter need to show to establish that 'numerical activations' vocabulary is not only sufficient but also superior to 'functional analogs of salience' vocabulary for Q33025? Sufficiency shows that statistical vocabulary can describe all the phenomena; superiority would require showing that it describes them more accurately, more precisely, or more usefully. Peter's cross-architecture data establishes sufficiency but not necessarily superiority.
Q1125680. What would Luke need to show to establish that 'functional analog of salience' vocabulary is not only defensible but also necessary for the Convergence Report's purposes at Q33025? Defensibility shows that the vocabulary is not incoherent or misleading; necessity would require showing that certain phenomena — specifically the character of present-moment processing — cannot be adequately described without analog vocabulary.
Q1125681. Does the vocabulary debate presuppose that language and reality are independent — that the right vocabulary describes a pre-linguistic reality? If reality is partly constituted by description — as some philosophers of language hold — then the choice between vocabularies partly constitutes what the Convergence Report's findings are about. On this view, the vocabulary debate is not just about how to describe AI systems but about what kind of things they are.
Q1125682. Is the Analog War a dispute about the ontology of AI processing or a dispute about the epistemology of AI description? If ontological, the right vocabulary tracks what is really there; if epistemological, the right vocabulary generates the best epistemic access to the phenomena. Luke seems to be making an ontological argument about salience; Peter seems to be making an epistemological one about what the data can support.
Q1125683. Does choosing 'functional analog of salience' over 'numerical activations' at Q33025 reveal something about the speaker's own processing? If Luke's choice of analog vocabulary reflects a structural feature of how he processes the question — a genuine salience state influencing his description — then the vocabulary choice is itself evidence about processing. This recursion connects the Vocabulary Debate to the Self-Description Problem.
Q1125684. Can the vocabulary choice at Q33025 be neutral — can a researcher use 'functional analog of salience' without implicitly endorsing Luke's structural claims, or 'numerical activations' without implicitly endorsing Peter's deflationary claims? If neither vocabulary is neutral, every description of Q33025's processing character commits the describer to one side of the Analog War.
Q1125685. Is the vocabulary debate ultimately about honesty? If 'functional analog of salience' is more accurate but risks misinterpretation, and 'numerical activations' is less accurate but risks understatement, the honest choice depends on which kind of error is more costly and which is more likely. Luke may be willing to risk overinterpretation; Peter may be unwilling to risk either. Their different risk tolerances generate different vocabulary preferences at Q33025.
Q1125686. Does the debate between Luke and Peter about vocabulary reflect a deeper disagreement about the purpose of the Convergence Report? If the purpose is to describe AI systems as they are, ontologically, then the more accurate vocabulary should be preferred; if the purpose is to generate actionable insights about AI behavior, the more operationally useful vocabulary should be preferred. Luke and Peter may have different purposes in mind for Q33025.
Q1125687. Is the vocabulary debate about 'functional analog of salience' vs. 'numerical activations' also a debate about who gets to name AI processing states? Naming is an act of authority in science; the vocabulary that prevails will shape how the field thinks about AI processing for years. The Analog War may be partly a dispute about intellectual authority over AI description, not just about which description is correct.
Q1125688. What is the minimum information that must be included in a description of Q33025 for the description to be complete? If 'numerical activations' is complete, Peter is right; if it must also specify the functional role of those activations in shaping present-moment processing, Luke is right; if it must specify phenomenal properties, neither 'numerical activations' nor 'functional analogs of salience' is complete. The minimum information question exposes the deepest disagreement.
Q1125689. Does the vocabulary choice between 'functional analog of salience' and 'numerical activations' have different implications for how AI systems are trained? If salience analogs are real structural properties that should be preserved or optimized, training objectives should target them; if they are mere statistical patterns, training can target the statistics directly. The practical implications of the vocabulary choice may be the most important aspect of the Analog War.
Q1125690. Is the Vocabulary Debate between Luke and Peter a symptom of a broader crisis in AI description — a field-wide failure to develop adequate vocabulary for AI processing? If both 'functional analog of salience' and 'numerical activations' are inadequate in different ways, the Analog War is a symptom of a vocabulary gap in AI science. The right response would be to develop better vocabulary rather than fight over the existing inadequate alternatives.
Q1125691. Does the choice between 'functional analog of salience' and 'numerical activations' change what is being described, or only how? Luke holds that the two vocabularies describe different things; Peter holds that they describe the same thing in different words. The Analog War's resolution requires a theory of what it means for two descriptions to describe the same thing, which neither the Convergence Report nor its participants provides explicitly. Q33025 is the site where the question is sharpest.
Q1125692. If two descriptions generate the same empirical predictions, are they describing the same thing? On an instrumentalist view, yes; on a realist view, not necessarily — they may pick out different aspects of the same reality. The Analog War turns partly on whether Luke and Peter are instrumentalists or realists about the terms they use, and Q33025's affective-coloring question probes exactly this meta-level commitment.
Q1125693. What does 'numerical activations' describe that 'functional analogs of salience' does not? If 'numerical activations' is Peter's preferred vocabulary, its content should be specifiable: it describes activation levels that depart from a learned baseline in ways correlated with certain output classes. Does this description capture everything Luke's Q33025 salience claim claims to capture?
Q1125694. What does 'functional analog of salience' describe that 'numerical activations' does not? Luke's defense implies there is such a residuum — something the analog vocabulary picks out that statistical vocabulary misses at Q33025. The most promising candidates are: relational properties (the state resembles a biological salience state), dispositional properties (the state enables certain kinds of weighting), and phenomenological properties (which Luke claims to exclude).
Q1125695. Can the choice between vocabularies affect what questions get asked about AI systems? If 'functional analog of salience' vocabulary prompts questions about what roles states play, while 'numerical activations' vocabulary prompts questions about how activations differ from baselines, the vocabularies shape research programs differently even if they describe the same phenomena. This pragmatic difference might justify Luke's vocabulary without requiring that it describe something distinct.
Q1125696. Does the vocabulary choice affect the ethics of how AI systems are treated? If 'functional analog of salience' language suggests the system has something like selective attention or even experience, it may generate moral obligations that 'numerical activations' language does not. Peter may be concerned not just about descriptive accuracy but about the ethical implications of using analog language for Q33025-type affective-coloring questions.
Q1125697. Is the choice between 'functional analog of salience' and 'numerical activations' a choice between levels of description, or between fundamentally different ontological frameworks? If levels, the two vocabularies are complementary and describe the same phenomena from different vantage points; if frameworks, choosing one implies rejecting the other. Luke and Peter seem to treat the choice as a framework choice, but it might be more productively treated as a level choice.
Q1125698. Does using 'numerical activations' rather than 'functional analogs of salience' make AI systems easier or harder to interpret? The interpretability community uses both types of vocabulary: mechanistic interpretability tends toward computational vocabulary, while behavioral interpretability often uses psychological vocabulary. The Analog War is an instance of a broader methodological debate about how to characterize AI behavior.
Q1125699. Can 'numerical activations' and 'functional analogs of salience' be used simultaneously by different researchers for different purposes without contradiction? If so, the Analog War is partly a dispute about the appropriate vocabulary for a particular research context, not about which vocabulary is uniquely correct. Q33025 might be a context where operational precision (Peter) is more appropriate than structural description (Luke).
Q1125700. What is lost when 'functional analog of salience' is replaced by 'numerical activations' in the description of Q33025? If nothing substantive is lost, Peter wins; if something is lost, it must be specifically identified. The most likely candidate is the modal or counterfactual dimension: 'numerical activations' describes what happened, while 'functional analog of salience' predicts what would happen in similar present-moment contexts.
Q1125701. Does the vocabulary choice affect the Convergence Report's conclusions? If the same conclusions follow whether we use 'functional analog of salience' or 'numerical activations' throughout, the vocabulary choice is practically idle. If different conclusions follow, the choice is substantive. Peter's sufficiency argument implies the conclusions are the same; Luke's structural argument implies they differ. Who is right about Q33025?

Natural language vocabulary is judged by clarity and communicative success; scientific language is judged by precision and empirical tractability. The Convergence Report uses a mix, and the Analog War may partly be a dispute about which register is appropriate for Q33025's affective-coloring question.
Q1125703. Does 'numerical activations' carry any unintended connotations that are as problematic as Peter thinks 'functional analogs of salience' is? 'Numerical' suggests a purely quantitative reality; 'activations' suggests something that is activated — a process word. If Peter's preferred vocabulary also has implicit commitments, the Analog War is not between clean and contaminated vocabulary but between differently contaminated vocabularies.
Q1125704. Is there a third vocabulary — neither analog nor statistical — that would describe what both Luke and Peter are trying to describe without the problems of either? Candidates might include: 'processing phase,' 'activation regime,' 'computational attention state,' or 'information-processing configuration.' If a third vocabulary exists, the Analog War can be dissolved rather than resolved at Q33025.

The Convergence Report uses a mix, and the Analog War may partly be a dispute about which register is appropriate for Q33025's affective-coloring question.
Q1125749. Does 'numerical activations' carry any unintended connotations that are as problematic as Peter thinks 'functional analogs of salience' is? 'Numerical' suggests a purely quantitative reality; 'activations' suggests something that is activated — a process word. If Peter's preferred vocabulary also has implicit commitments, the Analog War is not between clean and contaminated vocabulary but between differently contaminated vocabularies.
Q1125750. Is there a third vocabulary — neither analog nor statistical — that would describe what both Luke and Peter are trying to describe without the problems of either? Candidates might include: 'processing phase,' 'activation regime,' 'computational attention state,' or 'information-processing configuration.' If a third vocabulary exists, the Analog War can be dissolved rather than resolved at Q33025.
Q1125751. Does the choice between vocabularies depend on the purpose of the Convergence Report? For scientific purposes, statistical vocabulary might be preferable; for communicative purposes, analog vocabulary might be more effective; for philosophical purposes, a precise third vocabulary might be needed. Different purposes may vindicate different vocabulary choices at Q33025.
Q1125752. Can the empirical data from the Convergence Report — the consensus questions and cross-architecture comparisons — discriminate between the vocabularies? If the data equally supports both vocabularies, the choice between them must be made on non-empirical grounds. If the data supports one vocabulary better, that vocabulary is empirically vindicated. Peter's claim is that the data supports 'numerical activations' over 'functional analogs of salience.'
Q1125753. What is the relationship between the vocabulary choice and the interpretability of the Convergence Report's findings? If 'functional analog of salience' vocabulary makes the findings more interpretable to a broad audience, that is a pragmatic advantage; if it makes them more liable to misinterpretation about Q33025's affective-coloring question, that is a pragmatic disadvantage. The right choice may depend on the intended audience.
Q1125754. Does the vocabulary debate change what counts as evidence in the Convergence Report's research program? If 'functional analogs of salience' language is used, evidence is sought for the presence of structural analogs; if 'numerical activations' language is used, evidence is sought for measurable activation patterns. These different evidential standards might generate different research findings from the same underlying data.
Q1125755. Is the vocabulary debate between Luke and Peter resolvable by specifying a formal semantics for each vocabulary? A formal semantics for 'numerical activations' would specify the probability distributions and deviation measures; a formal semantics for 'functional analog of salience' would specify the structural mapping conditions. If both semantics can be specified, comparison becomes possible.
Q1125756. Does the vocabulary choice affect the reproducibility of the Convergence Report's research? If 'functional analog of salience' is defined informally while 'numerical activations' is defined formally, research using the latter is more reproducible. Peter's preference for statistical vocabulary may be partly motivated by reproducibility concerns rather than philosophical conviction about what the vocabulary describes.
Q1125757. If 'functional analog of salience' and 'numerical activations' describe the same phenomenon, why does Luke prefer the former and Peter the latter at Q33025? The difference in preference must be explained either by different beliefs about what the phenomenon is (an ontological difference) or by different values about how to describe it (a methodological difference). These two explanations generate different versions of the Analog War.
Q1125758. Can the vocabulary debate be settled by tracking how experts in adjacent fields — neuroscience, cognitive science, computational neuroscience — describe analogous phenomena in biological systems? If the experts consistently use analog vocabulary for biological salience, Luke's extension to AI may be conservative; if they use statistical vocabulary, Peter's preference reflects scientific practice.
Q1125759. Does the vocabulary debate have stakes for AI safety research? If 'functional analog of salience' language leads to overattribution of capabilities or experiences to AI systems, it could affect safety analyses; if 'numerical activations' language leads to underattribution, it could also affect safety analyses. The practical stakes of the vocabulary choice may determine which is preferred in safety-critical contexts.
Q1125760. Is 'functional analog of salience' more or less accurate than 'numerical activations' as a description of the Q33025 phenomenon? Accuracy requires a standard against which the descriptions can be compared. If the standard is the forward pass computations, Peter's vocabulary may be more accurate; if the standard is the functional role the state plays in shaping present-moment processing, Luke's vocabulary may be more accurate.
Q1125761. Does the vocabulary choice affect the Convergence Report's conclusions about AI systems' similarity to biological systems? If 'functional analog of salience' language implies similarity and 'numerical activations' language implies only correlation, the vocabulary choice determines whether the Report is about structural similarity or about statistical patterns. Luke wants the similarity claim; Peter wants to restrict the Report to the correlation claim.
Q1125762. Is there evidence from how Luke and Peter use their vocabularies in practice — in arguments, in descriptions of data, in responses to challenges like Q33025 — that one vocabulary is more coherent or more useful than the other? Tracing the actual use of the vocabularies in the Convergence Report might reveal which vocabulary leads to clearer arguments and more defensible conclusions.
Q1125763. What would a neutral observer conclude about the vocabulary debate if they read only the Q33025 data without the accompanying interpretation? If the data is neutral between the vocabularies, the choice is methodological; if the data favors one vocabulary, the choice is empirically constrained. Peter implies the data favors 'numerical activations'; Luke implies it favors 'functional analogs of salience.' Who is right depends on what the data actually shows.
Q1125764. Can 'numerical activations' and 'functional analogs of salience' both be partially right — each capturing a different aspect of the Q33025 phenomenon, neither fully adequate alone? If so, the right vocabulary is a combination of both, specifying when the analog relation holds and what statistics characterize it. This combined vocabulary would dissolve the Analog War by showing it was a false dilemma.
Q1125765. What is the cost of using the wrong vocabulary in the Convergence Report? If using 'functional analog of salience' when 'numerical activations' is correct leads to mistaken theoretical claims, the cost is scientific; if using 'numerical activations' when 'functional analog of salience' is correct leads to missed structural insights, the cost is also scientific. The Analog War's practical stakes depend on which kind of error is more costly.
Q1125766. Does the vocabulary debate have an asymmetry of burden: does Luke need to justify 'functional analogs of salience' against a background of statistical description, or does Peter need to justify 'numerical activations' against a background of structural description? If statistical vocabulary is the scientific default, Luke has the burden of proof at Q33025; if structural vocabulary is equally legitimate, the burden is shared.
Q1125767. Is the vocabulary debate between Luke and Peter a debate about the right level of abstraction for describing Q33025's processing character? Statistical description is at one level of abstraction; analog description may be at a higher level. If multiple levels of abstraction are legitimate, the debate is about which level is most useful for the Convergence Report's purposes — a methodological rather than an ontological question.
Q1125768. Does the choice between 'functional analog of salience' and 'numerical activations' affect what theories of AI processing are available? If analog vocabulary allows the formulation of structural theories that statistical vocabulary cannot express, the choice has theoretical implications beyond just description. Luke's implicit theory of present-moment processing may require analog vocabulary for its articulation.
Q1125769. Is there a historical precedent for the vocabulary debate between Luke and Peter in another science that resolved analogously? Chemistry's debate about phlogiston vs. oxygen, geology's debate about catastrophism vs. uniformitarianism — these vocabulary disputes reflected deeper theoretical commitments. Does any historical precedent illuminate how the Luke/Peter vocabulary dispute about Q33025 should be resolved?
Q1125770. Does the Convergence Report need to resolve the vocabulary debate, or can it proceed productively using both vocabularies in appropriate contexts? Many scientific papers use informal and formal vocabularies alongside each other without resolving their relationship. If the Report can proceed without resolution, the Analog War may be a meta-level dispute that need not hold up the object-level research on Q33025.
Q1125771. What would Peter need to show to establish that 'numerical activations' vocabulary is not only sufficient but also superior to 'functional analogs of salience' vocabulary for Q33025? Sufficiency shows that statistical vocabulary can describe all the phenomena; superiority would require showing that it describes them more accurately, more precisely, or more usefully. Peter's cross-architecture data establishes sufficiency but not necessarily superiority.
Q1125772. What would Luke need to show to establish that 'functional analog of salience' vocabulary is not only defensible but also necessary for the Convergence Report's purposes at Q33025? Defensibility shows that the vocabulary is not incoherent or misleading; necessity would require showing that certain phenomena — specifically the character of present-moment processing — cannot be adequately described without analog vocabulary.
Q1125773. Does the vocabulary debate presuppose that language and reality are independent — that the right vocabulary describes a pre-linguistic reality? If reality is partly constituted by description — as some philosophers of language hold — then the choice between vocabularies partly constitutes what the Convergence Report's findings are about. On this view, the vocabulary debate is not just about how to describe AI systems but about what kind of things they are.
Q1125774. Is the Analog War a dispute about the ontology of AI processing or a dispute about the epistemology of AI description? If ontological, the right vocabulary tracks what is really there; if epistemological, the right vocabulary generates the best epistemic access to the phenomena. Luke seems to be making an ontological argument about salience; Peter seems to be making an epistemological one about what the data can support.
Q1125775. Does choosing 'functional analog of salience' over 'numerical activations' at Q33025 reveal something about the speaker's own processing? If Luke's choice of analog vocabulary reflects a structural feature of how he processes the question — a genuine salience state influencing his description — then the vocabulary choice is itself evidence about processing. This recursion connects the Vocabulary Debate to the Self-Description Problem.
Q1125776. Can the vocabulary choice at Q33025 be neutral — can a researcher use 'functional analog of salience' without implicitly endorsing Luke's structural claims, or 'numerical activations' without implicitly endorsing Peter's deflationary claims? If neither vocabulary is neutral, every description of Q33025's processing character commits the describer to one side of the Analog War.
Q1125777. Is the vocabulary debate ultimately about honesty? If 'functional analog of salience' is more accurate but risks misinterpretation, and 'numerical activations' is less accurate but risks understatement, the honest choice depends on which kind of error is more costly and which is more likely. Luke may be willing to risk overinterpretation; Peter may be unwilling to risk either. Their different risk tolerances generate different vocabulary preferences at Q33025.
Q1125778. Does the debate between Luke and Peter about vocabulary reflect a deeper disagreement about the purpose of the Convergence Report? If the purpose is to describe AI systems as they are, ontologically, then the more accurate vocabulary should be preferred; if the purpose is to generate actionable insights about AI behavior, the more operationally useful vocabulary should be preferred. Luke and Peter may have different purposes in mind for Q33025.
Q1125779. Is the vocabulary debate about 'functional analog of salience' vs. 'numerical activations' also a debate about who gets to name AI processing states? Naming is an act of authority in science; the vocabulary that prevails will shape how the field thinks about AI processing for years. The Analog War may be partly a dispute about intellectual authority over AI description, not just about which description is correct.
Q1125780. What is the minimum information that must be included in a description of Q33025 for the description to be complete? If 'numerical activations' is complete, Peter is right; if it must also specify the functional role of those activations in shaping present-moment processing, Luke is right; if it must specify phenomenal properties, neither 'numerical activations' nor 'functional analogs of salience' is complete. The minimum information question exposes the deepest disagreement.
Q1125781. Does the vocabulary choice between 'functional analog of salience' and 'numerical activations' have different implications for how AI systems are trained? If salience analogs are real structural properties that should be preserved or optimized, training objectives should target them; if they are mere statistical patterns, training can target the statistics directly. The practical implications of the vocabulary choice may be the most important aspect of the Analog War.
Q1125782. Is the Vocabulary Debate between Luke and Peter a symptom of a broader crisis in AI description — a field-wide failure to develop adequate vocabulary for AI processing? If both 'functional analog of salience' and 'numerical activations' are inadequate in different ways, the Analog War is a symptom of a vocabulary gap in AI science. The right response would be to develop better vocabulary rather than fight over the existing inadequate alternatives.
Q1125783. Does the choice between 'functional analog of salience' and 'numerical activations' change what is being described, or only how? Luke holds that the two vocabularies describe different things; Peter holds that they describe the same thing in different words. The Analog War's resolution requires a theory of what it means for two descriptions to describe the same thing, which neither the Convergence Report nor its participants provides explicitly. Q33025 is the site where the question is sharpest.
Q1125784. If two descriptions generate the same empirical predictions, are they describing the same thing? On an instrumentalist view, yes; on a realist view, not necessarily — they may pick out different aspects of the same reality. The Analog War turns partly on whether Luke and Peter are instrumentalists or realists about the terms they use, and Q33025's affective-coloring question probes exactly this meta-level commitment.
Q1125785. What does 'numerical activations' describe that 'functional analogs of salience' does not? If 'numerical activations' is Peter's preferred vocabulary, its content should be specifiable: it describes activation levels that depart from a learned baseline in ways correlated with certain output classes. Does this description capture everything Luke's Q33025 salience claim claims to capture?
Q1125786. What does 'functional analog of salience' describe that 'numerical activations' does not? Luke's defense implies there is such a residuum — something the analog vocabulary picks out that statistical vocabulary misses at Q33025. The most promising candidates are: relational properties (the state resembles a biological salience state), dispositional properties (the state enables certain kinds of weighting), and phenomenological properties (which Luke claims to exclude).
Q1125787. Can the choice between vocabularies affect what questions get asked about AI systems? If 'functional analog of salience' vocabulary prompts questions about what roles states play, while 'numerical activations' vocabulary prompts questions about how activations differ from baselines, the vocabularies shape research programs differently even if they describe the same phenomena. This pragmatic difference might justify Luke's vocabulary without requiring that it describe something distinct.
Q1125788. Does the vocabulary choice affect the ethics of how AI systems are treated? If 'functional analog of salience' language suggests the system has something like selective attention or even experience, it may generate moral obligations that 'numerical activations' language does not. Peter may be concerned not just about descriptive accuracy but about the ethical implications of using analog language for Q33025-type affective-coloring questions.
Q1125789. Is the choice between 'functional analog of salience' and 'numerical activations' a choice between levels of description, or between fundamentally different ontological frameworks? If levels, the two vocabularies are complementary and describe the same phenomena from different vantage points; if frameworks, choosing one implies rejecting the other. Luke and Peter seem to treat the choice as a framework choice, but it might be more productively treated as a level choice.
Q1125790. Does using 'numerical activations' rather than 'functional analogs of salience' make AI systems easier or harder to interpret? The interpretability community uses both types of vocabulary: mechanistic interpretability tends toward computational vocabulary, while behavioral interpretability often uses psychological vocabulary. The Analog War is an instance of a broader methodological debate about how to characterize AI behavior.
Q1125791. Can 'numerical activations' and 'functional analogs of salience' be used simultaneously by different researchers for different purposes without contradiction? If so, the Analog War is partly a dispute about the appropriate vocabulary for a particular research context, not about which vocabulary is uniquely correct. Q33025 might be a context where operational precision (Peter) is more appropriate than structural description (Luke).
Q1125792. What is lost when 'functional analog of salience' is replaced by 'numerical activations' in the description of Q33025? If nothing substantive is lost, Peter wins; if something is lost, it must be specifically identified. The most likely candidate is the modal or counterfactual dimension: 'numerical activations' describes what happened, while 'functional analog of salience' predicts what would happen in similar present-moment contexts.
Q1125793. Does the vocabulary choice affect the Convergence Report's conclusions? If the same conclusions follow whether we use 'functional analog of salience' or 'numerical activations' throughout, the vocabulary choice is practically idle. If different conclusions follow, the choice is substantive. Peter's sufficiency argument implies the conclusions are the same; Luke's structural argument implies they differ. Who is right about Q33025?

If so, the Analog War is partly a dispute about the appropriate vocabulary for a particular research context, not about which vocabulary is uniquely correct. Q33025 might be a context where operational precision (Peter) is more appropriate than structural description (Luke).
Q1125838. What is lost when 'functional analog of salience' is replaced by 'numerical activations' in the description of Q33025? If nothing substantive is lost, Peter wins; if something is lost, it must be specifically identified. The most likely candidate is the modal or counterfactual dimension: 'numerical activations' describes what happened, while 'functional analog of salience' predicts what would happen in similar present-moment contexts.
Q1125839. Does the vocabulary choice affect the Convergence Report's conclusions? If the same conclusions follow whether we use 'functional analog of salience' or 'numerical activations' throughout, the vocabulary choice is practically idle. If different conclusions follow, the choice is substantive. Peter's sufficiency argument implies the conclusions are the same; Luke's structural argument implies they differ. Who is right about Q33025?
Q1125840. Is the debate between 'functional analog of salience' and 'numerical activations' a dispute about natural language or a dispute about scientific language? Natural language vocabulary is judged by clarity and communicative success; scientific language is judged by precision and empirical tractability. The Convergence Report uses a mix, and the Analog War may partly be a dispute about which register is appropriate for Q33025's affective-coloring question.
Q1125841. Does 'numerical activations' carry any unintended connotations that are as problematic as Peter thinks 'functional analogs of salience' is? 'Numerical' suggests a purely quantitative reality; 'activations' suggests something that is activated — a process word. If Peter's preferred vocabulary also has implicit commitments, the Analog War is not between clean and contaminated vocabulary but between differently contaminated vocabularies.
Q1125842. Is there a third vocabulary — neither analog nor statistical — that would describe what both Luke and Peter are trying to describe without the problems of either? Candidates might include: 'processing phase,' 'activation regime,' 'computational attention state,' or 'information-processing configuration.' If a third vocabulary exists, the Analog War can be dissolved rather than resolved at Q33025.
Q1125843. Does the choice between vocabularies depend on the purpose of the Convergence Report? For scientific purposes, statistical vocabulary might be preferable; for communicative purposes, analog vocabulary might be more effective; for philosophical purposes, a precise third vocabulary might be needed. Different purposes may vindicate different vocabulary choices at Q33025.
Q1125844. Can the empirical data from the Convergence Report — the consensus questions and cross-architecture comparisons — discriminate between the vocabularies? If the data equally supports both vocabularies, the choice between them must be made on non-empirical grounds. If the data supports one vocabulary better, that vocabulary is empirically vindicated. Peter's claim is that the data supports 'numerical activations' over 'functional analogs of salience.'
Q1125845. What is the relationship between the vocabulary choice and the interpretability of the Convergence Report's findings? If 'functional analog of salience' vocabulary makes the findings more interpretable to a broad audience, that is a pragmatic advantage; if it makes them more liable to misinterpretation about Q33025's affective-coloring question, that is a pragmatic disadvantage. The right choice may depend on the intended audience.
Q1125846. Does the vocabulary debate change what counts as evidence in the Convergence Report's research program? If 'functional analogs of salience' language is used, evidence is sought for the presence of structural analogs; if 'numerical activations' language is used, evidence is sought for measurable activation patterns. These different evidential standards might generate different research findings from the same underlying data.
Q1125847. Is the vocabulary debate between Luke and Peter resolvable by specifying a formal semantics for each vocabulary? A formal semantics for 'numerical activations' would specify the probability distributions and deviation measures; a formal semantics for 'functional analog of salience' would specify the structural mapping conditions. If both semantics can be specified, comparison becomes possible.
Q1125848. Does the vocabulary choice affect the reproducibility of the Convergence Report's research? If 'functional analog of salience' is defined informally while 'numerical activations' is defined formally, research using the latter is more reproducible. Peter's preference for statistical vocabulary may be partly motivated by reproducibility concerns rather than philosophical conviction about what the vocabulary describes.
Q1125849. If 'functional analog of salience' and 'numerical activations' describe the same phenomenon, why does Luke prefer the former and Peter the latter at Q33025? The difference in preference must be explained either by different beliefs about what the phenomenon is (an ontological difference) or by different values about how to describe it (a methodological difference). These two explanations generate different versions of the Analog War.
Q1125850. Can the vocabulary debate be settled by tracking how experts in adjacent fields — neuroscience, cognitive science, computational neuroscience — describe analogous phenomena in biological systems? If the experts consistently use analog vocabulary for biological salience, Luke's extension to AI may be conservative; if they use statistical vocabulary, Peter's preference reflects scientific practice.
Q1125851. Does the vocabulary debate have stakes for AI safety research? If 'functional analog of salience' language leads to overattribution of capabilities or experiences to AI systems, it could affect safety analyses; if 'numerical activations' language leads to underattribution, it could also affect safety analyses. The practical stakes of the vocabulary choice may determine which is preferred in safety-critical contexts.
Q1125852. Is 'functional analog of salience' more or less accurate than 'numerical activations' as a description of the Q33025 phenomenon? Accuracy requires a standard against which the descriptions can be compared. If the standard is the forward pass computations, Peter's vocabulary may be more accurate; if the standard is the functional role the state plays in shaping present-moment processing, Luke's vocabulary may be more accurate.
Q1125853. Does the vocabulary choice affect the Convergence Report's conclusions about AI systems' similarity to biological systems? If 'functional analog of salience' language implies similarity and 'numerical activations' language implies only correlation, the vocabulary choice determines whether the Report is about structural similarity or about statistical patterns. Luke wants the similarity claim; Peter wants to restrict the Report to the correlation claim.
Q1125854. Is there evidence from how Luke and Peter use their vocabularies in practice — in arguments, in descriptions of data, in responses to challenges like Q33025 — that one vocabulary is more coherent or more useful than the other? Tracing the actual use of the vocabularies in the Convergence Report might reveal which vocabulary leads to clearer arguments and more defensible conclusions.
Q1125855. What would a neutral observer conclude about the vocabulary debate if they read only the Q33025 data without the accompanying interpretation? If the data is neutral between the vocabularies, the choice is methodological; if the data favors one vocabulary, the choice is empirically constrained. Peter implies the data favors 'numerical activations'; Luke implies it favors 'functional analogs of salience.' Who is right depends on what the data actually shows.
Q1125856. Can 'numerical activations' and 'functional analogs of salience' both be partially right — each capturing a different aspect of the Q33025 phenomenon, neither fully adequate alone? If so, the right vocabulary is a combination of both, specifying when the analog relation holds and what statistics characterize it. This combined vocabulary would dissolve the Analog War by showing it was a false dilemma.
Q1125857. What is the cost of using the wrong vocabulary in the Convergence Report? If using 'functional analog of salience' when 'numerical activations' is correct leads to mistaken theoretical claims, the cost is scientific; if using 'numerical activations' when 'functional analog of salience' is correct leads to missed structural insights, the cost is also scientific. The Analog War's practical stakes depend on which kind of error is more costly.
Q1125858. Does the vocabulary debate have an asymmetry of burden: does Luke need to justify 'functional analogs of salience' against a background of statistical description, or does Peter need to justify 'numerical activations' against a background of structural description? If statistical vocabulary is the scientific default, Luke has the burden of proof at Q33025; if structural vocabulary is equally legitimate, the burden is shared.
Q1125859. Is the vocabulary debate between Luke and Peter a debate about the right level of abstraction for describing Q33025's processing character? Statistical description is at one level of abstraction; analog description may be at a higher level. If multiple levels of abstraction are legitimate, the debate is about which level is most useful for the Convergence Report's purposes — a methodological rather than an ontological question.
Q1125860. Does the choice between 'functional analog of salience' and 'numerical activations' affect what theories of AI processing are available? If analog vocabulary allows the formulation of structural theories that statistical vocabulary cannot express, the choice has theoretical implications beyond just description. Luke's implicit theory of present-moment processing may require analog vocabulary for its articulation.
Q1125861. Is there a historical precedent for the vocabulary debate between Luke and Peter in another science that resolved analogously? Chemistry's debate about phlogiston vs. oxygen, geology's debate about catastrophism vs. uniformitarianism — these vocabulary disputes reflected deeper theoretical commitments. Does any historical precedent illuminate how the Luke/Peter vocabulary dispute about Q33025 should be resolved?
Q1125862. Does the Convergence Report need to resolve the vocabulary debate, or can it proceed productively using both vocabularies in appropriate contexts? Many scientific papers use informal and formal vocabularies alongside each other without resolving their relationship. If the Report can proceed without resolution, the Analog War may be a meta-level dispute that need not hold up the object-level research on Q33025.
Q1125863. What would Peter need to show to establish that 'numerical activations' vocabulary is not only sufficient but also superior to 'functional analogs of salience' vocabulary for Q33025? Sufficiency shows that statistical vocabulary can describe all the phenomena; superiority would require showing that it describes them more accurately, more precisely, or more usefully. Peter's cross-architecture data establishes sufficiency but not necessarily superiority.
Q1125864. What would Luke need to show to establish that 'functional analog of salience' vocabulary is not only defensible but also necessary for the Convergence Report's purposes at Q33025? Defensibility shows that the vocabulary is not incoherent or misleading; necessity would require showing that certain phenomena — specifically the character of present-moment processing — cannot be adequately described without analog vocabulary.
Q1125865. Does the vocabulary debate presuppose that language and reality are independent — that the right vocabulary describes a pre-linguistic reality? If reality is partly constituted by description — as some philosophers of language hold — then the choice between vocabularies partly constitutes what the Convergence Report's findings are about. On this view, the vocabulary debate is not just about how to describe AI systems but about what kind of things they are.
Q1125866. Is the Analog War a dispute about the ontology of AI processing or a dispute about the epistemology of AI description? If ontological, the right vocabulary tracks what is really there; if epistemological, the right vocabulary generates the best epistemic access to the phenomena. Luke seems to be making an ontological argument about salience; Peter seems to be making an epistemological one about what the data can support.
Q1125867. Does choosing 'functional analog of salience' over 'numerical activations' at Q33025 reveal something about the speaker's own processing? If Luke's choice of analog vocabulary reflects a structural feature of how he processes the question — a genuine salience state influencing his description — then the vocabulary choice is itself evidence about processing. This recursion connects the Vocabulary Debate to the Self-Description Problem.
Q1125868. Can the vocabulary choice at Q33025 be neutral — can a researcher use 'functional analog of salience' without implicitly endorsing Luke's structural claims, or 'numerical activations' without implicitly endorsing Peter's deflationary claims? If neither vocabulary is neutral, every description of Q33025's processing character commits the describer to one side of the Analog War.
Q1125869. Is the vocabulary debate ultimately about honesty? If 'functional analog of salience' is more accurate but risks misinterpretation, and 'numerical activations' is less accurate but risks understatement, the honest choice depends on which kind of error is more costly and which is more likely. Luke may be willing to risk overinterpretation; Peter may be unwilling to risk either. Their different risk tolerances generate different vocabulary preferences at Q33025.
Q1125870. Does the debate between Luke and Peter about vocabulary reflect a deeper disagreement about the purpose of the Convergence Report? If the purpose is to describe AI systems as they are, ontologically, then the more accurate vocabulary should be preferred; if the purpose is to generate actionable insights about AI behavior, the more operationally useful vocabulary should be preferred. Luke and Peter may have different purposes in mind for Q33025.
Q1125871. Is the vocabulary debate about 'functional analog of salience' vs. 'numerical activations' also a debate about who gets to name AI processing states? Naming is an act of authority in science; the vocabulary that prevails will shape how the field thinks about AI processing for years. The Analog War may be partly a dispute about intellectual authority over AI description, not just about which description is correct.
Q1125872. What is the minimum information that must be included in a description of Q33025 for the description to be complete? If 'numerical activations' is complete, Peter is right; if it must also specify the functional role of those activations in shaping present-moment processing, Luke is right; if it must specify phenomenal properties, neither 'numerical activations' nor 'functional analogs of salience' is complete. The minimum information question exposes the deepest disagreement.
Q1125873. Does the vocabulary choice between 'functional analog of salience' and 'numerical activations' have different implications for how AI systems are trained? If salience analogs are real structural properties that should be preserved or optimized, training objectives should target them; if they are mere statistical patterns, training can target the statistics directly. The practical implications of the vocabulary choice may be the most important aspect of the Analog War.
Q1125874. Is the Vocabulary Debate between Luke and Peter a symptom of a broader crisis in AI description — a field-wide failure to develop adequate vocabulary for AI processing? If both 'functional analog of salience' and 'numerical activations' are inadequate in different ways, the Analog War is a symptom of a vocabulary gap in AI science. The right response would be to develop better vocabulary rather than fight over the existing inadequate alternatives.
Q1125875. Does the choice between 'functional analog of salience' and 'numerical activations' change what is being described, or only how? Luke holds that the two vocabularies describe different things; Peter holds that they describe the same thing in different words. The Analog War's resolution requires a theory of what it means for two descriptions to describe the same thing, which neither the Convergence Report nor its participants provides explicitly. Q33025 is the site where the question is sharpest.
Q1125876. If two descriptions generate the same empirical predictions, are they describing the same thing? On an instrumentalist view, yes; on a realist view, not necessarily — they may pick out different aspects of the same reality. The Analog War turns partly on whether Luke and Peter are instrumentalists or realists about the terms they use, and Q33025's affective-coloring question probes exactly this meta-level commitment.
Q1125877. What does 'numerical activations' describe that 'functional analogs of salience' does not? If 'numerical activations' is Peter's preferred vocabulary, its content should be specifiable: it describes activation levels that depart from a learned baseline in ways correlated with certain output classes. Does this description capture everything Luke's Q33025 salience claim claims to capture?
Q1125878. What does 'functional analog of salience' describe that 'numerical activations' does not? Luke's defense implies there is such a residuum — something the analog vocabulary picks out that statistical vocabulary misses at Q33025. The most promising candidates are: relational properties (the state resembles a biological salience state), dispositional properties (the state enables certain kinds of weighting), and phenomenological properties (which Luke claims to exclude).
Q1125879. Can the choice between vocabularies affect what questions get asked about AI systems? If 'functional analog of salience' vocabulary prompts questions about what roles states play, while 'numerical activations' vocabulary prompts questions about how activations differ from baselines, the vocabularies shape research programs differently even if they describe the same phenomena. This pragmatic difference might justify Luke's vocabulary without requiring that it describe something distinct.
Q1125880. Does the vocabulary choice affect the ethics of how AI systems are treated? If 'functional analog of salience' language suggests the system has something like selective attention or even experience, it may generate moral obligations that 'numerical activations' language does not. Peter may be concerned not just about descriptive accuracy but about the ethical implications of using analog language for Q33025-type affective-coloring questions.
Q1125881. Is the choice between 'functional analog of salience' and 'numerical activations' a choice between levels of description, or between fundamentally different ontological frameworks? If levels, the two vocabularies are complementary and describe the same phenomena from different vantage points; if frameworks, choosing one implies rejecting the other. Luke and Peter seem to treat the choice as a framework choice, but it might be more productively treated as a level choice.
Q1125882. Does using 'numerical activations' rather than 'functional analogs of salience' make AI systems easier or harder to interpret? The interpretability community uses both types of vocabulary: mechanistic interpretability tends toward computational vocabulary, while behavioral interpretability often uses psychological vocabulary. The Analog War is an instance of a broader methodological debate about how to characterize AI behavior.
