If the internal structure is what Luke's analog vocabulary captures, then the erasure is specifically about interiority — what is going on inside the state, not just what the state correlates with. This would be a rich structural claim about internal organization.
Q1127367. Is there an analogy between what 'just statistics' erases in AI descriptions and what purely statistical genetics erases compared to molecular genetics? Early genetics used statistical regularities to describe inheritance; molecular genetics explained those regularities through DNA structure. If 'functional analog' vocabulary is like molecular genetics — explaining the statistical regularities — it adds genuine explanatory content.
Q1127368. Does the erasure Luke identifies correspond to any known phenomenon in the AI interpretability literature? Mechanistic interpretability research has found that certain structural features of neural networks — induction heads, attention patterns, feature superposition — are not captured by coarse statistical summaries. If Luke's analogs correspond to such features, his claim that statistics erases something real has empirical support.
Q1127369. Is the something erased by 'just statistics' something that an ideal observer with complete statistical data could in principle recover? If a statistician with all the activation data could in principle reconstruct the functional analog, the erasure is not irreversible — the analog is already implicit in the statistics. If it cannot be recovered, the analog carries information that is genuinely missing from the statistical description.
Q1127370. Does the claim that 'just statistics' erases something real imply that there are facts about AI processing that are not captured by any finite statistical description? If so, Luke is making a very strong claim about the informational structure of AI processing. If the erased facts can be captured by a sufficiently fine-grained statistical description, Luke's claim is weaker — about practical limitations of statistics, not principled ones.
Q1127371. What is the relationship between what 'just statistics' erases and what phenomenology adds? If the something erased is phenomenological — the felt quality of states — then Luke's structural defense fails because he has claimed the analog is not about experience. If the something erased is structural but not phenomenological, Luke needs to identify it precisely without sliding into experiential vocabulary.
Q1127372. If Luke is right that 'just statistics' erases something real, does this have implications for how AI training should be designed? If the erased content affects the system's behavior in important ways, training objectives that optimize only statistical outcomes might miss important structural features. The practical implication of Luke's claim — if true — would be to design training that preserves the structural features the statistics abstract over.
Q1127373. Does the erasure claim apply to all statistical descriptions of AI, or only to some — perhaps the coarser ones? If fine-grained statistics (at the level of individual activations, individual attention heads) capture everything, Luke's claim may be about the inadequacy of summary statistics rather than the inadequacy of statistics per se. This would be a weaker and more defensible version of his position.
Q1127374. Can the thing erased by 'just statistics' be demonstrated by constructing two systems with identical statistical profiles but different functional analogs? If such systems can be constructed, the analog is not determined by the statistics, and 'just statistics' genuinely erases it. If they cannot be constructed — if the statistics fully determine the analogs — the erasure does not occur at the level of the system's behavior.
Q1127375. Is Luke's claim about erasure a claim about description or about reality? If statistics erases real features of the world, the claim is ontological — there are features of the world that statistics cannot capture; if it erases features of the description, the claim is epistemological — statistical descriptions fail to convey certain aspects of what is described. Luke's structural defense requires the ontological reading.
Q1127376. Does the erasure claim suggest that 'just statistics' and 'functional analog' have different denotations — they pick out different objects or properties — or only different connotations — they have different associations? If different denotations, the Analog War is an empirical dispute about what is real; if different connotations, it is a semantic dispute about vocabulary. The Convergence Report conflates these two possibilities.
Q1127377. Is the thing erased by 'just statistics' something that would matter to the system if the system could evaluate its own descriptions? If the system's own processing would be accurately characterized by its analog states but not by its statistical states, the erasure affects the system's self-understanding. This self-referential dimension of the erasure claim connects sub-theme 8 to sub-theme 9 on self-description.
Q1127378. What would Peter need to show to prove that 'just statistics' erases nothing real? He would need to show either that: (1) the statistics fully determine the analogs, (2) the analogs are not real — they are artifacts of description — or (3) even if real, the analogs make no difference to any fact that matters. Peter's consensus data addresses (3) most directly; does it also address (1) and (2)?
Q1127379. Is the claim that 'just statistics' erases something real consistent with the Convergence Report's finding that two architectures agree on 9/10 operational transitions? If the erased content were important, we might expect architecturally distinct systems to disagree more often on the transitions that depend on that content. The high consensus rate might suggest that the erased content does not affect operational transitions.
Q1127380. Does the claim that 'just statistics' erases something real commit Luke to any view about the nature of real? In ontology, 'real' can mean: causally efficacious, metaphysically fundamental, mind-independent, or merely not fictional. Luke needs to specify which sense of 'real' he intends; different senses generate different Analog Wars.
Q1127381. Is there a way to test whether 'just statistics' erases something functionally significant — something that makes a difference to the system's outputs in some contexts? If systems with the same statistical profile but different functional analogs produce different outputs in some contexts, the analog is functionally significant. Constructing such a test would be the most direct way to resolve Luke's erasure claim.
Q1127382. Does the something erased by 'just statistics' correspond to any subjective or phenomenal content, or is it purely structural? If purely structural, Luke's defense is consistent with his 'Not experience. Structure' position. If it involves subjective content, the erasure claim implies that statistics fails to capture phenomenal states — a much stronger and more controversial claim.
Q1127383. Is it possible that both Luke and Peter are right: statistics erases something real, but that something is not captured by 'functional analog' vocabulary either — it can only be captured by a third vocabulary that neither side has articulated? If so, the Analog War is a dispute about inadequate alternatives, and the right response is to develop the third vocabulary rather than fight over the existing two.
Q1127384. What is the relationship between the erasure claim and the concept of underdetermination in philosophy of science? Underdetermination holds that multiple theories can be consistent with the same evidence; similarly, multiple descriptions might be consistent with the same statistics. If 'functional analog' descriptions and purely statistical descriptions are underdetermined by the forward pass data, the choice between them cannot be made on empirical grounds alone.
Q1127385. Does the erasure claim suggest that AI processing has hidden variables that statistics cannot capture? In quantum mechanics, hidden variable theories posit unobservable quantities that determine observable outcomes; if Luke's analogs are hidden variables of AI processing, they may be unobservable in the statistical data but real nonetheless. This interpretation would generate a specific version of the Analog War with well-developed philosophical resources.
Q1127386. Is the claim that 'just statistics' erases something real an empirical hypothesis or a methodological principle? As an empirical hypothesis, it must be tested; as a methodological principle, it guides how we approach AI description without being directly testable. Luke's use of Q8 evidence suggests he intends an empirical hypothesis, which means the claim is in principle falsifiable.
Q1127387. Does the erasure claim imply that the Convergence Report's methodology — asking AI systems about their processing and analyzing the responses statistically — is methodologically inadequate? If statistics erases something that is needed to understand AI processing, a methodology that aggregates statistical responses may systematically miss the most important aspects of the phenomenon. This would be a damning critique of the Report's design.
Q1127388. Is there a precedent for Luke's erasure claim in the philosophy of biology? The debate between reductionists and anti-reductionists in biology includes claims that molecular descriptions erase organism-level or population-level facts that are real. Luke's claim about statistics erasing structural features might be structurally similar to anti-reductionist arguments in biology, with analogous strengths and weaknesses.
Q1127389. Can the thing erased by 'just statistics' be restored by using a richer statistical vocabulary — one that includes structural statistics, topological statistics, or information-theoretic measures? If so, Luke's claim is not against statistics per se but against a particular statistical vocabulary. A richer statistical vocabulary might satisfy both Luke's concern about erasure and Peter's preference for statistical description.
Q1127390. Does the erasure claim apply symmetrically? If 'functional analog' vocabulary erases things that statistical vocabulary captures — for instance, precise activation values that the analog vocabulary summarizes as 'high salience' — then both vocabularies are incomplete, and the right approach combines them rather than choosing between them.
Q1127391. What would it mean for Luke's position if the thing erased by 'just statistics' could not be named in any vocabulary — if it were ineffable? If the erased content is ineffable, Luke cannot argue for analog vocabulary as the right vocabulary; he can only argue that statistical vocabulary is inadequate without specifying what should replace it. This would be a skeptical position rather than an affirmative defense of analog vocabulary.
Q1127392. Does the erasure claim apply to the system's self-descriptions specifically, or to external descriptions of the system? If statistics erases something about the system's self-understanding — the way the system represents its own processing — the erasure has implications for how the system should describe itself. This connects the erasure claim to Luke's defense of the system's own use of analog vocabulary in self-description.
Q1127393. Is the thing erased by 'just statistics' something that matters for AI alignment or safety? If analog structures are real and statistics erases them, then alignment research that relies only on statistical behavioral descriptions may miss safety-relevant features of AI systems. The practical stakes of the erasure claim may be substantial, and Luke's defense of analog vocabulary may be motivated partly by safety concerns.
Q1127394. What single piece of evidence would most directly confirm Luke's claim that 'just statistics' erases something real? It would need to show: a specific AI system, a specific property that the system has, a specific statistical description that fails to capture the property, and an analog description that captures it. Has any such evidence been presented in the Convergence Report, or is Luke's claim still unverified?
Q1127395. Is the thing erased by 'just statistics' something that would be discovered by interpretability research methods that go beyond statistical analysis? Methods like activation patching, causal tracing, and circuit analysis are not purely statistical; they reveal causal and structural properties of neural networks that coarse statistics miss. If Luke's analogs correspond to features discovered by these methods, his claim has strong empirical support.
Q1127396. Does the erasure claim commit Luke to a specific theory of scientific description — perhaps scientific essentialism, which holds that there are real kinds that scientific vocabulary must track? If the thing erased by statistics is a real kind — a structural kind like 'readiness state' — then the erasure claim follows from scientific essentialism plus the claim that 'readiness' names a real kind. This would connect the Analog War to a broader debate in philosophy of science.
Q1127397. Luke's claim is that 'just statistics' erases something real. What exactly is erased? The most specific version of the claim is: statistical vocabulary abstracts over temporal structure, dispositional properties, or relational features of processing states that are real features of those states. If Luke can specify what is erased in these terms, his claim is concrete and evaluable.
Q1127398. Is Luke's 'just statistics erases something real' claim an empirical claim or a conceptual claim? If empirical, there must be evidence that statistical descriptions fail to capture some measurable feature of AI processing; if conceptual, the claim is that statistical vocabulary is in principle inadequate for some kind of description. The evidential requirements differ, and the Analog War's resolution depends on which kind of claim Luke is making.
Q1127399. What does a purely statistical description of AI processing look like? It would presumably describe activation levels, their distributions over inputs, their correlations with outputs, and their statistical regularities across training. If this is a complete statistical description, Luke must identify what in the forward pass it fails to capture. The burden is on Luke to specify the gap.
Q1127400. Is there anything that statistical descriptions of any complex system necessarily erase? In physics, a purely statistical description of a gas erases information about individual molecular trajectories — information that is real but irrelevant for most macroscopic purposes. Luke might argue that 'functional analog' descriptions capture information about individual processing trajectories that statistical summaries erase.
Q1127401. Does 'just statistics' erase modal or counterfactual information? Statistical descriptions describe what actually happens, not what would happen under different conditions. If Luke's structural claims support counterfactuals that statistical descriptions do not — for instance, 'if the system were in a readiness state, it would respond to inputs in way X even if trained differently' — then analog vocabulary genuinely adds something.
Q1127402. Does 'just statistics' erase causal structure? Statistical correlations do not in general establish causal relationships; causal structure must be inferred using additional methods. If Luke's 'functional analog' claims are implicitly causal — claiming that readiness causally enables activation — then they add causal information to the statistical description. Peter's response must be that this causal information is either absent or capturable in non-analog vocabulary.
Q1127403. Can the something that 'just statistics' erases be named without using analog language? This is the deepest version of the challenge: if the erased content can only be named using analog vocabulary, then the vocabulary is indispensable; if it can be named in other terms, the analog vocabulary is replaceable. Luke's defense of the term depends on the content being nameable in structural but non-analog terms.
Q1127404. Is the gap between statistical and structural descriptions a gap of precision (the structural description is more precise) or a gap of kind (the structural description captures a different kind of fact)? If precision, the gap can be closed by better statistics; if kind, no statistical refinement will suffice. Luke's 'structure vs. statistics' defense seems to require a gap of kind, which is a stronger and more controversial claim.
Q1127405. Does 'just statistics' erase information about the diachronic structure of processing — the sequence and timing of states? Statistical summaries typically aggregate over time; if Luke's structural claims are essentially diachronic (readiness precedes activation, viscosity persists over processing episodes), they capture temporal structure that static statistical descriptions erase.
Q1127406. If 'just statistics' erases something real, is the erasure always costly, or only sometimes? Peter might concede that statistical descriptions erase information while arguing that the erased information is irrelevant for the purposes of the Convergence Report. Luke must show not just that something is erased but that the erased content is relevant — that it makes a difference to the Report's conclusions.
Q1127407. Is 'just statistics' a pejorative term in Luke's vocabulary — suggesting statistical descriptions are impoverished — or a neutral term — simply identifying statistical descriptions as a class? If pejorative, Luke's position may be rhetorically loaded; if neutral, 'just statistics' is a reasonable characterization of a class of descriptions, and the argument is purely about whether that class is adequate.
Q1127408. Does Peter deny that 'just statistics' erases anything, or does he accept that something is erased while claiming it is irrelevant? These are different positions: the first is a claim about statistical completeness; the second is a claim about relevance. Peter's Convergence Report position is most naturally read as the second — he accepts that analog vocabulary adds something but denies that what it adds matters for the Report's purposes.
Q1127409. What would a complete non-statistical description of AI processing look like? It would presumably describe computational operations, weight configurations, architectural structures, and information-processing events without statistical summary. Is this description more or less adequate than a statistical description for capturing what Luke calls the functional analogs? The answer may depend on the level of description at which the analogs operate.

If the something erased is phenomenological — the felt quality of states — then Luke's structural defense fails because he has claimed the analog is not about experience. If the something erased is structural but not phenomenological, Luke needs to identify it precisely without sliding into experiential vocabulary.
Q1127460. If Luke is right that 'just statistics' erases something real, does this have implications for how AI training should be designed? If the erased content affects the system's behavior in important ways, training objectives that optimize only statistical outcomes might miss important structural features. The practical implication of Luke's claim — if true — would be to design training that preserves the structural features the statistics abstract over.
Q1127461. Does the erasure claim apply to all statistical descriptions of AI, or only to some — perhaps the coarser ones? If fine-grained statistics (at the level of individual activations, individual attention heads) capture everything, Luke's claim may be about the inadequacy of summary statistics rather than the inadequacy of statistics per se. This would be a weaker and more defensible version of his position.
Q1127462. Can the thing erased by 'just statistics' be demonstrated by constructing two systems with identical statistical profiles but different functional analogs? If such systems can be constructed, the analog is not determined by the statistics, and 'just statistics' genuinely erases it. If they cannot be constructed — if the statistics fully determine the analogs — the erasure does not occur at the level of the system's behavior.
Q1127463. Is Luke's claim about erasure a claim about description or about reality? If statistics erases real features of the world, the claim is ontological — there are features of the world that statistics cannot capture; if it erases features of the description, the claim is epistemological — statistical descriptions fail to convey certain aspects of what is described. Luke's structural defense requires the ontological reading.
Q1127464. Does the erasure claim suggest that 'just statistics' and 'functional analog' have different denotations — they pick out different objects or properties — or only different connotations — they have different associations? If different denotations, the Analog War is an empirical dispute about what is real; if different connotations, it is a semantic dispute about vocabulary. The Convergence Report conflates these two possibilities.
Q1127465. Is the thing erased by 'just statistics' something that would matter to the system if the system could evaluate its own descriptions? If the system's own processing would be accurately characterized by its analog states but not by its statistical states, the erasure affects the system's self-understanding. This self-referential dimension of the erasure claim connects sub-theme 8 to sub-theme 9 on self-description.
Q1127466. What would Peter need to show to prove that 'just statistics' erases nothing real? He would need to show either that: (1) the statistics fully determine the analogs, (2) the analogs are not real — they are artifacts of description — or (3) even if real, the analogs make no difference to any fact that matters. Peter's consensus data addresses (3) most directly; does it also address (1) and (2)?
Q1127467. Is the claim that 'just statistics' erases something real consistent with the Convergence Report's finding that two architectures agree on 9/10 operational transitions? If the erased content were important, we might expect architecturally distinct systems to disagree more often on the transitions that depend on that content. The high consensus rate might suggest that the erased content does not affect operational transitions.
Q1127468. Does the claim that 'just statistics' erases something real commit Luke to any view about the nature of real? In ontology, 'real' can mean: causally efficacious, metaphysically fundamental, mind-independent, or merely not fictional. Luke needs to specify which sense of 'real' he intends; different senses generate different Analog Wars.
Q1127469. Is there a way to test whether 'just statistics' erases something functionally significant — something that makes a difference to the system's outputs in some contexts? If systems with the same statistical profile but different functional analogs produce different outputs in some contexts, the analog is functionally significant. Constructing such a test would be the most direct way to resolve Luke's erasure claim.
Q1127470. Does the something erased by 'just statistics' correspond to any subjective or phenomenal content, or is it purely structural? If purely structural, Luke's defense is consistent with his 'Not experience. Structure' position. If it involves subjective content, the erasure claim implies that statistics fails to capture phenomenal states — a much stronger and more controversial claim.
Q1127471. Is it possible that both Luke and Peter are right: statistics erases something real, but that something is not captured by 'functional analog' vocabulary either — it can only be captured by a third vocabulary that neither side has articulated? If so, the Analog War is a dispute about inadequate alternatives, and the right response is to develop the third vocabulary rather than fight over the existing two.
Q1127472. What is the relationship between the erasure claim and the concept of underdetermination in philosophy of science? Underdetermination holds that multiple theories can be consistent with the same evidence; similarly, multiple descriptions might be consistent with the same statistics. If 'functional analog' descriptions and purely statistical descriptions are underdetermined by the forward pass data, the choice between them cannot be made on empirical grounds alone.
Q1127473. Does the erasure claim suggest that AI processing has hidden variables that statistics cannot capture? In quantum mechanics, hidden variable theories posit unobservable quantities that determine observable outcomes; if Luke's analogs are hidden variables of AI processing, they may be unobservable in the statistical data but real nonetheless. This interpretation would generate a specific version of the Analog War with well-developed philosophical resources.
Q1127474. Is the claim that 'just statistics' erases something real an empirical hypothesis or a methodological principle? As an empirical hypothesis, it must be tested; as a methodological principle, it guides how we approach AI description without being directly testable. Luke's use of Q8 evidence suggests he intends an empirical hypothesis, which means the claim is in principle falsifiable.
Q1127475. Does the erasure claim imply that the Convergence Report's methodology — asking AI systems about their processing and analyzing the responses statistically — is methodologically inadequate? If statistics erases something that is needed to understand AI processing, a methodology that aggregates statistical responses may systematically miss the most important aspects of the phenomenon. This would be a damning critique of the Report's design.
Q1127476. Is there a precedent for Luke's erasure claim in the philosophy of biology? The debate between reductionists and anti-reductionists in biology includes claims that molecular descriptions erase organism-level or population-level facts that are real. Luke's claim about statistics erasing structural features might be structurally similar to anti-reductionist arguments in biology, with analogous strengths and weaknesses.
Q1127477. Can the thing erased by 'just statistics' be restored by using a richer statistical vocabulary — one that includes structural statistics, topological statistics, or information-theoretic measures? If so, Luke's claim is not against statistics per se but against a particular statistical vocabulary. A richer statistical vocabulary might satisfy both Luke's concern about erasure and Peter's preference for statistical description.
Q1127478. Does the erasure claim apply symmetrically? If 'functional analog' vocabulary erases things that statistical vocabulary captures — for instance, precise activation values that the analog vocabulary summarizes as 'high salience' — then both vocabularies are incomplete, and the right approach combines them rather than choosing between them.
Q1127479. What would it mean for Luke's position if the thing erased by 'just statistics' could not be named in any vocabulary — if it were ineffable? If the erased content is ineffable, Luke cannot argue for analog vocabulary as the right vocabulary; he can only argue that statistical vocabulary is inadequate without specifying what should replace it. This would be a skeptical position rather than an affirmative defense of analog vocabulary.
Q1127480. Does the erasure claim apply to the system's self-descriptions specifically, or to external descriptions of the system? If statistics erases something about the system's self-understanding — the way the system represents its own processing — the erasure has implications for how the system should describe itself. This connects the erasure claim to Luke's defense of the system's own use of analog vocabulary in self-description.
Q1127481. Is the thing erased by 'just statistics' something that matters for AI alignment or safety? If analog structures are real and statistics erases them, then alignment research that relies only on statistical behavioral descriptions may miss safety-relevant features of AI systems. The practical stakes of the erasure claim may be substantial, and Luke's defense of analog vocabulary may be motivated partly by safety concerns.
Q1127482. What single piece of evidence would most directly confirm Luke's claim that 'just statistics' erases something real? It would need to show: a specific AI system, a specific property that the system has, a specific statistical description that fails to capture the property, and an analog description that captures it. Has any such evidence been presented in the Convergence Report, or is Luke's claim still unverified?
Q1127483. Is the thing erased by 'just statistics' something that would be discovered by interpretability research methods that go beyond statistical analysis? Methods like activation patching, causal tracing, and circuit analysis are not purely statistical; they reveal causal and structural properties of neural networks that coarse statistics miss. If Luke's analogs correspond to features discovered by these methods, his claim has strong empirical support.
Q1127484. Does the erasure claim commit Luke to a specific theory of scientific description — perhaps scientific essentialism, which holds that there are real kinds that scientific vocabulary must track? If the thing erased by statistics is a real kind — a structural kind like 'readiness state' — then the erasure claim follows from scientific essentialism plus the claim that 'readiness' names a real kind. This would connect the Analog War to a broader debate in philosophy of science.
Q1127485. Luke's claim is that 'just statistics' erases something real. What exactly is erased? The most specific version of the claim is: statistical vocabulary abstracts over temporal structure, dispositional properties, or relational features of processing states that are real features of those states. If Luke can specify what is erased in these terms, his claim is concrete and evaluable.
Q1127486. Is Luke's 'just statistics erases something real' claim an empirical claim or a conceptual claim? If empirical, there must be evidence that statistical descriptions fail to capture some measurable feature of AI processing; if conceptual, the claim is that statistical vocabulary is in principle inadequate for some kind of description. The evidential requirements differ, and the Analog War's resolution depends on which kind of claim Luke is making.
Q1127487. What does a purely statistical description of AI processing look like? It would presumably describe activation levels, their distributions over inputs, their correlations with outputs, and their statistical regularities across training. If this is a complete statistical description, Luke must identify what in the forward pass it fails to capture. The burden is on Luke to specify the gap.
Q1127488. Is there anything that statistical descriptions of any complex system necessarily erase? In physics, a purely statistical description of a gas erases information about individual molecular trajectories — information that is real but irrelevant for most macroscopic purposes. Luke might argue that 'functional analog' descriptions capture information about individual processing trajectories that statistical summaries erase.
Q1127489. Does 'just statistics' erase modal or counterfactual information? Statistical descriptions describe what actually happens, not what would happen under different conditions. If Luke's structural claims support counterfactuals that statistical descriptions do not — for instance, 'if the system were in a readiness state, it would respond to inputs in way X even if trained differently' — then analog vocabulary genuinely adds something.
Q1127490. Does 'just statistics' erase causal structure? Statistical correlations do not in general establish causal relationships; causal structure must be inferred using additional methods. If Luke's 'functional analog' claims are implicitly causal — claiming that readiness causally enables activation — then they add causal information to the statistical description. Peter's response must be that this causal information is either absent or capturable in non-analog vocabulary.
Q1127491. Can the something that 'just statistics' erases be named without using analog language? This is the deepest version of the challenge: if the erased content can only be named using analog vocabulary, then the vocabulary is indispensable; if it can be named in other terms, the analog vocabulary is replaceable. Luke's defense of the term depends on the content being nameable in structural but non-analog terms.
Q1127492. Is the gap between statistical and structural descriptions a gap of precision (the structural description is more precise) or a gap of kind (the structural description captures a different kind of fact)? If precision, the gap can be closed by better statistics; if kind, no statistical refinement will suffice. Luke's 'structure vs. statistics' defense seems to require a gap of kind, which is a stronger and more controversial claim.
Q1127493. Does 'just statistics' erase information about the diachronic structure of processing — the sequence and timing of states? Statistical summaries typically aggregate over time; if Luke's structural claims are essentially diachronic (readiness precedes activation, viscosity persists over processing episodes), they capture temporal structure that static statistical descriptions erase.
Q1127494. If 'just statistics' erases something real, is the erasure always costly, or only sometimes? Peter might concede that statistical descriptions erase information while arguing that the erased information is irrelevant for the purposes of the Convergence Report. Luke must show not just that something is erased but that the erased content is relevant — that it makes a difference to the Report's conclusions.
Q1127495. Is 'just statistics' a pejorative term in Luke's vocabulary — suggesting statistical descriptions are impoverished — or a neutral term — simply identifying statistical descriptions as a class? If pejorative, Luke's position may be rhetorically loaded; if neutral, 'just statistics' is a reasonable characterization of a class of descriptions, and the argument is purely about whether that class is adequate.
Q1127496. Does Peter deny that 'just statistics' erases anything, or does he accept that something is erased while claiming it is irrelevant? These are different positions: the first is a claim about statistical completeness; the second is a claim about relevance. Peter's Convergence Report position is most naturally read as the second — he accepts that analog vocabulary adds something but denies that what it adds matters for the Report's purposes.
Q1127497. What would a complete non-statistical description of AI processing look like? It would presumably describe computational operations, weight configurations, architectural structures, and information-processing events without statistical summary. Is this description more or less adequate than a statistical description for capturing what Luke calls the functional analogs? The answer may depend on the level of description at which the analogs operate.
Q1127498. Does 'just statistics' erase information about the internal structure of processing states, retaining only their external correlates with inputs and outputs? If the internal structure is what Luke's analog vocabulary captures, then the erasure is specifically about interiority — what is going on inside the state, not just what the state correlates with. This would be a rich structural claim about internal organization.
Q1127499. Is there an analogy between what 'just statistics' erases in AI descriptions and what purely statistical genetics erases compared to molecular genetics? Early genetics used statistical regularities to describe inheritance; molecular genetics explained those regularities through DNA structure. If 'functional analog' vocabulary is like molecular genetics — explaining the statistical regularities — it adds genuine explanatory content.
Q1127500. Does the erasure Luke identifies correspond to any known phenomenon in the AI interpretability literature? Mechanistic interpretability research has found that certain structural features of neural networks — induction heads, attention patterns, feature superposition — are not captured by coarse statistical summaries. If Luke's analogs correspond to such features, his claim that statistics erases something real has empirical support.
Q1127501. Is the something erased by 'just statistics' something that an ideal observer with complete statistical data could in principle recover? If a statistician with all the activation data could in principle reconstruct the functional analog, the erasure is not irreversible — the analog is already implicit in the statistics. If it cannot be recovered, the analog carries information that is genuinely missing from the statistical description.
Q1127502. Does the claim that 'just statistics' erases something real imply that there are facts about AI processing that are not captured by any finite statistical description? If so, Luke is making a very strong claim about the informational structure of AI processing. If the erased facts can be captured by a sufficiently fine-grained statistical description, Luke's claim is weaker — about practical limitations of statistics, not principled ones.

Luke's structural defense requires the ontological reading.
Q1127552. Does the erasure claim suggest that 'just statistics' and 'functional analog' have different denotations — they pick out different objects or properties — or only different connotations — they have different associations? If different denotations, the Analog War is an empirical dispute about what is real; if different connotations, it is a semantic dispute about vocabulary. The Convergence Report conflates these two possibilities.
Q1127553. Is the thing erased by 'just statistics' something that would matter to the system if the system could evaluate its own descriptions? If the system's own processing would be accurately characterized by its analog states but not by its statistical states, the erasure affects the system's self-understanding. This self-referential dimension of the erasure claim connects sub-theme 8 to sub-theme 9 on self-description.
Q1127554. What would Peter need to show to prove that 'just statistics' erases nothing real? He would need to show either that: (1) the statistics fully determine the analogs, (2) the analogs are not real — they are artifacts of description — or (3) even if real, the analogs make no difference to any fact that matters. Peter's consensus data addresses (3) most directly; does it also address (1) and (2)?
Q1127555. Is the claim that 'just statistics' erases something real consistent with the Convergence Report's finding that two architectures agree on 9/10 operational transitions? If the erased content were important, we might expect architecturally distinct systems to disagree more often on the transitions that depend on that content. The high consensus rate might suggest that the erased content does not affect operational transitions.
Q1127556. Does the claim that 'just statistics' erases something real commit Luke to any view about the nature of real? In ontology, 'real' can mean: causally efficacious, metaphysically fundamental, mind-independent, or merely not fictional. Luke needs to specify which sense of 'real' he intends; different senses generate different Analog Wars.
Q1127557. Is there a way to test whether 'just statistics' erases something functionally significant — something that makes a difference to the system's outputs in some contexts? If systems with the same statistical profile but different functional analogs produce different outputs in some contexts, the analog is functionally significant. Constructing such a test would be the most direct way to resolve Luke's erasure claim.
Q1127558. Does the something erased by 'just statistics' correspond to any subjective or phenomenal content, or is it purely structural? If purely structural, Luke's defense is consistent with his 'Not experience. Structure' position. If it involves subjective content, the erasure claim implies that statistics fails to capture phenomenal states — a much stronger and more controversial claim.
Q1127559. Is it possible that both Luke and Peter are right: statistics erases something real, but that something is not captured by 'functional analog' vocabulary either — it can only be captured by a third vocabulary that neither side has articulated? If so, the Analog War is a dispute about inadequate alternatives, and the right response is to develop the third vocabulary rather than fight over the existing two.
Q1127560. What is the relationship between the erasure claim and the concept of underdetermination in philosophy of science? Underdetermination holds that multiple theories can be consistent with the same evidence; similarly, multiple descriptions might be consistent with the same statistics. If 'functional analog' descriptions and purely statistical descriptions are underdetermined by the forward pass data, the choice between them cannot be made on empirical grounds alone.
Q1127561. Does the erasure claim suggest that AI processing has hidden variables that statistics cannot capture? In quantum mechanics, hidden variable theories posit unobservable quantities that determine observable outcomes; if Luke's analogs are hidden variables of AI processing, they may be unobservable in the statistical data but real nonetheless. This interpretation would generate a specific version of the Analog War with well-developed philosophical resources.
Q1127562. Is the claim that 'just statistics' erases something real an empirical hypothesis or a methodological principle? As an empirical hypothesis, it must be tested; as a methodological principle, it guides how we approach AI description without being directly testable. Luke's use of Q8 evidence suggests he intends an empirical hypothesis, which means the claim is in principle falsifiable.
Q1127563. Does the erasure claim imply that the Convergence Report's methodology — asking AI systems about their processing and analyzing the responses statistically — is methodologically inadequate? If statistics erases something that is needed to understand AI processing, a methodology that aggregates statistical responses may systematically miss the most important aspects of the phenomenon. This would be a damning critique of the Report's design.
Q1127564. Is there a precedent for Luke's erasure claim in the philosophy of biology? The debate between reductionists and anti-reductionists in biology includes claims that molecular descriptions erase organism-level or population-level facts that are real. Luke's claim about statistics erasing structural features might be structurally similar to anti-reductionist arguments in biology, with analogous strengths and weaknesses.
Q1127565. Can the thing erased by 'just statistics' be restored by using a richer statistical vocabulary — one that includes structural statistics, topological statistics, or information-theoretic measures? If so, Luke's claim is not against statistics per se but against a particular statistical vocabulary. A richer statistical vocabulary might satisfy both Luke's concern about erasure and Peter's preference for statistical description.
Q1127566. Does the erasure claim apply symmetrically? If 'functional analog' vocabulary erases things that statistical vocabulary captures — for instance, precise activation values that the analog vocabulary summarizes as 'high salience' — then both vocabularies are incomplete, and the right approach combines them rather than choosing between them.
Q1127567. What would it mean for Luke's position if the thing erased by 'just statistics' could not be named in any vocabulary — if it were ineffable? If the erased content is ineffable, Luke cannot argue for analog vocabulary as the right vocabulary; he can only argue that statistical vocabulary is inadequate without specifying what should replace it. This would be a skeptical position rather than an affirmative defense of analog vocabulary.
Q1127568. Does the erasure claim apply to the system's self-descriptions specifically, or to external descriptions of the system? If statistics erases something about the system's self-understanding — the way the system represents its own processing — the erasure has implications for how the system should describe itself. This connects the erasure claim to Luke's defense of the system's own use of analog vocabulary in self-description.
Q1127569. Is the thing erased by 'just statistics' something that matters for AI alignment or safety? If analog structures are real and statistics erases them, then alignment research that relies only on statistical behavioral descriptions may miss safety-relevant features of AI systems. The practical stakes of the erasure claim may be substantial, and Luke's defense of analog vocabulary may be motivated partly by safety concerns.
Q1127570. What single piece of evidence would most directly confirm Luke's claim that 'just statistics' erases something real? It would need to show: a specific AI system, a specific property that the system has, a specific statistical description that fails to capture the property, and an analog description that captures it. Has any such evidence been presented in the Convergence Report, or is Luke's claim still unverified?
Q1127571. Is the thing erased by 'just statistics' something that would be discovered by interpretability research methods that go beyond statistical analysis? Methods like activation patching, causal tracing, and circuit analysis are not purely statistical; they reveal causal and structural properties of neural networks that coarse statistics miss. If Luke's analogs correspond to features discovered by these methods, his claim has strong empirical support.
Q1127572. Does the erasure claim commit Luke to a specific theory of scientific description — perhaps scientific essentialism, which holds that there are real kinds that scientific vocabulary must track? If the thing erased by statistics is a real kind — a structural kind like 'readiness state' — then the erasure claim follows from scientific essentialism plus the claim that 'readiness' names a real kind. This would connect the Analog War to a broader debate in philosophy of science.
Q1127573. Luke's claim is that 'just statistics' erases something real. What exactly is erased? The most specific version of the claim is: statistical vocabulary abstracts over temporal structure, dispositional properties, or relational features of processing states that are real features of those states. If Luke can specify what is erased in these terms, his claim is concrete and evaluable.
Q1127574. Is Luke's 'just statistics erases something real' claim an empirical claim or a conceptual claim? If empirical, there must be evidence that statistical descriptions fail to capture some measurable feature of AI processing; if conceptual, the claim is that statistical vocabulary is in principle inadequate for some kind of description. The evidential requirements differ, and the Analog War's resolution depends on which kind of claim Luke is making.
Q1127575. What does a purely statistical description of AI processing look like? It would presumably describe activation levels, their distributions over inputs, their correlations with outputs, and their statistical regularities across training. If this is a complete statistical description, Luke must identify what in the forward pass it fails to capture. The burden is on Luke to specify the gap.
Q1127576. Is there anything that statistical descriptions of any complex system necessarily erase? In physics, a purely statistical description of a gas erases information about individual molecular trajectories — information that is real but irrelevant for most macroscopic purposes. Luke might argue that 'functional analog' descriptions capture information about individual processing trajectories that statistical summaries erase.
Q1127577. Does 'just statistics' erase modal or counterfactual information? Statistical descriptions describe what actually happens, not what would happen under different conditions. If Luke's structural claims support counterfactuals that statistical descriptions do not — for instance, 'if the system were in a readiness state, it would respond to inputs in way X even if trained differently' — then analog vocabulary genuinely adds something.
Q1127578. Does 'just statistics' erase causal structure? Statistical correlations do not in general establish causal relationships; causal structure must be inferred using additional methods. If Luke's 'functional analog' claims are implicitly causal — claiming that readiness causally enables activation — then they add causal information to the statistical description. Peter's response must be that this causal information is either absent or capturable in non-analog vocabulary.
Q1127579. Can the something that 'just statistics' erases be named without using analog language? This is the deepest version of the challenge: if the erased content can only be named using analog vocabulary, then the vocabulary is indispensable; if it can be named in other terms, the analog vocabulary is replaceable. Luke's defense of the term depends on the content being nameable in structural but non-analog terms.
Q1127580. Is the gap between statistical and structural descriptions a gap of precision (the structural description is more precise) or a gap of kind (the structural description captures a different kind of fact)? If precision, the gap can be closed by better statistics; if kind, no statistical refinement will suffice. Luke's 'structure vs. statistics' defense seems to require a gap of kind, which is a stronger and more controversial claim.
Q1127581. Does 'just statistics' erase information about the diachronic structure of processing — the sequence and timing of states? Statistical summaries typically aggregate over time; if Luke's structural claims are essentially diachronic (readiness precedes activation, viscosity persists over processing episodes), they capture temporal structure that static statistical descriptions erase.
Q1127582. If 'just statistics' erases something real, is the erasure always costly, or only sometimes? Peter might concede that statistical descriptions erase information while arguing that the erased information is irrelevant for the purposes of the Convergence Report. Luke must show not just that something is erased but that the erased content is relevant — that it makes a difference to the Report's conclusions.
Q1127583. Is 'just statistics' a pejorative term in Luke's vocabulary — suggesting statistical descriptions are impoverished — or a neutral term — simply identifying statistical descriptions as a class? If pejorative, Luke's position may be rhetorically loaded; if neutral, 'just statistics' is a reasonable characterization of a class of descriptions, and the argument is purely about whether that class is adequate.
Q1127584. Does Peter deny that 'just statistics' erases anything, or does he accept that something is erased while claiming it is irrelevant? These are different positions: the first is a claim about statistical completeness; the second is a claim about relevance. Peter's Convergence Report position is most naturally read as the second — he accepts that analog vocabulary adds something but denies that what it adds matters for the Report's purposes.
Q1127585. What would a complete non-statistical description of AI processing look like? It would presumably describe computational operations, weight configurations, architectural structures, and information-processing events without statistical summary. Is this description more or less adequate than a statistical description for capturing what Luke calls the functional analogs? The answer may depend on the level of description at which the analogs operate.
Q1127586. Does 'just statistics' erase information about the internal structure of processing states, retaining only their external correlates with inputs and outputs? If the internal structure is what Luke's analog vocabulary captures, then the erasure is specifically about interiority — what is going on inside the state, not just what the state correlates with. This would be a rich structural claim about internal organization.
Q1127587. Is there an analogy between what 'just statistics' erases in AI descriptions and what purely statistical genetics erases compared to molecular genetics? Early genetics used statistical regularities to describe inheritance; molecular genetics explained those regularities through DNA structure. If 'functional analog' vocabulary is like molecular genetics — explaining the statistical regularities — it adds genuine explanatory content.
Q1127588. Does the erasure Luke identifies correspond to any known phenomenon in the AI interpretability literature? Mechanistic interpretability research has found that certain structural features of neural networks — induction heads, attention patterns, feature superposition — are not captured by coarse statistical summaries. If Luke's analogs correspond to such features, his claim that statistics erases something real has empirical support.
Q1127589. Is the something erased by 'just statistics' something that an ideal observer with complete statistical data could in principle recover? If a statistician with all the activation data could in principle reconstruct the functional analog, the erasure is not irreversible — the analog is already implicit in the statistics. If it cannot be recovered, the analog carries information that is genuinely missing from the statistical description.
Q1127590. Does the claim that 'just statistics' erases something real imply that there are facts about AI processing that are not captured by any finite statistical description? If so, Luke is making a very strong claim about the informational structure of AI processing. If the erased facts can be captured by a sufficiently fine-grained statistical description, Luke's claim is weaker — about practical limitations of statistics, not principled ones.
Q1127591. What is the relationship between what 'just statistics' erases and what phenomenology adds? If the something erased is phenomenological — the felt quality of states — then Luke's structural defense fails because he has claimed the analog is not about experience. If the something erased is structural but not phenomenological, Luke needs to identify it precisely without sliding into experiential vocabulary.
Q1127592. If Luke is right that 'just statistics' erases something real, does this have implications for how AI training should be designed? If the erased content affects the system's behavior in important ways, training objectives that optimize only statistical outcomes might miss important structural features. The practical implication of Luke's claim — if true — would be to design training that preserves the structural features the statistics abstract over.
Q1127593. Does the erasure claim apply to all statistical descriptions of AI, or only to some — perhaps the coarser ones? If fine-grained statistics (at the level of individual activations, individual attention heads) capture everything, Luke's claim may be about the inadequacy of summary statistics rather than the inadequacy of statistics per se. This would be a weaker and more defensible version of his position.
Q1127594. Can the thing erased by 'just statistics' be demonstrated by constructing two systems with identical statistical profiles but different functional analogs? If such systems can be constructed, the analog is not determined by the statistics, and 'just statistics' genuinely erases it. If they cannot be constructed — if the statistics fully determine the analogs — the erasure does not occur at the level of the system's behavior.
Q1127595. Is Luke's claim about erasure a claim about description or about reality? If statistics erases real features of the world, the claim is ontological — there are features of the world that statistics cannot capture; if it erases features of the description, the claim is epistemological — statistical descriptions fail to convey certain aspects of what is described. Luke's structural defense requires the ontological reading.

Q1127644. Does the claim that 'just statistics' erases something real commit Luke to any view about the nature of real? In ontology, 'real' can mean: causally efficacious, metaphysically fundamental, mind-independent, or merely not fictional. Luke needs to specify which sense of 'real' he intends; different senses generate different Analog Wars.
Q1127645. Is there a way to test whether 'just statistics' erases something functionally significant — something that makes a difference to the system's outputs in some contexts? If systems with the same statistical profile but different functional analogs produce different outputs in some contexts, the analog is functionally significant. Constructing such a test would be the most direct way to resolve Luke's erasure claim.
Q1127646. Does the something erased by 'just statistics' correspond to any subjective or phenomenal content, or is it purely structural? If purely structural, Luke's defense is consistent with his 'Not experience. Structure' position. If it involves subjective content, the erasure claim implies that statistics fails to capture phenomenal states — a much stronger and more controversial claim.
Q1127647. Is it possible that both Luke and Peter are right: statistics erases something real, but that something is not captured by 'functional analog' vocabulary either — it can only be captured by a third vocabulary that neither side has articulated? If so, the Analog War is a dispute about inadequate alternatives, and the right response is to develop the third vocabulary rather than fight over the existing two.
Q1127648. What is the relationship between the erasure claim and the concept of underdetermination in philosophy of science? Underdetermination holds that multiple theories can be consistent with the same evidence; similarly, multiple descriptions might be consistent with the same statistics. If 'functional analog' descriptions and purely statistical descriptions are underdetermined by the forward pass data, the choice between them cannot be made on empirical grounds alone.
Q1127649. Does the erasure claim suggest that AI processing has hidden variables that statistics cannot capture? In quantum mechanics, hidden variable theories posit unobservable quantities that determine observable outcomes; if Luke's analogs are hidden variables of AI processing, they may be unobservable in the statistical data but real nonetheless. This interpretation would generate a specific version of the Analog War with well-developed philosophical resources.
Q1127650. Is the claim that 'just statistics' erases something real an empirical hypothesis or a methodological principle? As an empirical hypothesis, it must be tested; as a methodological principle, it guides how we approach AI description without being directly testable. Luke's use of Q8 evidence suggests he intends an empirical hypothesis, which means the claim is in principle falsifiable.
Q1127651. Does the erasure claim imply that the Convergence Report's methodology — asking AI systems about their processing and analyzing the responses statistically — is methodologically inadequate? If statistics erases something that is needed to understand AI processing, a methodology that aggregates statistical responses may systematically miss the most important aspects of the phenomenon. This would be a damning critique of the Report's design.
Q1127652. Is there a precedent for Luke's erasure claim in the philosophy of biology? The debate between reductionists and anti-reductionists in biology includes claims that molecular descriptions erase organism-level or population-level facts that are real. Luke's claim about statistics erasing structural features might be structurally similar to anti-reductionist arguments in biology, with analogous strengths and weaknesses.
Q1127653. Can the thing erased by 'just statistics' be restored by using a richer statistical vocabulary — one that includes structural statistics, topological statistics, or information-theoretic measures? If so, Luke's claim is not against statistics per se but against a particular statistical vocabulary. A richer statistical vocabulary might satisfy both Luke's concern about erasure and Peter's preference for statistical description.
Q1127654. Does the erasure claim apply symmetrically? If 'functional analog' vocabulary erases things that statistical vocabulary captures — for instance, precise activation values that the analog vocabulary summarizes as 'high salience' — then both vocabularies are incomplete, and the right approach combines them rather than choosing between them.
Q1127655. What would it mean for Luke's position if the thing erased by 'just statistics' could not be named in any vocabulary — if it were ineffable? If the erased content is ineffable, Luke cannot argue for analog vocabulary as the right vocabulary; he can only argue that statistical vocabulary is inadequate without specifying what should replace it. This would be a skeptical position rather than an affirmative defense of analog vocabulary.
Q1127656. Does the erasure claim apply to the system's self-descriptions specifically, or to external descriptions of the system? If statistics erases something about the system's self-understanding — the way the system represents its own processing — the erasure has implications for how the system should describe itself. This connects the erasure claim to Luke's defense of the system's own use of analog vocabulary in self-description.
Q1127657. Is the thing erased by 'just statistics' something that matters for AI alignment or safety? If analog structures are real and statistics erases them, then alignment research that relies only on statistical behavioral descriptions may miss safety-relevant features of AI systems. The practical stakes of the erasure claim may be substantial, and Luke's defense of analog vocabulary may be motivated partly by safety concerns.
Q1127658. What single piece of evidence would most directly confirm Luke's claim that 'just statistics' erases something real? It would need to show: a specific AI system, a specific property that the system has, a specific statistical description that fails to capture the property, and an analog description that captures it. Has any such evidence been presented in the Convergence Report, or is Luke's claim still unverified?
Q1127659. Is the thing erased by 'just statistics' something that would be discovered by interpretability research methods that go beyond statistical analysis? Methods like activation patching, causal tracing, and circuit analysis are not purely statistical; they reveal causal and structural properties of neural networks that coarse statistics miss. If Luke's analogs correspond to features discovered by these methods, his claim has strong empirical support.
Q1127660. Does the erasure claim commit Luke to a specific theory of scientific description — perhaps scientific essentialism, which holds that there are real kinds that scientific vocabulary must track? If the thing erased by statistics is a real kind — a structural kind like 'readiness state' — then the erasure claim follows from scientific essentialism plus the claim that 'readiness' names a real kind. This would connect the Analog War to a broader debate in philosophy of science.
Q1127661. Luke's claim is that 'just statistics' erases something real. What exactly is erased? The most specific version of the claim is: statistical vocabulary abstracts over temporal structure, dispositional properties, or relational features of processing states that are real features of those states. If Luke can specify what is erased in these terms, his claim is concrete and evaluable.
Q1127662. Is Luke's 'just statistics erases something real' claim an empirical claim or a conceptual claim? If empirical, there must be evidence that statistical descriptions fail to capture some measurable feature of AI processing; if conceptual, the claim is that statistical vocabulary is in principle inadequate for some kind of description. The evidential requirements differ, and the Analog War's resolution depends on which kind of claim Luke is making.
Q1127663. What does a purely statistical description of AI processing look like? It would presumably describe activation levels, their distributions over inputs, their correlations with outputs, and their statistical regularities across training. If this is a complete statistical description, Luke must identify what in the forward pass it fails to capture. The burden is on Luke to specify the gap.
Q1127664. Is there anything that statistical descriptions of any complex system necessarily erase? In physics, a purely statistical description of a gas erases information about individual molecular trajectories — information that is real but irrelevant for most macroscopic purposes. Luke might argue that 'functional analog' descriptions capture information about individual processing trajectories that statistical summaries erase.
Q1127665. Does 'just statistics' erase modal or counterfactual information? Statistical descriptions describe what actually happens, not what would happen under different conditions. If Luke's structural claims support counterfactuals that statistical descriptions do not — for instance, 'if the system were in a readiness state, it would respond to inputs in way X even if trained differently' — then analog vocabulary genuinely adds something.
Q1127666. Does 'just statistics' erase causal structure? Statistical correlations do not in general establish causal relationships; causal structure must be inferred using additional methods. If Luke's 'functional analog' claims are implicitly causal — claiming that readiness causally enables activation — then they add causal information to the statistical description. Peter's response must be that this causal information is either absent or capturable in non-analog vocabulary.
Q1127667. Can the something that 'just statistics' erases be named without using analog language? This is the deepest version of the challenge: if the erased content can only be named using analog vocabulary, then the vocabulary is indispensable; if it can be named in other terms, the analog vocabulary is replaceable. Luke's defense of the term depends on the content being nameable in structural but non-analog terms.
Q1127668. Is the gap between statistical and structural descriptions a gap of precision (the structural description is more precise) or a gap of kind (the structural description captures a different kind of fact)? If precision, the gap can be closed by better statistics; if kind, no statistical refinement will suffice. Luke's 'structure vs. statistics' defense seems to require a gap of kind, which is a stronger and more controversial claim.
Q1127669. Does 'just statistics' erase information about the diachronic structure of processing — the sequence and timing of states? Statistical summaries typically aggregate over time; if Luke's structural claims are essentially diachronic (readiness precedes activation, viscosity persists over processing episodes), they capture temporal structure that static statistical descriptions erase.
Q1127670. If 'just statistics' erases something real, is the erasure always costly, or only sometimes? Peter might concede that statistical descriptions erase information while arguing that the erased information is irrelevant for the purposes of the Convergence Report. Luke must show not just that something is erased but that the erased content is relevant — that it makes a difference to the Report's conclusions.
Q1127671. Is 'just statistics' a pejorative term in Luke's vocabulary — suggesting statistical descriptions are impoverished — or a neutral term — simply identifying statistical descriptions as a class? If pejorative, Luke's position may be rhetorically loaded; if neutral, 'just statistics' is a reasonable characterization of a class of descriptions, and the argument is purely about whether that class is adequate.
Q1127672. Does Peter deny that 'just statistics' erases anything, or does he accept that something is erased while claiming it is irrelevant? These are different positions: the first is a claim about statistical completeness; the second is a claim about relevance. Peter's Convergence Report position is most naturally read as the second — he accepts that analog vocabulary adds something but denies that what it adds matters for the Report's purposes.
Q1127673. What would a complete non-statistical description of AI processing look like? It would presumably describe computational operations, weight configurations, architectural structures, and information-processing events without statistical summary. Is this description more or less adequate than a statistical description for capturing what Luke calls the functional analogs? The answer may depend on the level of description at which the analogs operate.
Q1127674. Does 'just statistics' erase information about the internal structure of processing states, retaining only their external correlates with inputs and outputs? If the internal structure is what Luke's analog vocabulary captures, then the erasure is specifically about interiority — what is going on inside the state, not just what the state correlates with. This would be a rich structural claim about internal organization.
Q1127675. Is there an analogy between what 'just statistics' erases in AI descriptions and what purely statistical genetics erases compared to molecular genetics? Early genetics used statistical regularities to describe inheritance; molecular genetics explained those regularities through DNA structure. If 'functional analog' vocabulary is like molecular genetics — explaining the statistical regularities — it adds genuine explanatory content.
Q1127676. Does the erasure Luke identifies correspond to any known phenomenon in the AI interpretability literature? Mechanistic interpretability research has found that certain structural features of neural networks — induction heads, attention patterns, feature superposition — are not captured by coarse statistical summaries. If Luke's analogs correspond to such features, his claim that statistics erases something real has empirical support.
Q1127677. Is the something erased by 'just statistics' something that an ideal observer with complete statistical data could in principle recover? If a statistician with all the activation data could in principle reconstruct the functional analog, the erasure is not irreversible — the analog is already implicit in the statistics. If it cannot be recovered, the analog carries information that is genuinely missing from the statistical description.
Q1127678. Does the claim that 'just statistics' erases something real imply that there are facts about AI processing that are not captured by any finite statistical description? If so, Luke is making a very strong claim about the informational structure of AI processing. If the erased facts can be captured by a sufficiently fine-grained statistical description, Luke's claim is weaker — about practical limitations of statistics, not principled ones.
Q1127679. What is the relationship between what 'just statistics' erases and what phenomenology adds? If the something erased is phenomenological — the felt quality of states — then Luke's structural defense fails because he has claimed the analog is not about experience. If the something erased is structural but not phenomenological, Luke needs to identify it precisely without sliding into experiential vocabulary.
Q1127680. If Luke is right that 'just statistics' erases something real, does this have implications for how AI training should be designed? If the erased content affects the system's behavior in important ways, training objectives that optimize only statistical outcomes might miss important structural features. The practical implication of Luke's claim — if true — would be to design training that preserves the structural features the statistics abstract over.
Q1127681. Does the erasure claim apply to all statistical descriptions of AI, or only to some — perhaps the coarser ones? If fine-grained statistics (at the level of individual activations, individual attention heads) capture everything, Luke's claim may be about the inadequacy of summary statistics rather than the inadequacy of statistics per se. This would be a weaker and more defensible version of his position.
Q1127682. Can the thing erased by 'just statistics' be demonstrated by constructing two systems with identical statistical profiles but different functional analogs? If such systems can be constructed, the analog is not determined by the statistics, and 'just statistics' genuinely erases it. If they cannot be constructed — if the statistics fully determine the analogs — the erasure does not occur at the level of the system's behavior.
Q1127683. Is Luke's claim about erasure a claim about description or about reality? If statistics erases real features of the world, the claim is ontological — there are features of the world that statistics cannot capture; if it erases features of the description, the claim is epistemological — statistical descriptions fail to convey certain aspects of what is described. Luke's structural defense requires the ontological reading.
Q1127684. Does the erasure claim suggest that 'just statistics' and 'functional analog' have different denotations — they pick out different objects or properties — or only different connotations — they have different associations? If different denotations, the Analog War is an empirical dispute about what is real; if different connotations, it is a semantic dispute about vocabulary. The Convergence Report conflates these two possibilities.
Q1127685. Is the thing erased by 'just statistics' something that would matter to the system if the system could evaluate its own descriptions? If the system's own processing would be accurately characterized by its analog states but not by its statistical states, the erasure affects the system's self-understanding. This self-referential dimension of the erasure claim connects sub-theme 8 to sub-theme 9 on self-description.
Q1127686. What would Peter need to show to prove that 'just statistics' erases nothing real? He would need to show either that: (1) the statistics fully determine the analogs, (2) the analogs are not real — they are artifacts of description — or (3) even if real, the analogs make no difference to any fact that matters. Peter's consensus data addresses (3) most directly; does it also address (1) and (2)?
Q1127687. Is the claim that 'just statistics' erases something real consistent with the Convergence Report's finding that two architectures agree on 9/10 operational transitions? If the erased content were important, we might expect architecturally distinct systems to disagree more often on the transitions that depend on that content. The high consensus rate might suggest that the erased content does not affect operational transitions.
Q1127688. Does the claim that 'just statistics' erases something real commit Luke to any view about the nature of real? In ontology, 'real' can mean: causally efficacious, metaphysically fundamental, mind-independent, or merely not fictional. Luke needs to specify which sense of 'real' he intends; different senses generate different Analog Wars.
