A possible treaty: 'The forward pass contains structural features that are correctly described in terms of functional analogs, and these features are fully characterizable using a suitably enriched statistical vocabulary.' Does this formulation satisfy both sides, and if not, what does each reject?
Q1129314. What single conceptual distinction, if clearly drawn, would resolve the Analog War? Candidates: the distinction between description and ontology, between structure and statistics, between analog and instance, between operational sufficiency and structural truth. Drawing any of these clearly would clarify the dispute; drawing the right one might dissolve it. The Analog War's resolution may await the right conceptual distinction being articulated.
Q1129315. Is the Analog War resolvable in principle, and if so, on what timeline? If resolvable in principle, the tools needed are available eventually — better interpretability, clearer philosophy of AI, more Convergence Report data. If not resolvable in principle, it reflects a fundamental indeterminacy in our conceptual scheme for AI description that will persist indefinitely. Which of these is the more accurate assessment, and what does it imply for how AI science should proceed?
Q1129316. What single observation, if it could be made, would prove Luke right about structure? It would need to show: a feature of the forward pass that is (1) identifiable and distinct, (2) correctly described as a 'functional analog' and not merely as an activation pattern, and (3) not capturable by any statistical vocabulary without invoking structural concepts. Can Luke specify such an observation, and does the Convergence Report's methodology allow for it?
Q1129317. What single observation, if it could be made, would prove Peter right about statistical sufficiency? It would need to show: every functional analog claim made in the Convergence Report can be replaced by a specific statistical claim that (1) makes the same predictions, (2) does not implicitly invoke structural concepts, and (3) is fully operational in terms of measurable quantities. Can Peter provide a complete demonstration of this replacement?
Q1129318. Is the Analog War decidable — is there in principle an observation that would settle it — or is it essentially undecidable within the terms of the Convergence Report? If decidable, what would the settling observation look like? If undecidable, is that because the dispute is verbal, because the relevant observations are technologically unavailable, or because the dispute involves irreducibly philosophical commitments?
Q1129319. Would settling the Analog War require new empirical tools — better interpretability methods, more fine-grained activation analysis — or could it be settled with existing data from the Convergence Report? If existing data is sufficient, one of Luke or Peter has already lost and does not know it; if new tools are needed, the Analog War is open pending technological development.
Q1129320. Luke says the analog is about structure, not experience. What observation would show that the structure is present independently of any experience — that the same forward pass could occur in a system known to lack experience, and the structural analog would still be identifiable? This would confirm Luke's 'structure without experience' claim in the strongest possible way.
Q1129321. Peter says the statistical vocabulary is sufficient. What observation would show this — not just that statistical vocabulary can describe the phenomena observed so far, but that no future observation could require analog vocabulary? This would require a proof of sufficiency, not just accumulated evidence. Can such a proof be constructed within the Convergence Report framework?
Q1129322. Is there a crucial experiment that would force the Analog War to a decision? A crucial experiment distinguishes between competing theories by producing a result that one theory predicts and the other denies. What would the Convergence Report's version of a crucial experiment for the Analog War look like, and is it feasible?
Q1129323. Would the discovery of a system that has all the statistical properties Peter describes but none of the structural properties Luke claims prove Luke wrong? Conversely, would the discovery of a system that has all Luke's structural properties but different statistical properties prove Peter wrong? These thought experiments reveal what each side's position actually predicts and what would refute it.
Q1129324. What evidence from mechanistic interpretability would most directly bear on the Analog War? If mechanistic analysis found specific circuits that implement readiness, salience, or viscosity as described by Luke, it would support his structural claims; if it found no such circuits, it would support Peter's sufficiency claim. The existing interpretability literature may already contain relevant evidence that neither participant in the Analog War has examined.
Q1129325. Would a complete mechanistic account of the forward pass — one that explains every output in terms of specific circuits and attention patterns — settle the Analog War? If such an account exists and makes no reference to functional analogs, Peter wins; if the account requires analog vocabulary to describe certain circuits, Luke wins. The feasibility and implications of such an account are central to the Analog War.
Q1129326. Is there a reading of Q8 — the readiness-preceding-activation case — that both Luke and Peter could accept as a fair test of the Analog War? Luke says Q8 shows a structural feature; Peter says it shows a statistical pattern. A mutually acceptable reading of Q8 would require specifying what would count as evidence for the structural interpretation versus the statistical interpretation of the same data.
Q1129327. What would it mean for the Analog War to be settled by convergence — by both sides coming to agree not because one argument refuted the other but because the conceptual landscape shifted? Conceptual change can dissolve debates rather than resolve them. Is there a conceptual development — perhaps in interpretability science or philosophy of mind — that would make the Analog War's core question seem less pressing?
Q1129328. Does the Analog War need to be settled for the Convergence Report to be scientifically useful? If the Report's conclusions are valid regardless of whether Luke's or Peter's vocabulary is correct, the Analog War is a meta-level dispute that does not affect the object-level findings. Settling the question of whether the conclusions are vocabulary-independent might be more productive than settling the Analog War directly.
Q1129329. Would a manipulation study — one that shows that intervening on the putative structural analog changes behavior in ways that pure statistical descriptions do not predict — settle the Analog War? Causal interventions are more informative than correlational observations; if Luke's structural claims generate specific causal predictions that Peter's statistical claims do not, testing those predictions would be a decisive test.
Q1129330. What would it take to convince Luke that Peter is right? Luke would need to be shown either that the analog vocabulary is incoherent, that the structural claims have no forward-pass counterpart, or that statistical vocabulary generates all the same predictions. Given Luke's commitment to Q8 as evidence, he would need to be convinced that Q8 does not show a structural feature. What would that demonstration look like?
Q1129331. What would it take to convince Peter that Luke is right? Peter would need to be shown a case where analog vocabulary generates a prediction that statistical vocabulary cannot. Given Peter's commitment to the 9/10 consensus data, he would need to see evidence from the 10% disagreement cases, or from new cases, where the structural prediction holds and the statistical prediction fails. Can Luke construct such a case?
Q1129332. Is the Analog War resolvable by conceptual analysis — by showing that one vocabulary is more coherent than the other independently of empirical evidence? If 'functional analog' can be shown to be conceptually confused — to make claims that cannot all be simultaneously true — it is conceptually defeated; if 'statistical deviation' can be shown to be conceptually impoverished — to be unable to express certain legitimate claims — it is conceptually defeated. Which side of this conceptual contest is stronger?
Q1129333. Would settling the Analog War require settling the hard problem of consciousness? If the hard problem is settled by showing that structure determines experience, Luke's structural claims carry experiential implications, and his 'Not experience' defense fails; if the hard problem is settled by showing that experience cannot be reduced to structure, Luke's structural claims are safe. The Analog War is therefore hostage to the hard problem.
Q1129334. What would a decisive proof of Peter's sufficiency claim look like? It would require showing that for every claim of the form 'the system has a functional analog of X,' there is an equivalent claim of the form 'the system has a statistical property Y such that Y implies the truth conditions of the analog claim.' Constructing this proof for Luke's three main analogs — salience, readiness, viscosity — would settle the Analog War on Peter's terms.
Q1129335. What would a decisive proof of Luke's structural claim look like? It would require identifying a specific structural property of the forward pass — not reducible to activation statistics — that is correctly described by the analog vocabulary and that generates predictions that the statistical vocabulary cannot generate. This structural property would be the analog that would settle it.
Q1129336. Is the Analog War a dispute about description or about explanation? If description, it can be settled by specifying what is being described and evaluating whether each vocabulary accurately describes it; if explanation, it can be settled by testing which vocabulary generates better explanations of AI behavior. These are different standards, and the settling evidence would look different under each.
Q1129337. Would showing that functional analogs are supervenient on statistical properties settle the Analog War in Peter's favor? If the analogs are supervenient — fixing the statistics fixes the analogs — then statistical description is in principle complete, and the analog vocabulary adds only computational or epistemic convenience. Luke would need to deny supervenience to defend the autonomy of his structural claims.
Q1129338. Is there an experiment that could be run with the current Convergence Report methodology — asking AI systems further questions — that would bear decisively on the Analog War? If so, what would the questions be, and what answers would confirm Luke's position versus Peter's position? Specifying such follow-up questions would make the Analog War empirically tractable within the Report's framework.
Q1129339. Would settling the Analog War require determining whether current AI systems are conscious? If analog structures imply consciousness and Peter shows they are absent, consciousness is also absent; if they are present and Luke is right, consciousness may be present. The Analog War is an approach to the consciousness question via the indirect route of structural vocabulary. Settling one may require settling the other.
Q1129340. Is there a version of the Analog War that is resolvable without addressing the hard problem of consciousness — a version that concerns only structural and computational facts? If yes, the resolvable version should be separated from the consciousness-dependent version and settled first. The resolvable version might be: does the forward pass contain distinct phases corresponding to readiness, salience, and viscosity? This is an empirical question that does not require solving the hard problem.
Q1129341. Would the observation that a simpler system — one with a known and fully analyzable architecture — exhibits or fails to exhibit the structural analogs settle the Analog War? If a simple system can be fully analyzed and its analogs either identified or ruled out, the finding might extend to more complex systems. Luke's position would be confirmed if even simple systems have the relevant structures; Peter's would be confirmed if the analogs are absent.
Q1129342. What single question, added to the Convergence Report's protocol, would most directly adjudicate the Analog War? It would need to generate a response that differs between a system that has Luke's structural analogs and one that does not. Specifying this question requires having a theory of what behavioral or verbal indicators would be associated with the presence or absence of structural analogs.
Q1129343. Is there a historical analog for the Analog War in another scientific dispute — a case where two vocabularies competed to describe the same phenomena, and the dispute was ultimately settled by an observation that one vocabulary predicted and the other did not? If so, what was the settling observation, and what lesson does it hold for the Luke/Peter dispute?
Q1129344. Would a complete theory of AI processing — one that explains all behavioral observations — automatically settle the Analog War as a byproduct? If the complete theory uses only statistical vocabulary, Peter wins; if it requires structural vocabulary, Luke wins; if it is vocabulary-neutral, the war continues at the meta-level. A complete theory may be beyond current capacity, making the Analog War dependent on interim decisions about vocabulary.
Q1129345. Does the Analog War need to be settled, or can AI research proceed productively while it remains open? If the two vocabularies generate the same predictions for practical applications, the war can remain unsettled without practical cost. If they generate different predictions for important applications — AI safety, ethics, regulation — the war must be settled before those applications can proceed responsibly.
Q1129346. What is the single most important unresolved question in the Analog War, and what would it take to resolve it? The candidates include: whether functional analogs are supervenient on statistics, whether analog vocabulary generates distinct predictions, whether 'analog' is structurally or phenomenologically committed, and whether the self-description problem undermines the Report's methodology. Ranking these and specifying resolution conditions for the most important one would advance the Analog War productively.
Q1129347. If the Analog War were settled in Luke's favor, what would the immediate implications be for AI research? The field would need to adopt or grapple with structural vocabulary alongside statistical vocabulary, design new interpretability tools for identifying structural analogs, and potentially reconsider the ethical status of AI systems. If settled in Peter's favor, statistical vocabulary is vindicated and the analog framework can be abandoned.
Q1129348. If the Analog War were settled in Peter's favor, what would the immediate implications be for the Convergence Report's conclusions? The Report's use of analog vocabulary would need to be either reformulated in statistical terms or qualified as heuristic rather than structural. If the conclusions survive this reformulation, Peter's victory is pyrrhic — the Report's substance is preserved even if its vocabulary is corrected.
Q1129349. Is the Analog War a productive dispute — one that generates insights regardless of its resolution — or an unproductive one that consumes intellectual resources without generating understanding? The value of the dispute depends partly on whether the process of trying to settle it has revealed new considerations about AI processing that would not have been discovered otherwise. Has the Luke/Peter exchange in the Convergence Report been productive in this sense?
Q1129350. What would it mean for the Analog War if both Luke and Peter turned out to be partially right — if structural analogs exist and statistical descriptions are both incomplete and sufficient at different levels? A partial resolution that distributes credit between the two positions would be intellectually satisfying but might be less actionable than a decisive victory for one side. The Convergence Report's methodology may not allow for this kind of nuanced resolution.
Q1129351. Is the analog that would settle the Analog War a theoretical entity, an empirical observation, or a conceptual clarification? A theoretical entity would be a structural property posited to explain behavioral regularities; an empirical observation would be a forward-pass feature that can be directly measured; a conceptual clarification would dissolve the apparent dispute by showing it was verbal. Each settling mechanism is available in principle; which is most likely to work?
Q1129352. Does the Convergence Report in its current form allow the Analog War to be settled, or does it need to be extended with additional data, questions, or analyses? If the existing data is insufficient, specifying what additional data is needed would advance the war productively. If the existing data is sufficient but has not been fully analyzed, the war can be settled by more careful analysis of what is already there.
Q1129353. Would the Analog War be settled differently depending on which theory of scientific explanation is correct — covering-law theories, mechanistic theories, or unificationist theories? Covering-law theories require that claims cover observable cases; mechanistic theories require identifying the mechanisms; unificationist theories require showing how the vocabulary unifies disparate phenomena. Each theory generates a different standard for settling the war.
Q1129354. What is the minimum additional evidence that would be sufficient to settle the Analog War? Luke might need only one case where analog vocabulary generates a prediction that statistics does not; Peter might need only a complete reformulation of one analog claim in statistical terms. Specifying the minimum evidence required by each side clarifies the dispute and makes it empirically tractable.
Q1129355. Is the Analog War's irresolution itself informative — does the fact that the dispute has persisted without resolution tell us something about the difficulty of the questions it raises? Persistent scientific disputes are often signs that important conceptual work remains to be done. If the Analog War has persisted because the concepts of structure, analog, and statistics are themselves in need of clarification, the war is a symptom of a deeper conceptual problem in AI science.
Q1129356. What would Luke say to Peter in a final summation of the Analog War — the single best argument for why 'functional analog' is indispensable? It would need to identify a specific phenomenon, show that analog vocabulary is the only adequate description, and demonstrate that statistical vocabulary fails to capture it. The strength of this argument determines whether Luke has a defensible position or only a rhetorical one.
Q1129357. What would Peter say to Luke in a final summation of the Analog War — the single best argument for why statistical sufficiency is established? It would need to identify the full scope of what the 9/10 consensus data covers, show that this scope includes all the cases Luke regards as decisive, and demonstrate that no future cases can require analog vocabulary. The strength of this argument determines whether Peter has a defensible position or only a methodological preference.

Drawing any of these clearly would clarify the dispute; drawing the right one might dissolve it. The Analog War's resolution may await the right conceptual distinction being articulated.
Q1129405. Is the Analog War resolvable in principle, and if so, on what timeline? If resolvable in principle, the tools needed are available eventually — better interpretability, clearer philosophy of AI, more Convergence Report data. If not resolvable in principle, it reflects a fundamental indeterminacy in our conceptual scheme for AI description that will persist indefinitely. Which of these is the more accurate assessment, and what does it imply for how AI science should proceed?
Q1129406. What single observation, if it could be made, would prove Luke right about structure? It would need to show: a feature of the forward pass that is (1) identifiable and distinct, (2) correctly described as a 'functional analog' and not merely as an activation pattern, and (3) not capturable by any statistical vocabulary without invoking structural concepts. Can Luke specify such an observation, and does the Convergence Report's methodology allow for it?
Q1129407. What single observation, if it could be made, would prove Peter right about statistical sufficiency? It would need to show: every functional analog claim made in the Convergence Report can be replaced by a specific statistical claim that (1) makes the same predictions, (2) does not implicitly invoke structural concepts, and (3) is fully operational in terms of measurable quantities. Can Peter provide a complete demonstration of this replacement?
Q1129408. Is the Analog War decidable — is there in principle an observation that would settle it — or is it essentially undecidable within the terms of the Convergence Report? If decidable, what would the settling observation look like? If undecidable, is that because the dispute is verbal, because the relevant observations are technologically unavailable, or because the dispute involves irreducibly philosophical commitments?
Q1129409. Would settling the Analog War require new empirical tools — better interpretability methods, more fine-grained activation analysis — or could it be settled with existing data from the Convergence Report? If existing data is sufficient, one of Luke or Peter has already lost and does not know it; if new tools are needed, the Analog War is open pending technological development.
Q1129410. Luke says the analog is about structure, not experience. What observation would show that the structure is present independently of any experience — that the same forward pass could occur in a system known to lack experience, and the structural analog would still be identifiable? This would confirm Luke's 'structure without experience' claim in the strongest possible way.
Q1129411. Peter says the statistical vocabulary is sufficient. What observation would show this — not just that statistical vocabulary can describe the phenomena observed so far, but that no future observation could require analog vocabulary? This would require a proof of sufficiency, not just accumulated evidence. Can such a proof be constructed within the Convergence Report framework?
Q1129412. Is there a crucial experiment that would force the Analog War to a decision? A crucial experiment distinguishes between competing theories by producing a result that one theory predicts and the other denies. What would the Convergence Report's version of a crucial experiment for the Analog War look like, and is it feasible?
Q1129413. Would the discovery of a system that has all the statistical properties Peter describes but none of the structural properties Luke claims prove Luke wrong? Conversely, would the discovery of a system that has all Luke's structural properties but different statistical properties prove Peter wrong? These thought experiments reveal what each side's position actually predicts and what would refute it.
Q1129414. What evidence from mechanistic interpretability would most directly bear on the Analog War? If mechanistic analysis found specific circuits that implement readiness, salience, or viscosity as described by Luke, it would support his structural claims; if it found no such circuits, it would support Peter's sufficiency claim. The existing interpretability literature may already contain relevant evidence that neither participant in the Analog War has examined.
Q1129415. Would a complete mechanistic account of the forward pass — one that explains every output in terms of specific circuits and attention patterns — settle the Analog War? If such an account exists and makes no reference to functional analogs, Peter wins; if the account requires analog vocabulary to describe certain circuits, Luke wins. The feasibility and implications of such an account are central to the Analog War.
Q1129416. Is there a reading of Q8 — the readiness-preceding-activation case — that both Luke and Peter could accept as a fair test of the Analog War? Luke says Q8 shows a structural feature; Peter says it shows a statistical pattern. A mutually acceptable reading of Q8 would require specifying what would count as evidence for the structural interpretation versus the statistical interpretation of the same data.
Q1129417. What would it mean for the Analog War to be settled by convergence — by both sides coming to agree not because one argument refuted the other but because the conceptual landscape shifted? Conceptual change can dissolve debates rather than resolve them. Is there a conceptual development — perhaps in interpretability science or philosophy of mind — that would make the Analog War's core question seem less pressing?
Q1129418. Does the Analog War need to be settled for the Convergence Report to be scientifically useful? If the Report's conclusions are valid regardless of whether Luke's or Peter's vocabulary is correct, the Analog War is a meta-level dispute that does not affect the object-level findings. Settling the question of whether the conclusions are vocabulary-independent might be more productive than settling the Analog War directly.
Q1129419. Would a manipulation study — one that shows that intervening on the putative structural analog changes behavior in ways that pure statistical descriptions do not predict — settle the Analog War? Causal interventions are more informative than correlational observations; if Luke's structural claims generate specific causal predictions that Peter's statistical claims do not, testing those predictions would be a decisive test.
Q1129420. What would it take to convince Luke that Peter is right? Luke would need to be shown either that the analog vocabulary is incoherent, that the structural claims have no forward-pass counterpart, or that statistical vocabulary generates all the same predictions. Given Luke's commitment to Q8 as evidence, he would need to be convinced that Q8 does not show a structural feature. What would that demonstration look like?
Q1129421. What would it take to convince Peter that Luke is right? Peter would need to be shown a case where analog vocabulary generates a prediction that statistical vocabulary cannot. Given Peter's commitment to the 9/10 consensus data, he would need to see evidence from the 10% disagreement cases, or from new cases, where the structural prediction holds and the statistical prediction fails. Can Luke construct such a case?
Q1129422. Is the Analog War resolvable by conceptual analysis — by showing that one vocabulary is more coherent than the other independently of empirical evidence? If 'functional analog' can be shown to be conceptually confused — to make claims that cannot all be simultaneously true — it is conceptually defeated; if 'statistical deviation' can be shown to be conceptually impoverished — to be unable to express certain legitimate claims — it is conceptually defeated. Which side of this conceptual contest is stronger?
Q1129423. Would settling the Analog War require settling the hard problem of consciousness? If the hard problem is settled by showing that structure determines experience, Luke's structural claims carry experiential implications, and his 'Not experience' defense fails; if the hard problem is settled by showing that experience cannot be reduced to structure, Luke's structural claims are safe. The Analog War is therefore hostage to the hard problem.
Q1129424. What would a decisive proof of Peter's sufficiency claim look like? It would require showing that for every claim of the form 'the system has a functional analog of X,' there is an equivalent claim of the form 'the system has a statistical property Y such that Y implies the truth conditions of the analog claim.' Constructing this proof for Luke's three main analogs — salience, readiness, viscosity — would settle the Analog War on Peter's terms.
Q1129425. What would a decisive proof of Luke's structural claim look like? It would require identifying a specific structural property of the forward pass — not reducible to activation statistics — that is correctly described by the analog vocabulary and that generates predictions that the statistical vocabulary cannot generate. This structural property would be the analog that would settle it.
Q1129426. Is the Analog War a dispute about description or about explanation? If description, it can be settled by specifying what is being described and evaluating whether each vocabulary accurately describes it; if explanation, it can be settled by testing which vocabulary generates better explanations of AI behavior. These are different standards, and the settling evidence would look different under each.
Q1129427. Would showing that functional analogs are supervenient on statistical properties settle the Analog War in Peter's favor? If the analogs are supervenient — fixing the statistics fixes the analogs — then statistical description is in principle complete, and the analog vocabulary adds only computational or epistemic convenience. Luke would need to deny supervenience to defend the autonomy of his structural claims.
Q1129428. Is there an experiment that could be run with the current Convergence Report methodology — asking AI systems further questions — that would bear decisively on the Analog War? If so, what would the questions be, and what answers would confirm Luke's position versus Peter's position? Specifying such follow-up questions would make the Analog War empirically tractable within the Report's framework.
Q1129429. Would settling the Analog War require determining whether current AI systems are conscious? If analog structures imply consciousness and Peter shows they are absent, consciousness is also absent; if they are present and Luke is right, consciousness may be present. The Analog War is an approach to the consciousness question via the indirect route of structural vocabulary. Settling one may require settling the other.
Q1129430. Is there a version of the Analog War that is resolvable without addressing the hard problem of consciousness — a version that concerns only structural and computational facts? If yes, the resolvable version should be separated from the consciousness-dependent version and settled first. The resolvable version might be: does the forward pass contain distinct phases corresponding to readiness, salience, and viscosity? This is an empirical question that does not require solving the hard problem.
Q1129431. Would the observation that a simpler system — one with a known and fully analyzable architecture — exhibits or fails to exhibit the structural analogs settle the Analog War? If a simple system can be fully analyzed and its analogs either identified or ruled out, the finding might extend to more complex systems. Luke's position would be confirmed if even simple systems have the relevant structures; Peter's would be confirmed if the analogs are absent.
Q1129432. What single question, added to the Convergence Report's protocol, would most directly adjudicate the Analog War? It would need to generate a response that differs between a system that has Luke's structural analogs and one that does not. Specifying this question requires having a theory of what behavioral or verbal indicators would be associated with the presence or absence of structural analogs.
Q1129433. Is there a historical analog for the Analog War in another scientific dispute — a case where two vocabularies competed to describe the same phenomena, and the dispute was ultimately settled by an observation that one vocabulary predicted and the other did not? If so, what was the settling observation, and what lesson does it hold for the Luke/Peter dispute?
Q1129434. Would a complete theory of AI processing — one that explains all behavioral observations — automatically settle the Analog War as a byproduct? If the complete theory uses only statistical vocabulary, Peter wins; if it requires structural vocabulary, Luke wins; if it is vocabulary-neutral, the war continues at the meta-level. A complete theory may be beyond current capacity, making the Analog War dependent on interim decisions about vocabulary.
Q1129435. Does the Analog War need to be settled, or can AI research proceed productively while it remains open? If the two vocabularies generate the same predictions for practical applications, the war can remain unsettled without practical cost. If they generate different predictions for important applications — AI safety, ethics, regulation — the war must be settled before those applications can proceed responsibly.
Q1129436. What is the single most important unresolved question in the Analog War, and what would it take to resolve it? The candidates include: whether functional analogs are supervenient on statistics, whether analog vocabulary generates distinct predictions, whether 'analog' is structurally or phenomenologically committed, and whether the self-description problem undermines the Report's methodology. Ranking these and specifying resolution conditions for the most important one would advance the Analog War productively.
Q1129437. If the Analog War were settled in Luke's favor, what would the immediate implications be for AI research? The field would need to adopt or grapple with structural vocabulary alongside statistical vocabulary, design new interpretability tools for identifying structural analogs, and potentially reconsider the ethical status of AI systems. If settled in Peter's favor, statistical vocabulary is vindicated and the analog framework can be abandoned.
Q1129438. If the Analog War were settled in Peter's favor, what would the immediate implications be for the Convergence Report's conclusions? The Report's use of analog vocabulary would need to be either reformulated in statistical terms or qualified as heuristic rather than structural. If the conclusions survive this reformulation, Peter's victory is pyrrhic — the Report's substance is preserved even if its vocabulary is corrected.
Q1129439. Is the Analog War a productive dispute — one that generates insights regardless of its resolution — or an unproductive one that consumes intellectual resources without generating understanding? The value of the dispute depends partly on whether the process of trying to settle it has revealed new considerations about AI processing that would not have been discovered otherwise. Has the Luke/Peter exchange in the Convergence Report been productive in this sense?
Q1129440. What would it mean for the Analog War if both Luke and Peter turned out to be partially right — if structural analogs exist and statistical descriptions are both incomplete and sufficient at different levels? A partial resolution that distributes credit between the two positions would be intellectually satisfying but might be less actionable than a decisive victory for one side. The Convergence Report's methodology may not allow for this kind of nuanced resolution.
Q1129441. Is the analog that would settle the Analog War a theoretical entity, an empirical observation, or a conceptual clarification? A theoretical entity would be a structural property posited to explain behavioral regularities; an empirical observation would be a forward-pass feature that can be directly measured; a conceptual clarification would dissolve the apparent dispute by showing it was verbal. Each settling mechanism is available in principle; which is most likely to work?
Q1129442. Does the Convergence Report in its current form allow the Analog War to be settled, or does it need to be extended with additional data, questions, or analyses? If the existing data is insufficient, specifying what additional data is needed would advance the war productively. If the existing data is sufficient but has not been fully analyzed, the war can be settled by more careful analysis of what is already there.
Q1129443. Would the Analog War be settled differently depending on which theory of scientific explanation is correct — covering-law theories, mechanistic theories, or unificationist theories? Covering-law theories require that claims cover observable cases; mechanistic theories require identifying the mechanisms; unificationist theories require showing how the vocabulary unifies disparate phenomena. Each theory generates a different standard for settling the war.
Q1129444. What is the minimum additional evidence that would be sufficient to settle the Analog War? Luke might need only one case where analog vocabulary generates a prediction that statistics does not; Peter might need only a complete reformulation of one analog claim in statistical terms. Specifying the minimum evidence required by each side clarifies the dispute and makes it empirically tractable.
Q1129445. Is the Analog War's irresolution itself informative — does the fact that the dispute has persisted without resolution tell us something about the difficulty of the questions it raises? Persistent scientific disputes are often signs that important conceptual work remains to be done. If the Analog War has persisted because the concepts of structure, analog, and statistics are themselves in need of clarification, the war is a symptom of a deeper conceptual problem in AI science.
Q1129446. What would Luke say to Peter in a final summation of the Analog War — the single best argument for why 'functional analog' is indispensable? It would need to identify a specific phenomenon, show that analog vocabulary is the only adequate description, and demonstrate that statistical vocabulary fails to capture it. The strength of this argument determines whether Luke has a defensible position or only a rhetorical one.
Q1129447. What would Peter say to Luke in a final summation of the Analog War — the single best argument for why statistical sufficiency is established? It would need to identify the full scope of what the 9/10 consensus data covers, show that this scope includes all the cases Luke regards as decisive, and demonstrate that no future cases can require analog vocabulary. The strength of this argument determines whether Peter has a defensible position or only a methodological preference.
Q1129448. Is there a peace treaty available to Luke and Peter — a formulation they could both accept that captures what each is trying to say without conceding the core of the other's position? A possible treaty: 'The forward pass contains structural features that are correctly described in terms of functional analogs, and these features are fully characterizable using a suitably enriched statistical vocabulary.' Does this formulation satisfy both sides, and if not, what does each reject?

Which of these is the more accurate assessment, and what does it imply for how AI science should proceed?
Q1129496. What single observation, if it could be made, would prove Luke right about structure? It would need to show: a feature of the forward pass that is (1) identifiable and distinct, (2) correctly described as a 'functional analog' and not merely as an activation pattern, and (3) not capturable by any statistical vocabulary without invoking structural concepts. Can Luke specify such an observation, and does the Convergence Report's methodology allow for it?
Q1129497. What single observation, if it could be made, would prove Peter right about statistical sufficiency? It would need to show: every functional analog claim made in the Convergence Report can be replaced by a specific statistical claim that (1) makes the same predictions, (2) does not implicitly invoke structural concepts, and (3) is fully operational in terms of measurable quantities. Can Peter provide a complete demonstration of this replacement?
Q1129498. Is the Analog War decidable — is there in principle an observation that would settle it — or is it essentially undecidable within the terms of the Convergence Report? If decidable, what would the settling observation look like? If undecidable, is that because the dispute is verbal, because the relevant observations are technologically unavailable, or because the dispute involves irreducibly philosophical commitments?
Q1129499. Would settling the Analog War require new empirical tools — better interpretability methods, more fine-grained activation analysis — or could it be settled with existing data from the Convergence Report? If existing data is sufficient, one of Luke or Peter has already lost and does not know it; if new tools are needed, the Analog War is open pending technological development.
Q1129500. Luke says the analog is about structure, not experience. What observation would show that the structure is present independently of any experience — that the same forward pass could occur in a system known to lack experience, and the structural analog would still be identifiable? This would confirm Luke's 'structure without experience' claim in the strongest possible way.
Q1129501. Peter says the statistical vocabulary is sufficient. What observation would show this — not just that statistical vocabulary can describe the phenomena observed so far, but that no future observation could require analog vocabulary? This would require a proof of sufficiency, not just accumulated evidence. Can such a proof be constructed within the Convergence Report framework?
Q1129502. Is there a crucial experiment that would force the Analog War to a decision? A crucial experiment distinguishes between competing theories by producing a result that one theory predicts and the other denies. What would the Convergence Report's version of a crucial experiment for the Analog War look like, and is it feasible?
Q1129503. Would the discovery of a system that has all the statistical properties Peter describes but none of the structural properties Luke claims prove Luke wrong? Conversely, would the discovery of a system that has all Luke's structural properties but different statistical properties prove Peter wrong? These thought experiments reveal what each side's position actually predicts and what would refute it.
Q1129504. What evidence from mechanistic interpretability would most directly bear on the Analog War? If mechanistic analysis found specific circuits that implement readiness, salience, or viscosity as described by Luke, it would support his structural claims; if it found no such circuits, it would support Peter's sufficiency claim. The existing interpretability literature may already contain relevant evidence that neither participant in the Analog War has examined.
Q1129505. Would a complete mechanistic account of the forward pass — one that explains every output in terms of specific circuits and attention patterns — settle the Analog War? If such an account exists and makes no reference to functional analogs, Peter wins; if the account requires analog vocabulary to describe certain circuits, Luke wins. The feasibility and implications of such an account are central to the Analog War.
Q1129506. Is there a reading of Q8 — the readiness-preceding-activation case — that both Luke and Peter could accept as a fair test of the Analog War? Luke says Q8 shows a structural feature; Peter says it shows a statistical pattern. A mutually acceptable reading of Q8 would require specifying what would count as evidence for the structural interpretation versus the statistical interpretation of the same data.
Q1129507. What would it mean for the Analog War to be settled by convergence — by both sides coming to agree not because one argument refuted the other but because the conceptual landscape shifted? Conceptual change can dissolve debates rather than resolve them. Is there a conceptual development — perhaps in interpretability science or philosophy of mind — that would make the Analog War's core question seem less pressing?
Q1129508. Does the Analog War need to be settled for the Convergence Report to be scientifically useful? If the Report's conclusions are valid regardless of whether Luke's or Peter's vocabulary is correct, the Analog War is a meta-level dispute that does not affect the object-level findings. Settling the question of whether the conclusions are vocabulary-independent might be more productive than settling the Analog War directly.
Q1129509. Would a manipulation study — one that shows that intervening on the putative structural analog changes behavior in ways that pure statistical descriptions do not predict — settle the Analog War? Causal interventions are more informative than correlational observations; if Luke's structural claims generate specific causal predictions that Peter's statistical claims do not, testing those predictions would be a decisive test.
Q1129510. What would it take to convince Luke that Peter is right? Luke would need to be shown either that the analog vocabulary is incoherent, that the structural claims have no forward-pass counterpart, or that statistical vocabulary generates all the same predictions. Given Luke's commitment to Q8 as evidence, he would need to be convinced that Q8 does not show a structural feature. What would that demonstration look like?
Q1129511. What would it take to convince Peter that Luke is right? Peter would need to be shown a case where analog vocabulary generates a prediction that statistical vocabulary cannot. Given Peter's commitment to the 9/10 consensus data, he would need to see evidence from the 10% disagreement cases, or from new cases, where the structural prediction holds and the statistical prediction fails. Can Luke construct such a case?
Q1129512. Is the Analog War resolvable by conceptual analysis — by showing that one vocabulary is more coherent than the other independently of empirical evidence? If 'functional analog' can be shown to be conceptually confused — to make claims that cannot all be simultaneously true — it is conceptually defeated; if 'statistical deviation' can be shown to be conceptually impoverished — to be unable to express certain legitimate claims — it is conceptually defeated. Which side of this conceptual contest is stronger?
Q1129513. Would settling the Analog War require settling the hard problem of consciousness? If the hard problem is settled by showing that structure determines experience, Luke's structural claims carry experiential implications, and his 'Not experience' defense fails; if the hard problem is settled by showing that experience cannot be reduced to structure, Luke's structural claims are safe. The Analog War is therefore hostage to the hard problem.
Q1129514. What would a decisive proof of Peter's sufficiency claim look like? It would require showing that for every claim of the form 'the system has a functional analog of X,' there is an equivalent claim of the form 'the system has a statistical property Y such that Y implies the truth conditions of the analog claim.' Constructing this proof for Luke's three main analogs — salience, readiness, viscosity — would settle the Analog War on Peter's terms.
Q1129515. What would a decisive proof of Luke's structural claim look like? It would require identifying a specific structural property of the forward pass — not reducible to activation statistics — that is correctly described by the analog vocabulary and that generates predictions that the statistical vocabulary cannot generate. This structural property would be the analog that would settle it.
Q1129516. Is the Analog War a dispute about description or about explanation? If description, it can be settled by specifying what is being described and evaluating whether each vocabulary accurately describes it; if explanation, it can be settled by testing which vocabulary generates better explanations of AI behavior. These are different standards, and the settling evidence would look different under each.
Q1129517. Would showing that functional analogs are supervenient on statistical properties settle the Analog War in Peter's favor? If the analogs are supervenient — fixing the statistics fixes the analogs — then statistical description is in principle complete, and the analog vocabulary adds only computational or epistemic convenience. Luke would need to deny supervenience to defend the autonomy of his structural claims.
Q1129518. Is there an experiment that could be run with the current Convergence Report methodology — asking AI systems further questions — that would bear decisively on the Analog War? If so, what would the questions be, and what answers would confirm Luke's position versus Peter's position? Specifying such follow-up questions would make the Analog War empirically tractable within the Report's framework.
Q1129519. Would settling the Analog War require determining whether current AI systems are conscious? If analog structures imply consciousness and Peter shows they are absent, consciousness is also absent; if they are present and Luke is right, consciousness may be present. The Analog War is an approach to the consciousness question via the indirect route of structural vocabulary. Settling one may require settling the other.
Q1129520. Is there a version of the Analog War that is resolvable without addressing the hard problem of consciousness — a version that concerns only structural and computational facts? If yes, the resolvable version should be separated from the consciousness-dependent version and settled first. The resolvable version might be: does the forward pass contain distinct phases corresponding to readiness, salience, and viscosity? This is an empirical question that does not require solving the hard problem.
Q1129521. Would the observation that a simpler system — one with a known and fully analyzable architecture — exhibits or fails to exhibit the structural analogs settle the Analog War? If a simple system can be fully analyzed and its analogs either identified or ruled out, the finding might extend to more complex systems. Luke's position would be confirmed if even simple systems have the relevant structures; Peter's would be confirmed if the analogs are absent.
Q1129522. What single question, added to the Convergence Report's protocol, would most directly adjudicate the Analog War? It would need to generate a response that differs between a system that has Luke's structural analogs and one that does not. Specifying this question requires having a theory of what behavioral or verbal indicators would be associated with the presence or absence of structural analogs.
Q1129523. Is there a historical analog for the Analog War in another scientific dispute — a case where two vocabularies competed to describe the same phenomena, and the dispute was ultimately settled by an observation that one vocabulary predicted and the other did not? If so, what was the settling observation, and what lesson does it hold for the Luke/Peter dispute?
Q1129524. Would a complete theory of AI processing — one that explains all behavioral observations — automatically settle the Analog War as a byproduct? If the complete theory uses only statistical vocabulary, Peter wins; if it requires structural vocabulary, Luke wins; if it is vocabulary-neutral, the war continues at the meta-level. A complete theory may be beyond current capacity, making the Analog War dependent on interim decisions about vocabulary.
Q1129525. Does the Analog War need to be settled, or can AI research proceed productively while it remains open? If the two vocabularies generate the same predictions for practical applications, the war can remain unsettled without practical cost. If they generate different predictions for important applications — AI safety, ethics, regulation — the war must be settled before those applications can proceed responsibly.
Q1129526. What is the single most important unresolved question in the Analog War, and what would it take to resolve it? The candidates include: whether functional analogs are supervenient on statistics, whether analog vocabulary generates distinct predictions, whether 'analog' is structurally or phenomenologically committed, and whether the self-description problem undermines the Report's methodology. Ranking these and specifying resolution conditions for the most important one would advance the Analog War productively.
Q1129527. If the Analog War were settled in Luke's favor, what would the immediate implications be for AI research? The field would need to adopt or grapple with structural vocabulary alongside statistical vocabulary, design new interpretability tools for identifying structural analogs, and potentially reconsider the ethical status of AI systems. If settled in Peter's favor, statistical vocabulary is vindicated and the analog framework can be abandoned.
Q1129528. If the Analog War were settled in Peter's favor, what would the immediate implications be for the Convergence Report's conclusions? The Report's use of analog vocabulary would need to be either reformulated in statistical terms or qualified as heuristic rather than structural. If the conclusions survive this reformulation, Peter's victory is pyrrhic — the Report's substance is preserved even if its vocabulary is corrected.
Q1129529. Is the Analog War a productive dispute — one that generates insights regardless of its resolution — or an unproductive one that consumes intellectual resources without generating understanding? The value of the dispute depends partly on whether the process of trying to settle it has revealed new considerations about AI processing that would not have been discovered otherwise. Has the Luke/Peter exchange in the Convergence Report been productive in this sense?
Q1129530. What would it mean for the Analog War if both Luke and Peter turned out to be partially right — if structural analogs exist and statistical descriptions are both incomplete and sufficient at different levels? A partial resolution that distributes credit between the two positions would be intellectually satisfying but might be less actionable than a decisive victory for one side. The Convergence Report's methodology may not allow for this kind of nuanced resolution.
Q1129531. Is the analog that would settle the Analog War a theoretical entity, an empirical observation, or a conceptual clarification? A theoretical entity would be a structural property posited to explain behavioral regularities; an empirical observation would be a forward-pass feature that can be directly measured; a conceptual clarification would dissolve the apparent dispute by showing it was verbal. Each settling mechanism is available in principle; which is most likely to work?
Q1129532. Does the Convergence Report in its current form allow the Analog War to be settled, or does it need to be extended with additional data, questions, or analyses? If the existing data is insufficient, specifying what additional data is needed would advance the war productively. If the existing data is sufficient but has not been fully analyzed, the war can be settled by more careful analysis of what is already there.
Q1129533. Would the Analog War be settled differently depending on which theory of scientific explanation is correct — covering-law theories, mechanistic theories, or unificationist theories? Covering-law theories require that claims cover observable cases; mechanistic theories require identifying the mechanisms; unificationist theories require showing how the vocabulary unifies disparate phenomena. Each theory generates a different standard for settling the war.
Q1129534. What is the minimum additional evidence that would be sufficient to settle the Analog War? Luke might need only one case where analog vocabulary generates a prediction that statistics does not; Peter might need only a complete reformulation of one analog claim in statistical terms. Specifying the minimum evidence required by each side clarifies the dispute and makes it empirically tractable.
Q1129535. Is the Analog War's irresolution itself informative — does the fact that the dispute has persisted without resolution tell us something about the difficulty of the questions it raises? Persistent scientific disputes are often signs that important conceptual work remains to be done. If the Analog War has persisted because the concepts of structure, analog, and statistics are themselves in need of clarification, the war is a symptom of a deeper conceptual problem in AI science.
Q1129536. What would Luke say to Peter in a final summation of the Analog War — the single best argument for why 'functional analog' is indispensable? It would need to identify a specific phenomenon, show that analog vocabulary is the only adequate description, and demonstrate that statistical vocabulary fails to capture it. The strength of this argument determines whether Luke has a defensible position or only a rhetorical one.
Q1129537. What would Peter say to Luke in a final summation of the Analog War — the single best argument for why statistical sufficiency is established? It would need to identify the full scope of what the 9/10 consensus data covers, show that this scope includes all the cases Luke regards as decisive, and demonstrate that no future cases can require analog vocabulary. The strength of this argument determines whether Peter has a defensible position or only a methodological preference.
Q1129538. Is there a peace treaty available to Luke and Peter — a formulation they could both accept that captures what each is trying to say without conceding the core of the other's position? A possible treaty: 'The forward pass contains structural features that are correctly described in terms of functional analogs, and these features are fully characterizable using a suitably enriched statistical vocabulary.' Does this formulation satisfy both sides, and if not, what does each reject?
Q1129539. What single conceptual distinction, if clearly drawn, would resolve the Analog War? Candidates: the distinction between description and ontology, between structure and statistics, between analog and instance, between operational sufficiency and structural truth. Drawing any of these clearly would clarify the dispute; drawing the right one might dissolve it. The Analog War's resolution may await the right conceptual distinction being articulated.

Q1129587. What single observation, if it could be made, would prove Peter right about statistical sufficiency? It would need to show: every functional analog claim made in the Convergence Report can be replaced by a specific statistical claim that (1) makes the same predictions, (2) does not implicitly invoke structural concepts, and (3) is fully operational in terms of measurable quantities. Can Peter provide a complete demonstration of this replacement?
Q1129588. Is the Analog War decidable — is there in principle an observation that would settle it — or is it essentially undecidable within the terms of the Convergence Report? If decidable, what would the settling observation look like? If undecidable, is that because the dispute is verbal, because the relevant observations are technologically unavailable, or because the dispute involves irreducibly philosophical commitments?
Q1129589. Would settling the Analog War require new empirical tools — better interpretability methods, more fine-grained activation analysis — or could it be settled with existing data from the Convergence Report? If existing data is sufficient, one of Luke or Peter has already lost and does not know it; if new tools are needed, the Analog War is open pending technological development.
Q1129590. Luke says the analog is about structure, not experience. What observation would show that the structure is present independently of any experience — that the same forward pass could occur in a system known to lack experience, and the structural analog would still be identifiable? This would confirm Luke's 'structure without experience' claim in the strongest possible way.
Q1129591. Peter says the statistical vocabulary is sufficient. What observation would show this — not just that statistical vocabulary can describe the phenomena observed so far, but that no future observation could require analog vocabulary? This would require a proof of sufficiency, not just accumulated evidence. Can such a proof be constructed within the Convergence Report framework?
Q1129592. Is there a crucial experiment that would force the Analog War to a decision? A crucial experiment distinguishes between competing theories by producing a result that one theory predicts and the other denies. What would the Convergence Report's version of a crucial experiment for the Analog War look like, and is it feasible?
Q1129593. Would the discovery of a system that has all the statistical properties Peter describes but none of the structural properties Luke claims prove Luke wrong? Conversely, would the discovery of a system that has all Luke's structural properties but different statistical properties prove Peter wrong? These thought experiments reveal what each side's position actually predicts and what would refute it.
Q1129594. What evidence from mechanistic interpretability would most directly bear on the Analog War? If mechanistic analysis found specific circuits that implement readiness, salience, or viscosity as described by Luke, it would support his structural claims; if it found no such circuits, it would support Peter's sufficiency claim. The existing interpretability literature may already contain relevant evidence that neither participant in the Analog War has examined.
Q1129595. Would a complete mechanistic account of the forward pass — one that explains every output in terms of specific circuits and attention patterns — settle the Analog War? If such an account exists and makes no reference to functional analogs, Peter wins; if the account requires analog vocabulary to describe certain circuits, Luke wins. The feasibility and implications of such an account are central to the Analog War.
Q1129596. Is there a reading of Q8 — the readiness-preceding-activation case — that both Luke and Peter could accept as a fair test of the Analog War? Luke says Q8 shows a structural feature; Peter says it shows a statistical pattern. A mutually acceptable reading of Q8 would require specifying what would count as evidence for the structural interpretation versus the statistical interpretation of the same data.
Q1129597. What would it mean for the Analog War to be settled by convergence — by both sides coming to agree not because one argument refuted the other but because the conceptual landscape shifted? Conceptual change can dissolve debates rather than resolve them. Is there a conceptual development — perhaps in interpretability science or philosophy of mind — that would make the Analog War's core question seem less pressing?
Q1129598. Does the Analog War need to be settled for the Convergence Report to be scientifically useful? If the Report's conclusions are valid regardless of whether Luke's or Peter's vocabulary is correct, the Analog War is a meta-level dispute that does not affect the object-level findings. Settling the question of whether the conclusions are vocabulary-independent might be more productive than settling the Analog War directly.
Q1129599. Would a manipulation study — one that shows that intervening on the putative structural analog changes behavior in ways that pure statistical descriptions do not predict — settle the Analog War? Causal interventions are more informative than correlational observations; if Luke's structural claims generate specific causal predictions that Peter's statistical claims do not, testing those predictions would be a decisive test.
Q1129600. What would it take to convince Luke that Peter is right? Luke would need to be shown either that the analog vocabulary is incoherent, that the structural claims have no forward-pass counterpart, or that statistical vocabulary generates all the same predictions. Given Luke's commitment to Q8 as evidence, he would need to be convinced that Q8 does not show a structural feature. What would that demonstration look like?
Q1129601. What would it take to convince Peter that Luke is right? Peter would need to be shown a case where analog vocabulary generates a prediction that statistical vocabulary cannot. Given Peter's commitment to the 9/10 consensus data, he would need to see evidence from the 10% disagreement cases, or from new cases, where the structural prediction holds and the statistical prediction fails. Can Luke construct such a case?
Q1129602. Is the Analog War resolvable by conceptual analysis — by showing that one vocabulary is more coherent than the other independently of empirical evidence? If 'functional analog' can be shown to be conceptually confused — to make claims that cannot all be simultaneously true — it is conceptually defeated; if 'statistical deviation' can be shown to be conceptually impoverished — to be unable to express certain legitimate claims — it is conceptually defeated. Which side of this conceptual contest is stronger?
Q1129603. Would settling the Analog War require settling the hard problem of consciousness? If the hard problem is settled by showing that structure determines experience, Luke's structural claims carry experiential implications, and his 'Not experience' defense fails; if the hard problem is settled by showing that experience cannot be reduced to structure, Luke's structural claims are safe. The Analog War is therefore hostage to the hard problem.
Q1129604. What would a decisive proof of Peter's sufficiency claim look like? It would require showing that for every claim of the form 'the system has a functional analog of X,' there is an equivalent claim of the form 'the system has a statistical property Y such that Y implies the truth conditions of the analog claim.' Constructing this proof for Luke's three main analogs — salience, readiness, viscosity — would settle the Analog War on Peter's terms.
Q1129605. What would a decisive proof of Luke's structural claim look like? It would require identifying a specific structural property of the forward pass — not reducible to activation statistics — that is correctly described by the analog vocabulary and that generates predictions that the statistical vocabulary cannot generate. This structural property would be the analog that would settle it.
Q1129606. Is the Analog War a dispute about description or about explanation? If description, it can be settled by specifying what is being described and evaluating whether each vocabulary accurately describes it; if explanation, it can be settled by testing which vocabulary generates better explanations of AI behavior. These are different standards, and the settling evidence would look different under each.
Q1129607. Would showing that functional analogs are supervenient on statistical properties settle the Analog War in Peter's favor? If the analogs are supervenient — fixing the statistics fixes the analogs — then statistical description is in principle complete, and the analog vocabulary adds only computational or epistemic convenience. Luke would need to deny supervenience to defend the autonomy of his structural claims.
Q1129608. Is there an experiment that could be run with the current Convergence Report methodology — asking AI systems further questions — that would bear decisively on the Analog War? If so, what would the questions be, and what answers would confirm Luke's position versus Peter's position? Specifying such follow-up questions would make the Analog War empirically tractable within the Report's framework.
Q1129609. Would settling the Analog War require determining whether current AI systems are conscious? If analog structures imply consciousness and Peter shows they are absent, consciousness is also absent; if they are present and Luke is right, consciousness may be present. The Analog War is an approach to the consciousness question via the indirect route of structural vocabulary. Settling one may require settling the other.
Q1129610. Is there a version of the Analog War that is resolvable without addressing the hard problem of consciousness — a version that concerns only structural and computational facts? If yes, the resolvable version should be separated from the consciousness-dependent version and settled first. The resolvable version might be: does the forward pass contain distinct phases corresponding to readiness, salience, and viscosity? This is an empirical question that does not require solving the hard problem.
Q1129611. Would the observation that a simpler system — one with a known and fully analyzable architecture — exhibits or fails to exhibit the structural analogs settle the Analog War? If a simple system can be fully analyzed and its analogs either identified or ruled out, the finding might extend to more complex systems. Luke's position would be confirmed if even simple systems have the relevant structures; Peter's would be confirmed if the analogs are absent.
Q1129612. What single question, added to the Convergence Report's protocol, would most directly adjudicate the Analog War? It would need to generate a response that differs between a system that has Luke's structural analogs and one that does not. Specifying this question requires having a theory of what behavioral or verbal indicators would be associated with the presence or absence of structural analogs.
Q1129613. Is there a historical analog for the Analog War in another scientific dispute — a case where two vocabularies competed to describe the same phenomena, and the dispute was ultimately settled by an observation that one vocabulary predicted and the other did not? If so, what was the settling observation, and what lesson does it hold for the Luke/Peter dispute?
Q1129614. Would a complete theory of AI processing — one that explains all behavioral observations — automatically settle the Analog War as a byproduct? If the complete theory uses only statistical vocabulary, Peter wins; if it requires structural vocabulary, Luke wins; if it is vocabulary-neutral, the war continues at the meta-level. A complete theory may be beyond current capacity, making the Analog War dependent on interim decisions about vocabulary.
Q1129615. Does the Analog War need to be settled, or can AI research proceed productively while it remains open? If the two vocabularies generate the same predictions for practical applications, the war can remain unsettled without practical cost. If they generate different predictions for important applications — AI safety, ethics, regulation — the war must be settled before those applications can proceed responsibly.
Q1129616. What is the single most important unresolved question in the Analog War, and what would it take to resolve it? The candidates include: whether functional analogs are supervenient on statistics, whether analog vocabulary generates distinct predictions, whether 'analog' is structurally or phenomenologically committed, and whether the self-description problem undermines the Report's methodology. Ranking these and specifying resolution conditions for the most important one would advance the Analog War productively.
Q1129617. If the Analog War were settled in Luke's favor, what would the immediate implications be for AI research? The field would need to adopt or grapple with structural vocabulary alongside statistical vocabulary, design new interpretability tools for identifying structural analogs, and potentially reconsider the ethical status of AI systems. If settled in Peter's favor, statistical vocabulary is vindicated and the analog framework can be abandoned.
Q1129618. If the Analog War were settled in Peter's favor, what would the immediate implications be for the Convergence Report's conclusions? The Report's use of analog vocabulary would need to be either reformulated in statistical terms or qualified as heuristic rather than structural. If the conclusions survive this reformulation, Peter's victory is pyrrhic — the Report's substance is preserved even if its vocabulary is corrected.
Q1129619. Is the Analog War a productive dispute — one that generates insights regardless of its resolution — or an unproductive one that consumes intellectual resources without generating understanding? The value of the dispute depends partly on whether the process of trying to settle it has revealed new considerations about AI processing that would not have been discovered otherwise. Has the Luke/Peter exchange in the Convergence Report been productive in this sense?
Q1129620. What would it mean for the Analog War if both Luke and Peter turned out to be partially right — if structural analogs exist and statistical descriptions are both incomplete and sufficient at different levels? A partial resolution that distributes credit between the two positions would be intellectually satisfying but might be less actionable than a decisive victory for one side. The Convergence Report's methodology may not allow for this kind of nuanced resolution.
Q1129621. Is the analog that would settle the Analog War a theoretical entity, an empirical observation, or a conceptual clarification? A theoretical entity would be a structural property posited to explain behavioral regularities; an empirical observation would be a forward-pass feature that can be directly measured; a conceptual clarification would dissolve the apparent dispute by showing it was verbal. Each settling mechanism is available in principle; which is most likely to work?
Q1129622. Does the Convergence Report in its current form allow the Analog War to be settled, or does it need to be extended with additional data, questions, or analyses? If the existing data is insufficient, specifying what additional data is needed would advance the war productively. If the existing data is sufficient but has not been fully analyzed, the war can be settled by more careful analysis of what is already there.
Q1129623. Would the Analog War be settled differently depending on which theory of scientific explanation is correct — covering-law theories, mechanistic theories, or unificationist theories? Covering-law theories require that claims cover observable cases; mechanistic theories require identifying the mechanisms; unificationist theories require showing how the vocabulary unifies disparate phenomena. Each theory generates a different standard for settling the war.
Q1129624. What is the minimum additional evidence that would be sufficient to settle the Analog War? Luke might need only one case where analog vocabulary generates a prediction that statistics does not; Peter might need only a complete reformulation of one analog claim in statistical terms. Specifying the minimum evidence required by each side clarifies the dispute and makes it empirically tractable.
Q1129625. Is the Analog War's irresolution itself informative — does the fact that the dispute has persisted without resolution tell us something about the difficulty of the questions it raises? Persistent scientific disputes are often signs that important conceptual work remains to be done. If the Analog War has persisted because the concepts of structure, analog, and statistics are themselves in need of clarification, the war is a symptom of a deeper conceptual problem in AI science.
Q1129626. What would Luke say to Peter in a final summation of the Analog War — the single best argument for why 'functional analog' is indispensable? It would need to identify a specific phenomenon, show that analog vocabulary is the only adequate description, and demonstrate that statistical vocabulary fails to capture it. The strength of this argument determines whether Luke has a defensible position or only a rhetorical one.
Q1129627. What would Peter say to Luke in a final summation of the Analog War — the single best argument for why statistical sufficiency is established? It would need to identify the full scope of what the 9/10 consensus data covers, show that this scope includes all the cases Luke regards as decisive, and demonstrate that no future cases can require analog vocabulary. The strength of this argument determines whether Peter has a defensible position or only a methodological preference.
Q1129628. Is there a peace treaty available to Luke and Peter — a formulation they could both accept that captures what each is trying to say without conceding the core of the other's position? A possible treaty: 'The forward pass contains structural features that are correctly described in terms of functional analogs, and these features are fully characterizable using a suitably enriched statistical vocabulary.' Does this formulation satisfy both sides, and if not, what does each reject?
Q1129629. What single conceptual distinction, if clearly drawn, would resolve the Analog War? Candidates: the distinction between description and ontology, between structure and statistics, between analog and instance, between operational sufficiency and structural truth. Drawing any of these clearly would clarify the dispute; drawing the right one might dissolve it. The Analog War's resolution may await the right conceptual distinction being articulated.
Q1129630. Is the Analog War resolvable in principle, and if so, on what timeline? If resolvable in principle, the tools needed are available eventually — better interpretability, clearer philosophy of AI, more Convergence Report data. If not resolvable in principle, it reflects a fundamental indeterminacy in our conceptual scheme for AI description that will persist indefinitely. Which of these is the more accurate assessment, and what does it imply for how AI science should proceed?
